THE WEEK'S WORK IN BRIEF. Turkey and geese eggs should now be set. Turkeys and geese hatched in May attain excellent weights by Christmas. Insects thrive apace in warm Weather; observe utter cleanliness in housing. Broodies are a bugbear this month; if not wanted take, them in hand early. May is the ideal month for growing stock. Keep the youngsters on the run; let nothing hinder their 'growth. Put all the time you . can spare into the poultry yard.—" The Poultry World." PROTECTION FOR THE LAYERS. It is a very wise proceeding to allow the stock to remain at liberty for as long a tin' as possible, for they will thus be well equipr- for winter laying and for rendering a good it• count of themselves in the breeding-pens when spring- time- arrives. With the approach of cold weather, however, the birds should be brought from all the outlying parts on the.f arm and placed in a position Where shelter may be had. The bringing of the fowls from the open fields is frequently unduly ,delayed, but it must be rgmembered that special care is necessary during the autumn and winter months. Not only does this apply to birds that have been selected for future breeders, though this is, of course, of the greatest importance, but it is imperative that the same care be given to the general laying flock. Their treatment should be somewhat different; at the same time the same care and attention should be lavished on both.— "Farm and Home."

were traced, not infrequently would it be found that inattention to this important mat- ter is at the root of the trouble. So far as is known tuberculosis descends from one genera- tion to another, and as the disease is not always apparent birds so affected may easily be bred from. Hence the evils of overcrowding chickens have a far-reaching affect. _ _ _

The remedy that immediately suggests itself is why not buy more appliances, and thus obviate the danger? This advice is very easy to give, but not always easy to follow, since with the majority of industrial poultry-keepers money must be considered. If a man wishes to develop more appliances must be obtained than are commensurate with the extent of his de- velopments, but very often people develop so far as rearing more •chickens is concerned, but do not develop in any other direction. If a man has space and accommodation for only a certain number of chickens, to attempt to rear more is a very foolish proceeding. The golden rule in chicken rearing is never to breed more than can be properly accommodated or than the land can safely carry.—" Farm and Home."

div.head: DON'T CANCEL SHOWS.
div.p: DON'T CANCEL SHOWS.

We have had nine months of European war- fare, and it may not be uninteresting at the moment to give some consideration to the position of the poultry industry as to how it has been affected by hostilities, and to hazard an opinion as to the future, says "The Feathered World." My view, is that those with sound, reliable studs of pedigree layers will be well advised to produce as many chickens as possible, because everything points to an increasing demand for this class of stock. The advertising columns at the present moment are alone sufficient to show the volume of business that is passing in this line, and every circumstance points to its ex- pansion. The section of the poultry industry that has probably suffered most severely is the fancy section, or that branch engaged upon the breed- ing of standard specimens. Much injury has been wrought through the spirit of " funk " being allowed to permeate the agricultural societies and exhibition committees. The im- portance of shows, even at times such as this, seems to have been lost sight of, arid some com- mittees have such a mistaken sense of their obligations as to imagine such affairs are merely merry-making things and carnivals that should be dropped during war time. I am a member of the committee of an agricultural society, and I have listened to such opinions. Shows are neither feasts nor fetes, but their object should be purely educational, and their office be to stimulate the breeding of , classical stock, for which this country has a woAd-wide reputation. A huge oversea business is annually carried on in British stock, which in volume must amount to millions, and it is by encouraging the main- tenance of our standard of breeding by exhibi- tions which permit comparison that our British reputation for stockbreeding can be fortified.

div.head: No Time for Pessimism.
div.p: No Time for Pessimism.

Those shows with funds—and there are many —who are dropping their fixtures at this im- portant time are failing in their duty to the stockbreeding industry, and merit the placing of their title upon the exhibitors' black list for future reference.

A war such as the one we are at present engaged upon must have its effect. This we are all prepared for, but I think the poultry-breeder who endeavours to maintain the strength of his stud during this temporarily slack time will adopt the most profitable course. Inquiries are now being received by breeders from Canada, South Africa, Spain, the Argentine, &c., and shipments are even now taking place, whilst I feel certain.—and all the signs are in that direc- tion—there will be a big rush from abroad for stock sooner or later. Pessimism neither won wars nor conducted a successful business, and articles full of depression, ,such as appeared from a well-known writer in an agricultural contemporary the other day, are a mistake. The suggestion that the poultry fancy is finished is, I think, distinctly erroneous, and at the most it is very premature. It has received a severe blow. there is no doubt, but I think it has passed through the severest time of strain, and the future is encouraging if not actually bright and rosy.

div.head: BITS FOR BEGINNERS.
div.p: BITS FOR BEGINNERS.

May is undoubtedly the best growing month of the year. Keep the chickens on the grow by adopting regular feeding times. Let them' want for nothing; see that they have plenty of fresh water to drink and plenty of grass range to obtain exercise, which promotes growth.

The older youngsters should receive attention. Separate the males from the females, giving each sex a run to itself. This is the only way to get the most from them. Cockerels are greedy customers and will steal all the food they can at the expense of the pullets. A winter layer Must be well handled from egg to maturity, and in this sentence you have the key to successful egg production during the winter months. By separating the cockerels from the pullets at an eally age the latter have every chance to make progress and mature normally.

The poultry yard will be entertaining visitors in the shape of insects, &c., when the warm weather comes. The houses and interior fittings should therefore be kept scrupulously clean, as dirty houses naturally invite the insects to make their stay a long one. There is plenty of work ahead of the poultry- keeper, whether he has 10, 100, or 1,000 head of stock. Attend to every detail and put all the time you possibly ca'n into the poultry-yard dur- ing May. You will never regret it !—" The Poultry World."

div.head: EVILS OF OVERCROWDING.
div.p: THE EVILS OF OVERCROWDING.

Whatever plan is adopted, the chickens must have plenty of space to allow of their full and proper development. If too many chickens are closely huddled together the oxygen quickly be- comes exhausted, and thus they are compelled to breathe the impure air over and over again. There is a great number of diseases that owe their origin to overcrowdin . Many of these diseases are not immediately apparent, but the seeds are sown which ultimately assert. them- selves. div.head: CORPORATION EMPLOYES AND THE WAR. Half Of The Eligible Clerical Staff Offer Their Services.
div.p: CORPORATION EMPLOYES AND THE WAR. Half Of The Eligible Clerical Staff Offer Their Services.

The General Purposes Committee reported at Tuesday evening's meeting of the Warrington, Town Council that it had been resolved that the Corporation, as employers, approved of the pro- posal to "give preference in filling up positions after the war to those who have served their country under arms or in making munitions of war." It was further resolved by the committee that Corporation vacancies now occurring be filled only by men who are ineligible to serve in His Majesty'B Forces. The Town Clerk reported to the committee that of the single men em- ployed on the clerical staffs of the Corporation. and eligible by age, just over 50 per cent. had either, enlisted or ,offered themselves for enlist- ment. That in these figures all of the military age had been included, although some had ap- parent physical defects. The committee ex- pressed their gratification at the figures, and further resolved that the war bonus in the case of those married employes of the Corporation. who have joined H.M. Forces, be added to the denendant's allowance. _ _ _

The MAYOR, in proposing the adoption of the committee's ~minutes, said that a return had been got out at his request, and it showed that over 50 per cent. of the single men employed in the clerical department had offered their ser- vices, and had either been accepted or rejected. A similar return relating to the single men em- ployed on the outside staff showed that 45 per cent. of those eligible had also either joined or had been rejected. Of the married men on the outside staff just 40 per cent. had offered.
The DEPUTY MAYOR seconded, and the corn mittee''s minutes were adopted.

div.head: ESPERANTO AND WAR.—Continued.

enjoyable evening was spent. The proceedings comprised music and dancing, and a capital programme of music was. gone through. The Esperanto choruses, "La Espero " and "Al la Esperantistaro," were enthusiastically sung by all the Esperantists. Miss Emily Taylor sang "There's only one England" and "Come, sweet morning," for which she was heartily applauded. Miss L. Snelling sang "Come back to Erin," which was greatly appreciated. Mrs. Applebaum delighted the audience with two short recitations in Esperanto, while Mr, R. P. Griffiths, also of LiVerpool, sang , " Flugintaj Revoj." Mr. Arthur Davis, as usual, earned hearty applause with "Up from Zummerset " and " Zummer- zetshire."

Mr. Will Smith (of Liscard) was heartily ap- plauded for his rendering of several Indian love lyrics, and Mr. Caldwell (the blind' pianist), sang "Somewhere a voice is calling." Three Belgian girls, who are members of the local society, sang the Brabanconne in Flemish, and they were warmly appreciated. The Misses Richardson, Applebaum and J. Corney acted as accompanists; Mr. Caldwell supplied the music for dancing, and Mr. R. P. Griffiths was M.C.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
ESPERANTO AND WAR
row Universal Language Might have Prevented Conflict.

div.head: LOCAL CONFERENCE.
div.p: LOCAL CONFERENCE.

We Esperantists maintain that the only cause of war is misunderstanding between nations; and that if we did away with this misunderstanding, by means of one language, such wars as the present one would be non- existent, or, at all events, much more remote.

These pointed words were spoken by the Lancashire and Cheshire Esperantists' Presi- dent, in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall, on Saturday afternoon. The occasion was the quarterly conference of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Esperantists. About 100 members attended from Blackburn, Bolton, Chester, Lancaster, Liverpool, Manchester, Leigh, Golborne; St. Helens, Eccles, Buxton, Stockport, Southport, Widnes, Wigan and Farn- worth. The representatives of the Warrington Society were the Rev. Father R. B. Primavesi (president), Miss Dora E. Parsonage (hon. secretary), Miss J. Corney (hon. treasurer), Miss Smith (vice-president) and the delegate for the Universal Association (Mr. .T. Smith). The chair was taken by the President of the Federation (Mr. Applebaum, of Liverpool), who was supported by Mr. Rhodes Marriott (of Manchester) and Mr. Sidney Taylor (of Bux- ton), vice-presidents, who serve on the com- mittee for two years after retiring.

div.head: "A PITY."
div.p: "A PITY."

The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) heartily welcomed the visitors. There was, he said half-apologetically, comparatively little attractiveness about Warrington—although on a finer day it did look more charming than it did at that moment. He was, however, pleased that the historic town had been honoured by the Esperanto Federation holding their quarterly meeting in it. Esperanto was a language which not only enabled the people of all countries to communicate with each other with greater freedom, but had had the effect of cementing friendships; it was a pity it was not used even more extensively than it was, for although hd did not think it would have pre- vented all wars, it might have had the effect of reducing their number. (Hear, hear.) In Father Prima vesi, concluded the Mayor, local Espe'rantists had an excellent supporter; and the Warrington Society he wished particularly every success. He also hoped that the delibera- tions that afternoon might strengthen the Esperanto movement. Ire Was glad to welcome the delegates to the good old town of Warring- ton. (Applause.) PRACTICAL AND ECONOMIC.

The President spoke of the Association's aims. These, he said, were at once practical and economic. In every walk of life men did their best to practise economy, and the only thing in the world in which it was not known was in the method of languages. Their proposition to the world was very practical. What they wanted was one international language, which every nation in the world should study. Those who had not the time, leisure or brains to study five, six or eight languages, should study one simple languagill in addition to their own. That language was in existence, and it was Esperanto (Applause.) They were not .Utopians, but had managed to make great strides. They had an Esperanto medical journal, as well as engineer- ing journals, and literary reviews with criti- cisms. These facilitated the exchange of ideas, and the general benefit on a scale otherwise im- possible.

div.head: Only _Cause of War.
div.p: Only _Cause of War.

"I think," concluded Mr. Applebaum, "it was Milton who said 'lt is only a third-grade man of affairs who is not inspired by and constant reference to the ideal'; and so we have also an ideal side—something spiritual in the movement." Having made use of the remarks quoted above, the speakin pointed out that the tendency of all literary publicists was towards that end; it was on account of the difference of languages that we were now fighting with Germany. (Hear, hear.) Then opportunities should be given by the municipalities for Esperanto to. be taught in the schools, _which would help to bring: about the realisation of their great ideals. (Applause.) ,

ALL ROADS LEAD TO WARRINGTON." The Rev. Father Primavesi, in moving a cordial vote of thanks to the Mayor for his kindness in welcoming the Federation and placing the use of the Town Hall at their dis- posal; said he had had no difficulty in obtaining his Worship's countenance and support for the conference; and mentioned that the Federation had met in Warrington—he was glad that was so because he considered that all road's led to Warrington. (Laughter.) Julius Csar 'dis- covered Warrington, and they had a Roman camp to show that he knew where to come. If he had been alive to-day, no doubt he would have given his countenance to Esperanto. (Laughter.) It was through the help of War- rington that other places got a local habitation and a name. as in the old posting days letters were directed to "Liverpool, near Warrington." That fact showed that all roads led to Wafting- ton. (Laughter.) , "I have," concluded Father Primavesi, I recently come in touch with his Worship with reference to the refugees, and he must have been struck by the difficulty of the differing languages. It is a great question, and I think we have solved it. I only wish it to be spread —by the help of local authorities." Mr. Horsley (of Eccles) seconded, expressing a hope for the furtherance of the movement. The motion was unanimously carried.

div.head: MAYOR MAY LEARN ESPERANTO.
div.p: MAYOR MAY LEARN ESPERANTO.

In replying, the Mayor declared that he had only done his duty.. The Town Hall was always at the disposal—while he was in office—of any society which he believed was working for the good of the community. If he had the time he would, when his mayoral duties were completed, probably learn Esperanto with a view to getting about the world. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Mayor also paid a fine tribute to the work done by Father Primavesi amongst the local refugees, saying that his services had been, very useful owing to his knowledge of languages in connection with the various people who had to be looked after. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: "KEEP BEAUTIFUL TORCH BURNING.
div.p: "KEEP BEAUTIFUL TORCH BURNING.
Alderman Peacock then , retired with an ex pression of regret. The conference which fol lowed, was conducted entirely in Esperanto.

The President, in the course of his address, alluded to the war, and drew the attention of the conference to the future propaganda of the Federation. 'They could not possibly ignore the circumstances, although "la Esperantistaro " was absolutely neutral, one of its bases being the brotherhood of mankind. They felt that a knowledge of Esperanto was more than ever absolutely necessary for humanity -at large. Pacifists had ,nothing to do while the cannon were roaring, but Esperantists could do their work as usual, and were preparing the way for the great movement which- was bound to take place at the conclusion of the war if their ideas as Esperantists were accepted by the world. They felt it therefore to be their bounden duty still to hold the lamp, pouring in the oil and continuing the burning of their beautiful torch. (Applause.) After much discussion it was decided that a special fund be raised for the purpose.

div.head: HANDSOME PRESENTATION.
div.p: HANDSOME PRESENTATION.

Mr. Rhodes Marriott then made the presenta- tion of a handsome mahogany writing-desk, bearing an inscribed silver plate, to Mr. G. It. Griffiths, of Liverpool, who, after three years' labours as hon. secretary of the Federation, has retired. Mr. Griffiths suitably acknowledged the splendid gift. The new secretary is Mr. Fred Parker, of Burnley.

div.head: TEA AT THE WINMARLEIGH.
div.p: TEA AT THE WINMARLEIGH.

After the conference the visitors adjourned to the Winmarleigh Cafe for tea, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the local society for their hospitality, on the motion of Mr. Marriott, seconded by Mr. Lewis. The Hon. Secretary (Miss Dora E. Parsonage) replied in Esperanto :—" On behalf of the War- rington Society I thank you very much for your kind and complimentary words. It is with very great pleasure that we welcome you here to-day, and I hope that you will all spend a most enjoy- able evening." (Applause.)

div.head: MUSIC AND DANCE.
div.p: MUSIC AND DANCE.

div.head: COMPLETED BRIDGE.
div.p: THE COMPLETED BRIDGE.
Councillor Pemberton's Allegation of Jobbery

div.head: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S RETORT.
div.p: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S RETORT.

An amendment that, when it came to voting, only found support from its proposer and seconder, occupied the major portion of the time devoted to the May meeting of the Warrington Town Council, which was held on Tuesday evening. The amendment was addressed to a non-contentious-looking minute in the report of the Bridges Committee, which recorded that the total cost of the contract with Messrs. Thorne and Sons, the contractors to whom was entrusted the work of building the bridge, amounted to £19,962 19s. 10d., that figure including the cost of additional works. The amendment was introduced by Coun- cillor Gough, and was seconded by Councillor Pemberton, both of whom indulged in criti- cism which was quite out of harmony with other utterances, which dilated upon the beauty of the structure, its noble width and the general pride with which it was regarded by Warringtonians.

time to build, but he thought the ends had justified the time, as well as the means. (Hear, hear.) It was much better that they should have hastened slowly, than that they should have had "scamped " work. As it was, he did not think anybody could point to a flaw in the bridge, and it truly represented a crowning triumph to Alderman Smethurst's long life of public activity. (Hear, hear.) The Alderman added that now that they had got the bridge he did hope that the Council would 'take a spacious view of the approaches and that they would be made worthy of so worthy a bridge. Councillor GOUGH moved that the minutes relating to the cost of the bridge be referred back to the committee and said that it had become a habit with some members of the Council to cry "Peace, peace!" A -MEMBER : What's that? Peas, peas! (Laughter.)

div.head: COUNCILLOR GOUGH CUT SHORT.
div.p: COUNCILLOR GOUGH CUT SHORT.

Councillor GOUGH : As I was saying, it has become a habit with some members of the Council to cry "Peace, peace !" whilst there has been no peace during the whole of ! the time the bridge has been under construe- ' tion. Now that the work was finished, the Councillor went on, some members would say "Why reap up all the failings and weaknesses of the past? Why not let sleeping diogs rest? Why cry stinking fish?" Not becaUse he de- lighted in being vindictive or in punishing men, but because he honestly believed that the end of a contract, just as the end of a year or of a life, was the right and proper time to take stock. Of all the loose undertakings the Corporation had entered into, the new bridge had been one of the most disreputable associated with the town. 'They Might readily classify it with the building of the Police Station and the Lawson contract. From the commencement of the construction of the bridge to the final settlement there had been a continuous wrangle about prices, extras, and not getting on with the work. In taking a retrospective view of the muddled dealings between the official, the contractor, and the engineer, the members of the Council had often been in a dilemma as to the right course to pursue. . The great curse the Corporation and the Council have to suffer and endure, and which has been going on for years, is that members of this Council who supply building materials
The MAYOR (ringing his bell) : "Now theli !" and cries of "Chair !"
Councillor GOUGH : Have helped and encour- aged—(" Chair, _chair.")
The MAYOR :: Order, order!

Councillor GOUGH: however, endeavoured to stick to the thread of his discourse, which he was reading from a somewhat bulky MS., but the only words that were audible amid an angry chorus of cries of "Chair, chair !" "Shut up !" and the like, were—" of the work done, and I say it is a shame—" The chorus of dissent at length grew so insistent that the Councillor broke off abruptly and announced his intention of resuming his seat, and did so; whereupon the MAYOR ob- served "Thank you; it would he better !"

div.head: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S ALLEGATIONS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON'S ALLEGATIONS.

Councillor PE3IBERTON seconded the amend- ment, remarking that one would think, from the fulsome praise bestowed upon "the people" connected with the bridge that the members who had spoken represented not the ratepayers, but the bridge builders. To give Alderman Smethurst his due, he was glad that he had emphasised the fact that the expenditure of nearly £20,000 referred only to the contract with Messrs. Thorne, because the bridge was going to _ .

cost nearer £27,000 than £20,000. TLet them face that fact; let them face the mimic! "Did Alderman Smethurst think for one moment that I would sit here and not say a word about a thing like this?" asked the Councillor. •" Be- cause, if so, I must tell him that it was positively ridiculous. I wonder what the pub- lic of Warrington are thinking; what they think of the sort of brain power they have on their Council, or what sort of brain power the Councillors think the public have. Only three months ago Alderman Smethurst agreed in this very Council Chamber with figures which I gave, and which showed the cost of the bridge to be something like £26,000. It was true that the amount paid to Messrs. Thorne alone was about £20,000. But the original contract was only £14,000. I was dead against the .contract being , exceeded. I was dead against any interference with it unless the whole thing was thrown open to be contracted for again. It was no use. The engineer's friends were too strong then; it could not be done. It was one of the greatest pieces of jobbery that was ever perpetrated. That is my opinion. It has taken over three years to build this bridge—and what's the good of saying otherwise—the time taken about the job was the laughing stock of Warrington. It was quite a local joke, and when one wanted to refer to the dim and distant futurelie used to say 'l'll do so and so when Warrington Bridge is finished.' (Laughter.) This passing of a congratulatory resolution is perfectly absurd. There are lots of men outside the Council quite intelligentas as those who are on' it—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and they have not such short memories as some think: Well, thf) bridge has taken three years, and some of the members were so friendly with the people con- cerned that, from their point of view, it would not have .mattered if 'the work had gone on for another three years. Every week this work was going on the Council were paying standing wages—not the contractor. If I had had my road I/ don't think it would have gone on a day longer than Was absolutely necessary. (Laugh- ter). Those who are laughing—and this is one of the peculiar things about these bodies—would not have more than one penny over- spent on one of their own • private contracts; indeed they. would want to hang a man if he charged them a sovereign above the contract price. - But in this matter of the bridge they are • not spending their own money; they are spending the public's money, and so it's a different story altogether. (Laugh- ter.) It's a fine bridge, we are told. Yes, and so it ought to be! But if only the public knew all and ,could vote on the matter, you would soon see what they thought about it. Alderman Smethurst has made a lot of the £1,600 value of the land that has been re-claimed. Why, it would not fetch 1,600 pence. I'll give £lO to Warrington Infirmary if Alderman Smethurst can prove that we shall have saved 1,600 pence. All sorts of red. herrings have been thrown across the trail. We were promised that if only we would have a wide bridge and takeout the centre arches would be given £4,000." A MEMBER: One thousand. •

Alderman SMETHURST : Three thousand. Councillor PEMBERTON : Where is it? We shan't get 3,000 pennies. Yet that promise was used as a great argument when we were talking about this bridge. Alderman SMETHURST : Not by me.

Councillor PEMBERTON : No; I'll give you your due, you didn't. No doubt that promise influ- enced the Council very much in passing that larger contract for a one-span bridge. It's the same old story!. Poor old ratepayers have to pay again They're a fine body of men; but how they stand it I don't know. (Laughter.)" I can see nothing for us to congratulate ourselves upon in this matter of the bridge. Councillor BROADHURST pointed out that the amendment at this late stage-when all the work was finished--could do no possible good. Maybe the Council had not made the best of their chances, hut it was too late to start re- tracting now, for the money had been paid, and they might as well let sleeping dogs bark. A VOICE: Lie. (Laughter.) Councillor BROADHURST : If there was any fault as to the variation of the original contract the whole Council must be held responsible.

div.head: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S REPLY
div.p: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S REPLY

Councillor ROBERTS: Mr. Mayor, we have been accustomed in this Council for years to charges of being corrupt and behaviour of the most dis- creditable kind. There was a time in Warring. to when a section of the public listened to

charges of that kind with a certain amount of credulity, even coming from the quarter they did. To-day the whole aspect of public opinion is changed, and nobody takes the slightest notice of a charge of this nature when it comes from the source from which it was made to- night. And, moreover, nobody ever will again. I feel it is only due to myself as a member of the Council, and to my colleagues, who try to walk honourably and honestly, whose word to- day is their bond, whose word does not need to be supported on oath, and then to be questioned, whose word is taken, fairly taken, by their col- leagues and associates and by the public gener- ally, and I repeat that Councillor Pemberton may go on making his statements alleging cor- ruption of the vilest possible character Councillor PEMBERTON : Mr. Mayor, I object to that. I have not made any such assertion. Councillor ROBERTS: I took your words down from your mouth; I am not in the habit of making statements I cannot prove. I can prove; my statements; some people cannot. You said "It was one of the greatest pieces of jobbery ever perpetrated in this Council." That is pretty tall talk, and if it does not imply corrup- tion on the part of members of the Council, I don't understand the English language; and I repeat—and I want it to be taken down—that you may go on making these charges as often as you like. They annoy and irritate to a cer- tain extent, although we are getting tolerably thick-skinned; but nobody outside the Council Chamber now, or at any future time, will attach very much importance to charges of this nature, coming from you. So much for Councillor Pemberton, and the same remark applies to a certain extent to Councillor Gough. He spoke about this as being one of the most disreput- able transactions that this Council ever had— well, he's a pretty article, with his reputation and past history, to come and make charges— Councillor GOUGH : Mr. Mayor Councillor ROBERTS: You have asked for it, and you are going to have it. Coun‘Allor GOUGH (to the Mayor) : You have allowed Harry Roberts a great deal of latitude. I wish you would give us the same privilege. We would wipe him as badly as lie can wipe us. You don't interfere with him.

The MAYOR: I think the public will be able to judge, now be.tween the various statements. Councillor ROBERTS: I quite agree, Mr. Mayor. I am quite satisfied to leave it at that. In regard to the job itself, the difference be- tween the amount of the original contract and the actual cost of the bridge had been made up of various items, every one of which had been the subject of discussion and consideration, until one was almost sick and weary of, it, by the Council. Every item of additional expendi- ture had received the deliberate and considered sanction of the Council. The retaining walls, which had cost £4,000, were one of the most beautiful features of the bridge, apart from their utilitarian value, which was almost in- calculable. The only cause for regret was that the wall on the north-east side was not carried a bit farther. It was quite correct that there were other expenses incidental to the making of a bridge 80 feet wide to supply the needs of three main roadways, which themselves had been con- siderably widened. The purchase of property and the acquisition of land had been necessary. but he said without hesitation that they had in the bridge not only an economical and a strong job, but one of the most valuable im- provements and most beautiful- pieces of work ever carried through in Warrington. If it had cost a few hundred pounds more than they had expected—and that was the extreme limit—they must admit they had a finished work which was a credit to everybody, and he was glad it had fallen to the lot of his old and dear friend, Alderman Smethurst, to have been in the scheme from its initiation to its completion. Councillor PEMBERtON, rising to a point of ex- planation, said he would like to make it clear that he and other members had objected to the extra expenditure all through the contract. He did not retract one single word he had said, in- cluding the word jobbery. Alderman BOLTON confessed that he could not make. Out what the amendment meant. The money had been spent and must be paid. Alderman SMETEURST interpolated, apropos of the discussion. a story of a friend of his who said to him "I should want £l,OOO a year for your job." (Laughter.) The amendment was put aid defeated, only the proposer and seconder—as reported above— voting for it. The minutes. were then adopted.-

div.head: COMPLETED BRIDGE.
div.p: THE COMPLETED BRIDGE.

Alderman SMETHURST, the chairman of the Bridges Committee, proposed the adoption of his committee's minutes, and said that many state- ments had been made with regard to the prob- able cost of the bridge, and not a few of them were extremely wide of the mark. Now that the structure was completed it was possible to give the exact cost, and, as a matter of fact, that was £19,962 19s. 10d. That total included the following items calculated upon schedule rates and figures in the original quantities:— Floor system, £1,076 3s. 7d.; cornice, balustrade, pylons, &c., £BOB 16s. 3d.; arch ribs, hinges, beam, columns, &c., 13,532 Bs.; foundations, abutments, piles, excavations, &c., £5,018 is. 3d.; general contractor's work, £3,394 7s. sd. Then there were extras, which had been report upon in detail, of £498, and extra works (par,-, ticulars of which had also been placad before the committee), totalling £1,403 19s. 111. In- surance (50 per cent. of the cost) amounted to £55 Os. 4d., and the cost of the retaining walls was £4,176 3s. Id. All these items Lronglit up the total cost of the structure and walls to £19,962 19s. 10d. The retention money r:n the original contract (10 per cent.) was £1,431: the amount paid to the contractors was £113,408 I9s. 10d., leaving a balance due at the last inneting of the committee of £123. Against the total cost the Corporation had a small asset to which he would like to draw the attention a the Coun- cil, and that had to do with the retaining walls. Those walls, as he had stated, cost over £4OOO. and against that outlay they could set an asset of 860 square yards of land which had been reclaimed, And which they were making use of at present, and of whion they make still further and profitable use in the future. lie thought they could, in fat, p;:t a value of something like £2 a yard )n that re claimed land., and that it could be usen as sites for warehouses, &c. At the price he had named, they would get a total return of £1,600, and, if they did so, he thought the Council would agree that, on the whole, the retaining walls had been a good investment. Alderman Smethurst went on to explain at length the circumstances in which the I,ridge was constructed to give direct access to Knutsford-road, and mentioned that he had in his pocket two small "cartoons," which were designed to show alternative posi- tions for the bridge at the time under discussion.
Leave them there.

Atelerinan BOLTON (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON : Let's see them. Alderman S3fETHURST : I cannot understand why, after my years of service ,and all the trouble I have gone to in connection with the bridge, the Council should not give me atten- tion without interruption. The MAYOR seconded the adoption of the committee's minutes.

Alfjprman BOLTON, in supporting, remarked that they had got a good bridge, and he thought both the town and the Corporation were to be congratulated upon the completion of one of the finest improvements ever effected in Warring- ton. Nothing surprised him more than to learn that the total cost was under £20,000, for which sum the town had got one of the finest ferro- concrete bridges in existence—a bridge that would facilitate river traffic, would bring more trade to the wharf, and would obviate the flooding of the Howley district, owing to the banking up of the river. Those outside the Corporation certainly owed the Bridges Com- mittee a vote of thanks, for they had done their best and, on the whole, had carried out the work entrusted to them most satisfactorily. (Hear, hear.) It was a good, lasting piece of work, and nothing but a German bomb--and it would have to be a big one at that; certainly bigger than usual—would do it much dataage. (Laugh- ter, and applause.) Councillor BROADHURST failed to see the reason why the Bridges Committee should pat themselves on the back and consider themselves a Mutual Admiration Society. The MAYOR: We are all on that committee. Councillor LOCKER: But we are not all an the tablet. •

Councillor BROADHURST went on to say that it had been stated repeatedly that the cost of the bridge would be something like J.:20,000. They all knew what the original tender was! He believed that the whole of the people of War- rington would agree with Alderman Bolton that in the bridge the town had something to be proud of, but they had paid enough for it; indeed, he thought they had paid too much for it. In his opinion they had paid at least £4,000 too much for it, and it was no use members coming there and making statements which would not, for a single minute, bear looking into. Let them be fair to themselves. They all knew that the Council were almost driven to taking the last extreme step that could be taken by a Council against a con- tractor. There could, however, be no doubt that the Chairman of the Bridges Committee had worked second to none in the matter and that he deserved the thanks of the Council and of hiS fellow-townsmen. There was one matter, however, to which he (the spegker) would like to draw the attention of the Coun- cil, and that was that when they were con- sidering the question of the construction of that bridge an offer was made them, from the Mayor's chair, that when the structure was completed they would, provided they built the bridge in a certain way—and they had built it that way—have a gift of £l,OOO from a certain -firm. COULteillOr PEMBERTON : £4,000. Alderman SMETHURST : £3,000. Alderman • Timms: The authorities do not agree. (Laughter.) Councillor BROADHURST : Well, I feel certain of £l,OOO. (Laughter.) I hope that firm, now that we have completed a single span bridge which is secon4 to none in England, will come forward and put down a cheque to assist the Chairman of the Bridges Committee to show a better balance sheets

RECRIMINATIONS OUT OF PLACE. Alderman BENNETT was sorry that there should be any recriminations, particularly On a night *hen, the bridge completed, there should be, nothing but mutual satisfaction. Of all the work which the Council had done, since he first became a member of it anyway, noth- ing had excited more general approval than the bridge. Councillor BROADHURST : cost of it. Alderman BENNETT : Well, I have not heard a single murmur as to the cost, except from Councillor Broadhurst, though I admit that the feeling of the general public was one of relief when they heard that the cost had actually worked out at less than £20,000. The Alderman went on to add that the original contract of £14,006 or ..1;15,000 did not include the river walls, or the strengthening of the whole fabric,. or, in fact, a good deal of the ornamentation which made the bridge such an object of beauty at the present time. He thought the town at large, no less than the Council, could corigratulate . themselves upon the stability and the beauty of the bridge, as well as, all things considered, the economy with Which so fine a structure had been built. div.head: PROSPEROUS WARRINGTON.
div.p: PROSPEROUS WARRINGTON.
Nearly £70,000 In Rates For Half-Year Despite The War.

At Tuesday's meeting of the Warrington Town Council, Councillor Wilkinson moved the adop- tion of the minutes of the Finance and Estate Committee, which contained what he described as "the most satisfactory" report of the Borough Collector for the half-year ended March 31st.

The Collector's report set forth that the abnormal conditions existing during the period covered by the half-year, October Ist to March 31st, might have suggested the possibility of the collection of the rates being anything but satis- factory, but he was glad to report that the results had net proved that view to he justified. The total amount collected was £68,863 6s. 10d.; and other items of interest were: Composftioa allowed, £4,442 6s. 4d.; allowances for empty property, £843 14s. Id.; allowances for assess- ments reduced, £295 25.; excusal of poor rate, on account of poverty, by the magistrates and Overseers, £lB 3s. 10d.; excusal of improvement rate, sewers rate and water rate, by the Finance Committee, £lO 14s. 3d.; allowances for de- molished property, &c., 2,89 is. 3d.; loss in collection, £26 ss. 9d.; and recoverable arrears, £l7l 18s. 2d. £755 MORE THAN LAST HALF-YEAR.
In comparison with the previous half-year,

the amount collected was £785 more, mainly on water meter accounts; the composition allowed £4,442 is the same; the empties are £147 more— due to four or five places,- such as Scotland-road Theatre, Carter's Warehouse, Mersey-street; Shepherd's shop, Market Gate, having been unoccupied since September last. The large amount for assessments reduced was principally due to the'L. and N.-W. Railway's appeal, being settled in the company'%favour. The excusals for poverty were £8 less than last half-year. These cases were given very careful considera- tion, and it was only when he was thoroughly satisfied of the absolute inability to pay, that _ _

they were put forward. Some of the Cases- were very sad ones, and showed a continuous struggle against adverse circumstances, and the amount allowed was really a very small fraction of the amount of the rate collectable. The arrears on
the whole were much less than last half-year, and had the full staff been available, he thought they would have been able to show even better results.

div.head: FEW DEFAULTERS.
div.p: FEW DEFAULTERS.

The loss in collection was £2655. 9d., and of that sum only £5 6s. 7d. was attributable to the half-year, one item in particular of £l3 2s. 10d. having been brought forward since September, 1913\ and now discharged, after the receipt of a small dividend. It was interesting to note that only ten summonses were issued as against afl average of 21 during the last three years. The results testified to the continued prosperity of the town, and the fairly even distribution of bnsiness amongst all sections of the community. The Collector was authorised to discharge as irrecoverable the sums of £lO 14s. 3d. (excused) and £26 ss. 9d. (loss in collection) referred to in the above report.

div.head: WAR-TIME COAL.
div.p: WAR-TIME COAL.
arrington Council Favour Restriction of Exports.

The Gas Committee of the Warrington Town Council decided, on the suggestion of the Man- chester District Institution of Gas Engineers, to urge upon the Government to consider the importance of taking immediate action, .with 3 view (1) to restricting the export of coal in order to ensure adequate supplies for the home demand, with particular reference to such pub- lic supplies as gas and electricity; (9) to ex- pediting matters, as urged by recent deputa- tions, to secure better railway transit and more regular supplies of coal from the collieries to meet the urgent and necessary requirements of gas and electricity departments; and (3) to take sich action as they may deem expedient to pre- vent such unnecessary increases in the price of coal for next year's requirements, as are now being quoted by the colliery owners, which will have a very serious effect upon the general welfare of the nation, as the increased workingO costs of public supply undertakings will neces- sarily lead to advanced charges for_ g electricity, &c. It was further decided thats.S. copy of the above be sent to the Prime Minister and to the Member for the Borough. The decision of the Gas Committee was 'ratted for the endorsement of the Town Coun- cil at their monthly meeting on Tuesday night, when Councillor Locker proposed that it be given, and Alderman John Evans seconded. , Alderman Bennett -gave his support to tne committee's proposal, and said that coal, in* the past, had been pouring out of the country, tf,' the great detriment of all classes, who had hee to be continually paying higher prices in con- sequence. He congratulated the committee 011, their attitude in the matter, and hoped that something tangible in the shape of restrictioo might result from it. The committee's action was unanimouslY approved. •

div.p: VOLUNTEER CORPS. - Should They Receive Aid From
The Rates? TOWN COUNCIL DEBATE
THE POINT.

An interesting discussion took place at the tannthly meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil nn Tuesday evening, as to whether muni- ci, Palities should contribute from the rates to the fund for equipping local Volunteer Corps— the Preparatory Training Corps, the Volunteer Training Corps, &c. The discussion arose out of a minute submitted bY the. General Purposes Committee. That tainute read as follows: "A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Ealing forwarding resolution passed by his Council urging the Government to promote legislation empowering Municipalities to contribute towards the equip- ment of Volunteer Corps, and requesting this committee to pass a similar resolution. It was resolved that no action be taken."

A MATTER OF GREAT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE. Alder Mall BENNETT said he thought it was a Pity that the General Purposes Committee had liot seen their way to give some support to the resolution, for he felt that the matter was one of such great public importance at the pre- sent time. Those volunteer corps were being raised all over the country, and they were doing useful and patriotic work; indeed, in some parts they were enormously strong and active. He was sorry, and rather ashamed, to feel that in Warrington the men had not by any means risen to the opportunities afforded them. An at- tempt was being made to infuse new life into the movement locally, and he hoped that the citizens who could not join the regular forces would do the next best thing by joining this volunteer force. div.head: HOUSING CONFERENCES.
div.p: HOUSING CONFERENCES.
Warrington Council Debate Their Usefulness, or Otherwise.

div.head: REAL PROBLEM.
div.p: THE REAL PROBLEM.

The question as to whether or not Warring- ton shall be represented at a conference on the subject of town planning to be held at Liverpool on May 12th and 13th, was debated at consider- able length at the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening.

div.head: IS HOUSING IN THE TOWN "APPALLING "? –
div.p: IS HOUSING IN THE TOWN "APPALLING "? -

Councillor ARCHER introduced the subject by drawing attention to a recommendation, put forward by the Street Improvement Committee, to the effect that the Chairman of the com- mittee (Alderman Bennett), the Deputy-chair- man (Councillor Joseph), Aldermen Jas. Evans and Councillors Gough and Pemberton be ap- pointed to attend the conference. "We have been sending to these conferences annually" said the Councillor, "but we seem to get no ` for'arder ' with regard to the question of dwelling-houses for the working class. There can be no doubt that the state of the town at the present time with regard to housing' is appalling." If the Councillors who attended the conference, he added, would only urge forward the matter of the housing of the workers, they would, un- doubtedly, be taking a step in the right direc- tion.

div.head: ARE THE CONFERENCES PRACTICAL?
div.p: ARE THE CONFERENCES PRACTICAL?

Alderman JAS. EVA.NS failed to see, that up to now, the conferences on town planning had helped in the matter of solving the housing difficulties to be met with in such congested areas as Warrington. It was all very well to spend time in discussing the laying out of dis- tricts where liouses were somethingllike half a mile apart, arid where new roads could be made at will, but what .had that got to do with places like Warrington? The Housing and Town Planning Act would have to be adopted by the Council before they could give to the working class of the town, all round, the suit- able, sanitary and decent houses that all would like to see them living in. He had attended one of the conferences, but he must confess that it did not help him to a solution of the problem— a problem, which was perplexing every Cor- poration in the country. The problem had to do with the demolition of undesirable dwellings and erection of others and more satisfactory ones in their stead. So far as he knew, these more or less academic conferences had not helped to solve the real housing question at all; that question which was concerned with the re-modelling of slum dwellings and slum areas.
The tiEPUTY Tows CLERK (Mr. A. T. Hallaway) explained that the conference would consider questions affecting housing during and after the war.

Alderman JAMES EVANS : I am afraid that the • members have only a smattering of knowledge as to what this conference is really for. I am afraid that it will be on the general lines of town planning, and that it will not be "a speciality" any more than any of the confer- ences that have preceded it, or that will follow it. What I want to know is, when is this town planning business going to come to the practical assistance of municipalities?

div.head: DO THE COUNCIL GET RETURN FOR THEIR MONEY?
div.p: DO THE COUNCIL GET RETURN FOR THEIR MONEY?

Councillor BROADHURST opined that the send 7 ing of delegates to these conferences amounted to the spending of money for.which the Council got no adequate return. What was the use of holding conferences unless there was some prac- tical outcome from them? There was plenty of scope for housing work in Warrington, if they set about it the proper way. IN knew for a positive fact, for he had been trying to get a house for a worker, and had found that it was impossible to get a suitable one for love or money in the town at the present time. If this conference on housing was' not going to lead to some practical result, he was of opinion that the money spent on sending delegates would not, to say the least of it. be well spent.

div.head: ROCK-BOTTOM FACT. _
div.p: THE ROCK-BOTTOM FACT. _

Councillor PEMBERTON agreed that it was time that "the town planning people" got down to the rock-bottom fact that the working classes of the country wanted houses. It was not the better classes who could afford to live in garden villages with whom conferences of this kind should concern themselves, but the working man —the £1 a week man—who could not get a house to live in. He used to be able to, but the source of supply was stopped, and he thought the con- ference would be doing very useful work If they inquired why. He remembered a time when there were 7,000 empty houses in Liverpool, and when the average number empty in Warring- ton as from 400 to 500. But the builders had stopp'ed building. There must be some reason for it, and if that conference was going to be of any practical use it must find out what the reason was. The working class were much nmprAd bpeanse of this stoppage in the supply of suitable houses. A TRIFLING COST.

Alderman BOLTON did not think the Council ought-to object to the• sending of the delegates Proposed, seeing that the cost was only al3.3nt 3s. per head. "If " he added amid laughter, "we can't spend 15s. on the best men on th,t Council to go to learn what experts have to say about housing, it's time for us to shut up !"

div.head: GOOD DONE BY THE CONFERENCES.
div.p: GOOD DONE BY THE CONFERENCES.

Alderman BENNETT said that the question of housing was one of the most serious of the many questions the country had to face, and surely that was an argument in favour of sending members of the Council to the conference, in order that they might get all the knowledge they could on the stibject. He thought the con- ferences had done an enormous amount of good. The National Housing and Town Planning Act was very largely due to the activity of the par- ticular body under whose auspices the con- ference was to be held. It was palpable to all that at the present time there was an enormous difficulty in dealing with the question of pro- viding adequate housing accommodation foie the workers, but he failed to see that that was any reason why they should not attend the con- ference; on the contrary it was a reason why they should. There were two or three factors which militated -directly against a solution of this housing problem, one of them being that conveyancing duties had to be paid on every purchase of land. Another, in the view of many people, was to be found in the land taxes, but a third—and this was perhaps the most important factor of the lot—was summed up in the word "rates." He had never been against spending any money if he saw \that the com- munity were going to get value for it—if they were going to get an equivalent return. He had long thought that the method in which muni- cipal revenues were raised was obsolete and unfair. Rates ought to be abolished and a municipal income tax sulfstituted. How- ever, let that pass. The immediate difficulty was that the -prices of materials and labour had risen, so that it was difficult to build a house to let at a rent which the working man could afford to pay. The committee's recommendation was adopted.

div.head: VOLUNTEER CORPS—continued.
div.p: VOLUNTEER CORPS—continued.

they would have been in a better position than they were to-day. The reason he would suggest for supporting the Ealing Council in their pro- posal was that if it were put into effect i would give them the opportunity of making a sub- scription should they so desire; it would not leave them, as a Corporation, barred out from doing so. One had to listen to a lot of talk about the rates going up and so on. Well, what if they did? Was not fheir national existence at ',stake; an existence which could only be maintained at a terrible cost of blood and trea§ure. The position to-day was of such extreme gravity as to demand from every one of them the most serious consideration of every proposition which lent itself to enlistment and to the strengthening of the forces at the coni- mand of the Crown; both for foreign and home service. The MAYOR seconded the amendment.

Councillor BROADHURST contended that the charge for the voluntary corps should, be a national one and should nbt be borne locally. Incidentally he mentioned that he was an old Volunteer of nearly twenty years' standing, and that he had held the rank. of Pioneer-Sergeant in the Liverpools. The -amendment was adopted, only three vot- ing against.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
WARTIME WALKING DAY.
HOW IT CAN BE AVOIDED.

Right-thinking people are unanimous in the opinion that, war or no war, the simple pleasures of the children must not be un- necessarily infringed upon. Walking Dar— essentially a children's festival, and in Warrington perhaps the outstanding event in the child's calendar—is in danger this year of being but a half-measure. It is contended —and there are firm grounds for the belief— that if Walking Day be held as usual, and on the usual day, a general holiday will be taken, a contingency that is undesirable in view of the fact that a very large number of the works of Warrington are at present engaged in industries relaxation in which would spell hindrance in the all-important matter of the output of war munitions. Various suggestions for averting a general holiday, and, at the same time, for preserving Walking Day for the sake of the children, were made on Tuesday at a meeting of the clergy and Sunday school superintendents of the Church of England.
The meeting was held in the Patten Hall, and the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis) pre- sided.
THE MAYOR'S LETTER.
At the outset, the Rector read the Mayor's letter on the subject, published in our last issue. It was as follows:

"I beg to inform you that representations have been made to, me by some of the large Works in the town as to the advisability of postponing 'Walking Day for this year on the ground of the loss of time and the inter- ference with Works, a large number of which are busily engaged on Government contracts. I presume that owing to all railway facilities and cheap trains being withheld by Railway Companies, no 'Workmen's trips will take place, and consequently there will be no, neces- sity for a two days' holiday as in previous years. If the workmen would keep to their work on .` Walking Day,' I see no .reason why the children should not have their usual holi- day; but it is doubtful whether the men could be expected to work under the circumstances. It has occurred to me that it might be possible to have Walking Day fixed for August Bank Holiday. Perhaps you will let me have your views on the whole matter, after which I pro- pose to call a meeting at an early date."
Need The Children's Pleasure Be Spoiled ?

intercession; that, he thought, would raise the tone of the whole gathering. At Wigan it was done in that way every year. It would add to the dignity of the occasion if the clergy wore their vestments.

div.head: SATURDAY SUGGESTED INSTEAD OF
div.p: SATURDAY SUGGESTED INSTEAD OF
FRIDAY.

The Rector went on to observe that those present would have seen that the Nonconform- ists wished to have Walking Day as usual on the Friday nearest to July Ist. On the other hand it was reported that the Roman Catho- lics were in favour of giving up Walking Day altogether this year. He thought it would be well to call a meeting of the Church officers on Sunday evening, and after careful consid- eration of the matter all were unanimously in favour of holding Walking Day as usual, but upon Saturday, July 3rd, instead of the Friday. If Friday, the usual day, was fixed this year, there would be several objections which could be raised. One was that it would interfere with work, and would entail, possibly, heavy cost. Further, he thought the feeling of all at the present time was against having a Walk- ing Day such as they had been accustpmed to have. He was inclined to favour the fixing of Walking Day on a Saturday, because there would not be the difficulty with regard to work. Parents would be able to enjoy the sight, and the children also would have their usual enjoyment. A great objection to the Saturday, however, was that if they had a procession such as was usually held on a Friday it would interfere with the business of the town on what was S. market day—a very serious consideration which was not taken note of at the meeting on Sunday.

div.head: Rector's Proposal.
div.p: The Rector's Proposal.

He would put before the meeting a proposal— it might possibly raise doubts in their minds at 'first, but he was very strongly inclined to feel that the proposition was a good one—and it was that they should have tea and games for the children on Saturday afternoon, and a procession of a religious character on the Sunday. He, fttrther, suggested that the scholars should meet at the schools at two o'clock, go to the Town Hall, assembling at about 2.30, then having a procession on the usual lines, and over the usual course, return to the respective ,churches for service at about 3.30. That course would not interfere with work, and thus the Government would benefit; for they felt it most important at present not to interfere with Government con- tracts. Secondly the proposal would benefit tradesmen, whom they were anxious should not suffer. They would get the benefit of pro- viding what was necessary in the way of dress and food. Thirdly, the proposed arrangement would benefit the parents, who would be obi to see their children walk, as they much- wished to do. FOurthly, the children would have their usual holiday and enjoyment, though, perhaps, it would be modi4ed. There would also be very little cost. It would not be necessary to provide a band or lorries for the infants. They would not need nearly so much money as usual, and as most of the People in the town were never better off, if they widened the basis' of subscriptions they would get a considerable amount from the parents tliemselves.

div.head: Dcmonstration of a Religious Character.
div.p: A Dcmonstration of a Religious Character.

It was strongly- felt that the demonstration should be of a religious character, suitable to the occasion, and a demonstration that tended to put before everybody their duty at the present time. Therefore, 'instead of having a band and a fancy procession, the children should wear their ordinary Sunday school dress, and they could sing hymns in the pro- cession and thus give a religious character to the event that would be worthy of the day. If thought advisable they might have a little service at the Town Hall and sing the National Anthem before the procession resumed. The suggestion was not his own; it had been made to him, but the more he consider6d it the more he felt that it was an excellent one; indeed, he could see no objection to it. He could, on the other hand, see great objections to the selection of Friday or Saturday for the holding of the procession.

div.head: WHAT THOSE AT THE FRONT WOULD
div.p: WHAT THOSE AT THE FRONT WOULD
WISH.

Mr. W. H. Stansfield (St. James', Latchford) said that the scheme outlined by the Rector coincided to a great extent with the idea in his own mind. He felt that Walking Day ought not to be given up altogether—that 'their fathers, sons and brothers who had gone to the Front would think of, them, at that time as enjoying Walking Day, and would be the first to wish that the great event should not altogether be dropped, though a. modification of the usual mode of procedure was desirable. They did not want the manufacture of war • munitions to be stopped or checked, as it would'be if Walking Day were held on the Friday, in which case the men would certainly Want to keep holiday. If they had tea and games on the Saturday after- noon, They would have their usual. helpers, who would be free for. the afternoon. The idea of having the procession on Sunday was excellent, as such a course would involve disorganisation of nothing but Sunday school; they would have a real Sunday ,school procession. He thought that a dignified procession, with each school marching behind its own banner, and with pne band, would admirably meet the situation, and the. walk could be fittingly concluded by the singing of a few hymns and the National' Anthem, and, perhaps, with a few prayers of

div.head: SPECIAL TIMES DEMAND SPECIAL METHODS.
div.p: SPECIAL TIMES DEMAND SPECIAL METHODS.

The Rev. B. Percival said that he had always felt that the event should not be entirely dropped, but he agreed that the occasion called for modification of the customary programme, and his own ideas on the matter were in harmony with the scheme the Rector ,had sug- gested. He did not over much care for Sunday processions, but the times were special, and special methods had to be adopted to fit in. He would not like it, however, to be regarded as a precedent that might be . followed on future occasions. He was in favour of having a short service after the procession. They wanted the proceedings to be a demonstration to the people of their earnestness in the matter.

div.head: PAROCHIAL PROCESSIONS PROPOSED.
div.p: PAROCHIAL PROCESSIONS PROPOSED.

The Rev. Davies (vicar of St. Ann's) suggested that each parish should have its own procession —to be confined to the parish. To march round the town in one united Procession would take 'three hours. Arrangements could be made for the scholars of each parish to start at a certain point, and all parts of the town would then be perambulated. He thought there ought to be no ostentation. They wanted the, little ones, as well as the grown-ups, to realise the seriousness of the occasion. After the scholars had marched rouncl their parish, they could go to the church.

div.head: PROBLEMS THAT BESET A PARSON.
div.p: PROBLEMS THAT BESET A PARSON.

The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth remarked that mention had been made of bands and lorries; they did not concern him, as he always took the children of his school away from War- rington for their treat, and got excursion rates. He was told that excursion rates would be allowed on any day except Saturday. If he took his children on Saturday he would have to pay perhaps double. If he did not take the children away, he was faced with the difficulty of finding a suitable field in which they could have their treat at home. Those who made a practice of holding the treat in a field at home were not faced with that problem. He liked the pro- posals that had been made, and he would like to vote for the scheme outlined by the Rector, but there were one or two points on which he had a question to ask: first, would the shops be closed on Saturday afternoon? (A Voice: "No." If not, a good number of their helpers would be unable to join in the proceedings. In the matter of the suggestion that each parish should have its own procession, he differed. His own parish had only two main streets—Lovely-lane and Priestlev-street—and he thought it would be far less dignified to march up one and down the other than to meet altogether on the lawn in the Park. Then, what about the other religious bodies? Were they (the Church of England) going to act separiitely or amalgamate, as in voars gone by, with Nonconformists and Roman Catholics?

div.head: TREATS "AS USUAL?"
div.p: TREATS "AS USUAL?"

Mr. Baskerville contended that there was no reason why each school should not give its children their treat in the usual way. He was connected with the Children's Care Committee, and had had communications from the railway companies stating that, on no day would excur- sion rates be allowed.

The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth asked for the date of Mr. Baskerville's information in the matter of the railway qharges, and the reply was "Last week," whereat the reverend gentleman admitted that the information was later than his own.

div.head: MATTER FOR MASTERS AND MEN.
div.p: A MATTER FOR MASTERS AND MEN.

The Rev. E. C. E. .Carleton said he thought Walking Day might be kept this year without any procession. The matter of whether the men would take the Friday off if that day were to be chosen for the fete day, was a question -Tor the masters and the men to decide between them; the business of the Churches was simply to look after the children, but if they gave up the idea of the procession altogether, the mere fact That the children were having a day in the fields would not draw the men from their work. He did not feel inclined to tie himself to a resolu- tion; it was a serious matter, and only oome- thing very general should be submitted to that meeting.

div.head: WALKING DAY AND "THE HOLIDAY
div.p: WALKING DAY AND "THE HOLIDAY
SPIRIT."

Mr. G. Brown (of the National School) said he had spoken to two employers of labour, and they said that it was impossible to separate the spirit • of Walking. Day from the holiday of the men. The men would assuredly cease work on the Friday, if the children had their Walking Day •as usual. One read that the various shows were being postponed this year. He (the 'speaker) felt very strongly in the matter. He felt that a procession would be very much out of place. He could not allow himself to walk in any procession of the kind with conditions as they were at present. He felt it would be well to abandon the festival altogether this year. The Rev. B. Percival observed that he thought they ought to try and keep things going as usual, or at least something like as usual. The festival ought to be a religious affair. He did not see why the children should have to go without their treat.

Mr. Stansfield- suggested that a general ap- peal might be made to the parents to contri- bute something to the children's tea. War- rington had not been unfavourably affetled by the war, and the majority of the parents could afford to pay sobiething in the direction indi- cated.
OPPORTUNITY FOR CONVEYING A SERIOUS MESSAGE.
The Rev. H. B. Firth submitted that it would be a great opportunity of conveying a very serious message to the people—that it was really a religious' event rather than a proces- sion for show.

The Rector said, in reply to a question as to whether it would be possible to makl the necessary arrangements for the direction of the traffic, that the Mayor had promised to make all necessary arrangements with the police. The procession ought to be a solemn demonstration of earnestness. They could learn from France and Germany the import- ance of taking the war seriously. He was fully persuaded that this nation did not realise the full significance of the task that lay before the Allies. The procession should be made the medium of a solemn appeal to the people to do their duty.

The Rev. Davies contended thai by adopting the method of each parish having its own separate procession more people would see something of the festival than ever before. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton proposed an adjournment for consideration of the sugges- tions made.

div.head: •PURPOSE OF THE MEETING.
div.p: THE •PURPOSE OF THE MEETING.

Mr. Stansfield said that the idea, of assemb- ling together that night was not to get the meeting. to. bind itself to the support of any particular course of action, but to test the feeling and to discuss ways and means so that when they went to the town's meeting they would know their minds. The Rector: We don't settle the matter. It is only for us to pass a resolution and forward it to the Mayor.

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton said that he had been thinking of proposing a resolution to the effect that the clergy and superintendents thought it would be advisable and more appro- priate to have no procession of the scholars while the war was in progress, and that Walk- ing Day would this year be sufficiently kept if each school provided tea and games for its scholars in the usual way. However, he would not move that resolution as the major- ity seemed in favour Of having a procession. The original resolution was carried, on a show of hands.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
" ROLLING-STONE " ROAN LAND.

div.head: Xth entures Of A Three-Florin Watch
div.p: Xth entures Of A Three-Florin Watch
In connection with an alleged theft from the shop of Benedict Tyrer, 100, Buttermarke street,

Rowland George Partridge, an electrician, o 5, St. Mary's-street, Warrington, was brough up on remand before the Borough Bench, on Saturday. He was charged with stealing a lady's silver watch, value 6s. Gd. Prisoner, pleaded that he was under the in- fluence of drink and did not know what he was doing. The Clerk: That's no excuse.
When the Shop Was Unguarded.

The Chief Constable reminded the Bench that prisoner had been remanded from the be- ginning of the week in. order that inquiries might be made in regard to him. At half-past nine on the night of the previous Saturday prisoner went to the shop in question and asked to be shown some boys' metal watches. Mr. Cooper, the assistant, produced for his inspection three watches, which he examined and then asked to be shown something better. Two lady's silver watches were produced, and he looked at those. He decided to buy a watch at 3s. and paid the money. Then he asked to ex- change the watch for a better one. The assist- ant went to the manager to ask whether the exchange could take place, and the manager consented. The exchange took place, and prisoner left the shop. Immediately he had gone the assistant started putting back the wares he had produced for prisoner's inspection. when he found that one of the lady's silver watches was missing. He went after prisoner, but failed to find any trace of him. Detective- Sergeant Summers and Detective Skelton visited prisoner's lodgings on the Sunday, and before they could say anything, he remarked: " Oh, have you come about the watch?" He I admitted he had it, and went upstairs to fetch it. He said he had no intention of stealing it, and took it when under the influence of drink. The shop assistant would have told the Bench, if he had been called on to give evidence, that prisoner was not in drink at all. He knew per- fectly well what he was doing. Defendant said he was very sorry. He had had seine drink. but admitted 'lie was not properly drunk. He had suffered from rheuma- tism end a bad head, and if he had a little drink be didn't realise what he was doing. He would promise to abstain from drink and bad 'com- pany, and make a fresh start in life if he was given a chance to redeem himself.
t. If

div.head: Had Gathered No Moss.
div.p: Had Gathered No Moss.

The Chief Constable stated that inquiries had been made and prisoner was a rolling stone, though he had evidently gathered no moss. He enlisted in the Cheshire Regiment on the 25th of August, at Birkenhead, but was discharged at Chester as medically unfit. He went to a few places and obtained small sums of money from charitably"-disposed persons. He went to see Mr. Spinks (who is in charge of the administration of local war relief) at the Parr Hall, and was given Gs., saying, on that' occasion he was an electrician, and wanted work. Mr. Spinks approached Mr. Mathias, the borough electrical engineer, who promised to give prisoner a job, but prisoner never went for it. He left an address somewhere at Sutton, near Chester. Mr. Spinks wrote to him and finally obtained the 6s. back. Since then prisoner had been travel- ling from place to place by rail, without paying his fare, and getting small sums of money by "telling the tale." He came to Warrington on the 15th March, and the police were unable to find that he had done any work at all since then. He had been convicted several times, but not for some years. The police didn't wish to blacken prisoner's character more than neces- sary, but he (Mr. Nicholls) certainly thought Prisoner ought to be nunished to bring it home to him that he could not do 'as he had been doing with impunity.

div.head: If He Wanted to Go Straight.
div.p: If He Wanted to Go Straight.

Mr. Nicholls finally observed that if prisoner was realfy desirous of leading a straight life afterwards, the Police Court Missionary would give him every assistance. A man did not have to possess many or high qualifications nowadays to get work; it was practically thrown at him. Prisoner said that he had been ill, and that was why he had been unable to do any work. There had been days and days pass without his being able to go out at all.
The Chief Constable: He can explain any- thing away. _He's a master hand at it.
Prisoner': I don't want to explain anything away; T_only want to have another chance.
The Chair-man (Mr. R. T. Fairclou. gh) in pro- nouncing sentence of fourteen days' imprison- ment, said he hoped prisoner would be a better man when he came out.

div.head: TOOK "FRENCH LEAVE." Soldiers Before The Magistrates.
div.p: TOOK "FRENCH LEAVE." Soldiers Before The Magistrates.
THREE TIMES AN ABSENTEE.

That he had been absent without leave since May Ist, from his battery of the Royal Garrison Artillery, was the charge preferred against Gunner John Burgess, at the Warrington Police Court on Monday.—" Right, sir!" he said with a salute, when the magistrates' clerk read the charge over to him.—At 3.15 a.m., so it was stated in evidence, a police constable saw the man coming from the direction of Bank Quay Station to a railway embankment. The officer stopped him and asked him for his pass, where- upon he admitted that he was absent from his regiment without leave. He added that he had travelled from Euston Station, London, without paying his fare. The constable took him to the booking clerk at Bank Quay Station, and then locked him up.—The Chief Constable told the Bench that this was the third time the man had absented himself from his regiment in five weeks.—He was ordered to be handed over to an escort, the Chairman of the Bench (the Mayor) remarking "I hope you will be sent to the Front!" to which the prisoner 4-etorted "Thank you, sir!"

div.head: Hadn't a Pass.
div.p: Hadn't a Pass.

At the same Court, Robert Cunningham admitted being an absentee from the Argyle and Sutherland Highlanders.—The evidence showed that at 3.20 on Monday morning a police officer saw the prisoner on Bank Quay Station and asked him to produce his pass. He said he had not got one, and admitted that he had been absent from his regiment since April 22nd.—He was ordered to be handed over to an.escort.

div.head: Two Dublin Fusiliers Astray.
div.p: Two Dublin Fusiliers Astray.

Two members of the Dublin Fusiliers (4th Battalion)—Jas. O'Donnell and John FaTring- ton—admitted to the Warrington magistrates on Monday that they were absentees, and were ordered to be handed over to the military authorities.—The evidence showed that they should have been back on May Ist. but at 3.20 a.m. on Monday morning a constable saw them at Bank Quay Station, and asked them for their passes, when they said they had lost them. The men were taken into custody, but it required the assistance of three officers to get them to the Police Station.—The men were ordered to the cells pending the arrival of a military escort.

div.head: WEEK-END TOPERS.
div.p: WEEK-END TOPERS.
Batch 01 Men Who "Refreshed" " \of %Visely, But Too %Veil!"

A batch of week-end " drunks " were dis- posed of by the Warrington magistrates on Monday morning, the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) being in the chair and having as his colleagues on the Bench Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton, Bennett, Pierpoint and James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. S. Wright, G. Pilling, A. J. Jolley, W. Roberts, W. Fur- ness, T. Locker and C. Jackson Holmes. Kelly, The Obtuse! •

Being drunk and disorderly on Saturday cost Peter Nly 10s., or, in the alternative. seven days' imprisonment. Detective-Sergeant Reddington said that at 5.15 on the evening of the day in question he went into the Britannia Inn and there saw the prisoner in company with two other men ; indeed, noticing their condition—for all three were drunk—he followed them in and warned the licensee not to serve them. One of them

planked a shilling on the counter and de- manded drinks, but the landlord refused to serve them and put them out. Two of the men went away quietly, but Kelly refused to follow their example, saying that Ile would not budge an inch for witness, or anybody like him. A crowd gathered round and witness was forced to lock the man up. The Chief Constable said there was one pre- vious conviction, for a similar offence, against the man.
