div.head: Wanted to Fight a Woman.
div.p: Wanted to Fight a Woman.

George Harrison, giving an address in Ship- yard, and against whom, the Chief Constable said, there were ten previous convictions—the last being dated 1908; when he went to prison for six months for cruelty to his children— was fined 125., or seven days' imprisonment, for having been drunk and disorderly in Ship- yard on Saturday.—The evidence was that the man, who was very drunk and who made use of filthy language, .was wanting to fight a woman when he was taken into custody. • . Not a 'Sweet Street Singer.

Louis Mellop, a stranger to the town, was fined 7s. 6d./,' or seven days' hard labour, for having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge- street on Saturday.—According to the constable' who arrested him, the man was making his unsteady Way along Bridge-street at 9.5 at night and was jostling people off the footpath and shouting and singing at the top of his voice. He was badly drunk and three times refused to go away when spoken to by the officer.—The Chief Constable said the man was in such a -state that it would really be a charity to fine him 7s. 6d.
Saved in the Nick of Time.

Thomas Cornall, according to a police wit- ness, was so drunk in Sankey-street on Satur- day night that he reeled off the footpath and got clean in the track of a motor car and would have been run over had the witness not pulled him out of the way in the nick of time. He had not got far along the street after his providential escape when he fell full length into the roadway and had to be taken to the lock-up.--He was fined 65., with the alternative of seven days' hard labour.

div.head: Disorderly Lodger.
div.p: A Disorderly Lodger.

At 11.20 p.m. on Saturday, so the evidence ran, John Gaskell had to be ejected from a common lodging-house because he was drunk and would not refrain from quarrelling with another lodger. Before being turned out he was given his "kip money" back. When in the street he proceeded to behave in a most disorderly manner, and, in consequence, was arrested.—He was fined 55., with seven days' imprisonment as the alternative.

div.head: Not Drunk and Not Solver.
div.p: Not Drunk and Not Solver.

"I was not what you could call drunk !" ob- served Frederick Dutton when called -upon to plead to a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Gibson-street at 11.40 on Satur- day night. "If you were not what could be called drunk," queried the Clerk, "were you what could be called sober?"

"No; I wasn't that either !" the prisoner replied, amid laughter, and the Court decided to construe his answer into a plea of 'guilty. The evidence was that the man was shout- ing at the top of his voice, and was, gener- ally, creating a disturbance, being undoubtedly drunk. A police officer tried to persuade him to go indoors quietly, but he would, not take good advice. He was fined 6s. or seven days, these being two previous convictions for "drunkenness against him.
His Mind A Blank.

At 12.10 a.m. on Sunday a policeman found Thomas McDonald, a labourer, lying in a drunken state against a wall in Dallam-lane. Ile was asked what by was doing there at that time, but he did not seem to know where he was, why he was there, or anything about it. As he seemed quite incapable of taking care of himself he was'locked up.—He was fined 65., or seven days' imprisonment.

div.head: BIRCII FOR BAD BOYS.
div.p: BIRCII FOR BAD BOYS.
Quartet Of Youthful Market Thieves.

At a special Children's Court, held after Wed- nesday's Borough Police Court, four boys, aged, respectively, 9, 10, 11 and 12, were charged with being concerned together in stealing thirty-six oranges, the property of Joseph Kitchen, a wholesale fruiterer, parrying on business in Warrington Market. Superintendent Williamson said that on the night of Thursday, April 22nd, Mr. Kitchen sheeted his stall in the market over and put boards round it. When he went to the stall the following morning he found that the sheeting had been cut—damage being done t 9 the cloth to the extent of about 38.—and that from 30 to 40 oranges had been stolen. Detective Green made inquiries, and getting on the track of one of the boy thieves, soon got to know who the others were. All the boys admitted participation in the robbery, one saying that he had twelve

The elder boy, whose home surroundings were not all that could be desired, was a confirmed market thief, and had been caught in the act twice before, once when he had his pocket full of peas, and again when they were stuffed with carrots.

The father of the eldest boy said he was "a good lad "at home, and the parents of the other boys gave their offsprings similar characters, one mother adding that her son had been neglected a bit and had gone a little wild owing to the fact that he had been left without control for ten weeks whilst she had been in hospital. The eldest boy was remanded in order that arrangements may be made for sending him to an industrial school, and the other lads were each ordered six strokes of the birch-rod.

div.head: SOON BACK AGAIN.
div.p: SOON BACK AGAIN.
Fini,(l on MondaS-; Sent to Gaol on Wednesday.

Before Messrs. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), W. T. Williams, IL Thornton and C. Jackson Holmes, Louis YeHop, a diminutive man of the labouring class, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Friars' Green the pre- vious day.

The evidence was to the effect that at 2.15 on Tuesday afternoon the man was seen in Bridge- street in a very drunken state, shouting and singing. Re was cautioned by a policeman, but insisted on going into a confectioner's shop, which he was only persuaded to leave with a great deal of difficulty. He next went into a public-house, from which he had to be ejected. Supt. Williamson said the man was before the Court on Monday, and was then fined 7s. 60. When brought into the Police Station on Tues- day he was in a hopeless state of drunkenness, although it was only just after two o'clock in the afternoon.
The man was ordered 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour.

div.head: CRUELTY TO A DOG.
div.p: CRUELTY TO A DOG.
Struck It With A "Lead" And "Nearly
Closed Its Eye lip."

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday, before Messrs. A. J. Jolley (in the ;lair), W. Roberts and W. T. Williams, and Dr. Naden, William Charnock, of 25, Langdin-street, was fined ss. and ss. costs (representing two wit- nesses' fees 'at 2s. 6d each) for cruelly beating a dog on April 23rd.—He pleaded "guilty, but, with no intention of damaging the dog." The evidence was to the effect that the defendant was seen to hit the dog with a dc.g- lead, which had a piece of metal at the end of it, catching the animal "across the eye and cutting it." "He nearly closed the dog's eye up, and it was bleeding." To a brother of the owner he expressed himself as "very sorry if hea'had done anything," but whilst so expressing his sorrow, said the brother in giving evidence, "another little dog came up and he hit that one also."
Defendant's excuse was that a number of dogs got round his legs—because he was walking with a pup of his own—and he struck at them with- out any intention of damaging either of them.

MARKET AND SHOPS.
Demand For Conditions To Allow Of Early Closing.

Mr. E. Thomas, local secretary of the National Union of Shop Assistants, Warehousemen and Clerks, 141, Cumberland-street, sends us the fol- lowing copy of a letter he has sent to the Mayor and Chief' Constable of Warrington, also Col. Moggridge, commanding the district, re the earlier closing of shops on Saturday nights. "Anticipating a meeting of shopkeepers being called by the Shops Committee appointed by Earl Kitchener on the question of releasing Men of military age in the distributing trade for service with the forces, may, we suggest that the Market stallholders and Markets Committee be asked to attend at the same time to try and arrange an earlier closing of shops throughout the town on Saturday nights? It is a well- known fact that the open market of this town is the present cause of the late closing of shops. Shopkeepers, having to pay more than the stall- holders for rates, taxes and lighting, naturally do not like to close their establishments earlier than the Markets. By doing so they would be sending their customers from the shops to the -Markets.

div.head: KENDAL
div.p: KENDAL
Ten O'clock Late Enough.
"We know for a fact that the majority of shop proprietors would willingly close their premises at 10 o'clock if the Market Committee would decide and enforce the closing of the Market at this hour.

"Hotels and public-houses now being closed at 10 p.m., the majority Of customers served at the shops' and stalls after this hour must have left their purchasing of the necessities of life until they could no longer obtain drink. At any rate, that is the impression they give the shop assistant.

"The earlier closing of shops would be a great boon to the female assistants now taking the place of the males, who are doing their bit for King and country, also for the assistants who are working short-handed for the same reason, several of whom have been refused by the Army doctors owing to illness, &c., caused through working such abnormal long hours and confinement in stuffy shops. It would also give our brave lads something to look forward to on their return to civil life.

"Surely 10 p.m. is late enough for everybody. Even this hour means a 14-hour day for the assistants, who commence duties at S a.m. "At a meeting of the Union of Shop Assist- ants I was instructed to write to you requesting your support in the above movement.—Tours faithfully, E. Thomas."

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAX 8, 1915.

div.head: DUST.
div.p: DUST.

There are many kinds of dust, from the metaphorical kinds that are said to be thrown into people's eyes to deceive their mental vision, to the literal dust, of which we mor- tals are all composed. Few people, however, can have any idea of the large varieties of dust, their causes and their uses, that exist between these two extremes. Most of them are passed in review in an entertaining and apparently exhaustive article which appeared in the April number of "' Knowledge," from the pen of Mr. WILLIAM SWAINE, of 62, Liver- pool-road, an old Warrington Secondary School boy, who is now a student at Man- chester University. Now that the event is passed, and the object in view achieved, Mr. SWAINE may forgive us if we mention that it was he who inspired by means of letters to the Editor, the plea of "The Examiner" nearly two years ago for the institution of local municipal scholarships to the Univer- sities, so that the brains of brilliant but poor scholars might not be wasted. The plea was so well justified that the public scholarships were founded by the Education Committee, and one is already in active operation. It does not often happen that one is able to do a permanent piece of good work for the com- munity -so early in life as Mr. SWAINE was thus able to do.

His article on dust gives high promise of future progress along both scientific and literary channels. It deals with dust on the roads and on the ocean, harmless and even fattening dust, and harmful and poisonous dust. The dangers of coal dust and of flour dust—which is even more explosive--are treated with the help of such authorities as TYNDALL, WATT, CUTLER and LODGE. Chemical dust, mill dust, atmospheric pollution arising from the emissions 'of chimneys, volcanic dust, .cosmic dust—the disintegration of meteorites—and their effects upon the air, are all dealt with in detail, but we must refer our readers to the original article for fuller satisfaction.

"And what would our world appear like if there were no duszt ?" asks the writer. "Very probably the sky would not have its delicate blue colour, but would be black with the sun glaring down on the earth without any (jiff u- sion, whilst the stars would be visible during both day and night; and no gloriously tinted sunrise or sunset for the poet or man of science to contemplate. On the other hand, no smoky towns, no dusty highways or furni- ture, and no fog. But which dusts cause the aztstbetic results? Chiefly the volcanic and cosmic—those which we cannot help. And which dust is it that causes us so much an- noyance, and which is so familiar? That which we can'help, by altering our roads or locomotion, our domestic fires and our fac- tories. However, such is the progress of civilisation, and truly God made the coun- try and man made the town.' "

div.head: ADULTERATION DECREASINC.
div.p: ADULTERATION DECREASINC.

Dr. JOSEPH complimented the shopkeepers and congratulated the town, at the Council meeting on Tuesday night, upon the fact that the analyst's annual report showed that the adulteration of food locally had practically disappeared. He figuratively patted trades- men on the back as an encouragement for them to continue in the straight path of hon- esty which means not only full value to pur- chasers, but uninjured health for the com- munity. The great bulk of tradesmen peed no supervision, threatening or coaxing; it is here, as in so many walks of life, that a very small minority do the mischief. Much of the adulteration is unintentional, too, for, as Dr. JOSEPH specially pointed out, following the explanation of a year ago that coffee might be so largely charged with chicory as to turn what is a tonic and a nourishing beverage into a depressant and dangerous drink, par-
ticularly for people with heart trouble, the adulteration of coffee has, this year, reached the negligible stage..

div.head: HOUSING QUESTION.
div.p: THE HOUSING QUESTION.

A curiously irregular, though interesting discussion took place on Tuesday evening at the Town Council on the question of the hous- ing of the working classes. The Street Im- provement Committee recommended that five of its members be appointed a deputation to attend a Town Planning Conference to be held in Liverpool next Wednesday and Thursday. One would have thought that the question to be decided was as to the suitability of the gentlemen selected, but, on the point whether it was worth while sending representatives to conferences that meet and meet and leave the shortage of houses more pronounced than ever, much wider ground was covered. The contention was as irrelevant as the discussion was out of order, unless it was seriously held that it was not worth spending five fares to Liverpool to learn what the rest of the coun- try is thinking upon housing and town plan- ning problems. It would be a poor compli- ment to our experts in local government to put so low a price upon their collective wis- dom. Alderman BENNtrr stated what most people will regard as an elemental fact that ' the appalling state into which our house accommodation has got, pr will very soon get, is a strong reason why we should join hands with those who are endeavouring, even by means of the much-derided conference, to find a solution and apply a remedy. The MAYOR tried to keep the Council to the question on the agenda, but the debate got so far astray las Alderman BENNETT'S suggestion that local rates should be abolished and a municipal income tax set up to take their place. Coun- cillor PEMBERTON laid emphasis on the fact that whereas we used to have an average of 400 or 500 empty houses in Warrington, it is , DOW impossible, as Councillor BROADHURST put it, for a working man to get a house for love or money. Builders have stopped build- ing; but some owners have not stopped rais- ing their rents, in many cases unfairly and to a degree far in excess of the amount justified by the rise in the rates. All these questions were nicely woven around the subject of the appointment of a deputation; and it was understood that these gentlemen, who were duly appointed, would receive instruction from the committee as to the course they must adopt when at.the Liverpool gathering.

div.head: RATAN TATA.
div.p: RATAN TATA.

We have recently published several articles ' dealing with the social conditions of the people, with special reference to Warrington, but the war has effectually killed all interest in questions dealing with the ordinary affairs of life. Ordinarily the revelations contained in the book "Livelihood and Poverty," issued by the Ratan Tata Foundation, and re- viewed by us, would have made. a sensation at least for a few days, but the only interest, so far as we can discover, aroused now has been with regard to the curiously named foundation under which the information was given to the public. Who, what, or why is Ratan Tata? That is the question, rather than how can a large proportion of our fel- lows be put in the way .of decent living. Ratan Tata is the name of a wealthy Indian gentleman who set aside a large sum of money to be used in inquiring into the causes of poverty; and the resulting " foundation " is under the direction of PROFESSOR 11013110IISE, PROFESSOR lIRWIPK, Mr. TAWNEY, and others, and is worked through the London School of Economics. Already several very useful in- quiries have been made into the particular aspects of poverty regarding such questions as the feeding of school children and the 'practical working of the Trade Boards Act. The results are published in handy form at reasonable prices. The latest publication of the foundation deals with the result of in- quiries in four English towns, of which War- ringtori is one. Social reformers will find it useful to store for the time when the town is ready to listen to them.

div.head: HOUSE COAL BILL.
div.p: THE HOUSE COAL BILL.

From comments which we have received this week we gather that we cannot be far wrong if we estimate 2cwt. per household as the weekly minimum consumption of coal where one fire only is used. The average amount of coal actually burned in the work- ing Than's home would probably be well over 2cwt., especially in winter time. With very careful stoking, and a judicious mixture of coke and slack, less than 2cwt. will suffice, but it may be affirmed with cer- tainty that an allowance of lewt. per house- hold is insufficient, and that apparently is about the allowance made in the Ratan Tata Inquiry. It is questionable if the size of open grates is often permanently reduced by the intro- duction of fire bricks in the home of the wort-- ing man. Probably the middle classes have done more to reduce their coal bills during recent years when they have introduced modern grates. The manufacturers make con- sideiable claims to coal economies. Are these claims justified, and if so, are the wage- earners reaping any benefit from newer de- signs in fire grates? Now that the more genial days are upon us, it ought to be possible to discover the actual difference between the coal bills of summer and winter.

div.head: ST. ELPHIN'S PARK.
div.p: ST. ELPHIN'S PARK.

Councillor CRAIK put into concrete form a question that has been exercising the minds of a large number of the residents of Fair- field for some time. The strip of ground, for which we paid 23,000, and upon which we have spent a substantial sum of money, is still closed to the public—except for the bowling green end. The paths have been made, but left in a rough cindered condition; and the gates remain closed. A choice col- lection of tulips are blooming gaily, and the grass in the little bark is of the greenest, but those are reasons which only aggravate the case of the men and women who are longing to make use of the grounds. Councillor CRAIK asked for information as to the probable date of opening, but was told by the MAYOR that he must give notice of such a question, as it was not on the agenda. "No, and the park isn't opened either," said the Councillor, amid laughter. Councillor CRAIK was in a difficult position. At the annual meeting of the Council he was wrongly removed from several important corn-

mittee,s, and, as a protest against the injus- tice, he resigned from all the other com- mittees. He, therefore, knoWs nothing of what the committees are doing. If he wishes to ask for information at the Council meet- ing he must give five days' notice of his intention to do so; and as the agenda is printed five days before the Council meet, Councillor CRAIK wants to know where he is. It appears to us that notice is not required for such a simple question as that put by Coun- cillor CRAIK, as it does not involve the collec- tion of statistics or anything of that kind. In any case, a large portion of the towns- people would like the information Councillor CRAIK desired, and think they are entitled to it without going through the formality of sending notice to the Chairman of the Parks Committee. They have paid for the park, and they would like to see it unlocked.

div.head: VACANT CHAIR.
div.p: THE VACANT CHAIR.

When Alderman BOLTON rose at the Town Council meeting on Tuesday night to move the adoption of the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, of which he is chairman, a cheer went round the room. The worthy Alderman has, for a long time left his chair in the Council Chamber vacant—the Council have met, but missed him, for months. He did not quite understand the demonstra- tive welcome, but Councillor PEMBERTON ex- plained the situation by facetiously moving a vote of thanks to Alderman BOLTON "for being present to-night." This was not seconded; like Councillor CRAIK'S question, it was not on the agenda.

div.head: OUR UNIQUE BRIDGE.
div.p: OUR UNIQUE BRIDGE.

Alderman SMETHURST, chairman of the Bridges Committee, who has been fortunate enough to steer the bridge scheme to a final and successful conclusion, was able to report on Tuesday night that the total cost of the bridge, now completed, was t.. 19,962 19s. 10d. The original contract was £14,310, but before a start was made the conditions were so varied that the estimated price became to begin with £16,02; and thenceforward the original con- , tract really stood in abeyance. Other im- provements have been added from time to time, always with the consent of the Council, which has brought up the total to the sum at which it now, finally stands. No one will say that £20,000 is an excessive charge for a bridge that will be the finest in the pro- vinces and will have few to equal it in Lon- don. There have been many wild statements as to the ultimate cost of the bridge, some of them going to the extent of saying that it would be £30,000 or £40,000. To briitg the figure to anything like this amount every ex- penditure on or around the bridge had to bd pressed into service—but it is scarcely fair to tick on to the contract for building the bridge the cost of, say, laying car tracks and gas, water and electric mains across the river. We now know that the cost is just under £20,000, and, if all goes well, Warrington may, we think, congratulate itself upon being the possessor of a remarkably fine bridge, as well as upon having got full return for the money spent upon it. To Alderman SMETHURST the town owes a deep debt of gratitude. He has been largely instrumental in giving us this fine structure, which will in future share with the Parish Church—and the smoke—the privilege of giving Warrington its distinguishing features. It was the Alderman's own suggestion that resulted in altering the line of the bridge some 16ft. or 18ft. from the Stockton Heath side to the Latchford side, a decided improve- ment which was readily adopted by the authorities. As a set-off to the extra ex- penditure upon training walls we have re- claimed land from the river at all the four corners of the bridge, amounting to 810 square yards. This reclaimed land will be "laid out," and so allow us to see the bridge to the best advantage.

There was a nasty scene during the discus- sion, in which Councillors PEMBERTON, GOUGE, and ROBERTS took part. Readers will find a full report in another column of this most remarkable incident on an occasion which was meant to be one for self-congratulation upon the completion of one of the most important works ever undertaken by the Council.

div.head: TYPEWRITING EXTRAORDINARY.
div.p: TYPEWRITING EXTRAORDINARY.
993 Words a Minute.

At Wood's College, Bold-street, on Wednes- day evening, Miss Millicent Woodward, a former pupil of Mr. Wood, and now the cham- pion typist of the Unithd Kingdom, winner of the non-professional championship cup and the first lady operator in the pro- fessional contest, gold medalist and Underwood team cup winner, gave a demonstration of about a hour and a half's duration with some remarkable results. Mr. Thos. W. Ward, of the Pearson and Knowles' Coal and Iron Co. Engineering Department was in charge of the examination. All mistakes in the typing were deducted; the figures given being the number of words accurately written in the times stated. Miss Woodward's record for the evening was

One minute, copying from manuscript, mini- mum, 99 words; maximum, 119. One minute, from dictation, minimum, 98; maximum, 124. One minute, memorised matter, 223. Three minutes, copying from manuscript, 345 words, average 115 per minute. Commercial letter from dictation, 145 words, set out in paragraphs with figures and quota- tion marks, one minute, twenty-five seconds. Miss Woodward, at the request of the Editor of "The Examiner" (who checked the times) wrote a verse of poetry from memory at 112 words the minute.

The memorised test, in which the speed of 223 words was -attained, consisted of small words, but they were set out and spaced perfectly, and it was found that the operator had struck a key or space bar 667 times, depressed the shift-key for capitals eleven times, and pushed back the cvriage eleven times, so that she had done 689 separate acts with her fingers in one minute, or between eleven and twelve per second. At the end of the contest Miss Woodward copied a long passage at a high rate while Mr. Wood carried on a conversation with her, and the specimen came through without mistake. Miss Woodward's was a very fine performance, and the large company were very sincere in the vote of thanks which, at the close, they accorded her for the really brilliant manner in which she had entertained them.

div.head: Accident at Padgate Station.
div.p: Accident at Padgate Station.

A serious accident occurred on the Cheshire Lines Railway at Padgate Station on Wednes- day morning. When the 10.4 train was leaving the. station for Warrington an elderly lady— Errs. Betsy Crosby, of The Lodge, Fearnhead, aged 67—attempted to board the train whilst it was in motion, but unfortunately slipped and fell between the moving train and the platform. The driver immediately applied the brake and brought the train to a stand- still. Dr. Bennett was summoned immediately, and after an examination ordered the lady's removal to the Warrington Infirmary, where she is detained, suffering from severe injuries.

div.head: LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
The Leather Trade.
Generally speaking, the variation in the leather trade in this district last week was very small, but, as regards inquiries, and new business, it was a case of Army goods first, and the rest nowhere.

div.head: Red Flowers for the Aliar.
div.p: Red Flowers for the Aliar.

"Red (signifying the Pentecostal fire) is the liturgical colour for this season," says the Vicar of St. James', Latchford, in his Parish Maga- zine, "and so red flowers—though white ones are not out of place—are particularly appro- priate."

div.head: Late Mrs. Madeley.
div.p: The Late Mrs. Madeley.

Alderman Bennett, at Tuesday evening's meeting of the Town Council, referred to the loss sustained by the Chief Librarian (Mr. Madeley) in the death of his wife, and voiced the Council's condolency with him.

div.head: " Scarlet " and Diphtheria.
div.p: " Scarlet " and Diphtheria.

Last week the births in Warrington num- bered 34, and the deaths 25, twelve of the lat- ter being of persons over 65 years of age. Scarlet fever, of which disease there were 70 cases in hospital, accounted far seven deaths. There were six cases of diphtheria.

div.head: War-Dela3-ed Mission.
div.p: War-Dela3-ed Mission.

Owing to the shortage of labour caused by the war, the work on the new St. Hilda's Mission Church has not been able to be completed as soon as was expected. "However," says the Vicar of St. James' in the current issue of his Parish Magazine, "we cannot control such circumstances, and we hope that in a very short time the structure will be finished. Notice of the opening will be given at the earliest pos- sible moment."

div.head: Grocer's Failure.
div.p: Grocer's Failure.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court on Friday morning, Thomas O'Day, who formerly carried on business as a grocer, in Gorsey-lane, Warrington, appeared for his public examina- tion, being legally represented by Mr. A. Browne. His total liabilities amounted to about £2OO, and ,the examination was closed by Mr. Registrar Ridgway, subject to the CflM- pletion of the usual formalities.

div.head: Wheat Getting Scarce.
div.p: Wheat Getting Scarce.

Wheat remained firm at late prices on War- rington market on Wednesday, Bs. 4d. to Bs. 7d. per 701 b. being fetched. Supplies are getting scarce. Oats hardened on the week. 4s. 6d. to 4s. 71d. being offered. Straw was better and sold at from 355. to 375. 6d. per ton. Clover hay realised £4 15s. per ton, and meadow hay £4 ss. XX. flour fetched 495. 6d. per 2801 b., and best bran is. 51d. per 201 b. Eggs sold at 10 for a shilling.

div.head: Star Kinema.
div.p: Star Kinema.

One of the latest and funniest, not to mention one of the costliest films ever shown in War- rington, has been booked as the big attraction at the Star Kinema for the first three days of next week. The central character in it is taken by Charles Chaplin, whose fame as a cinema comedian is world-wide. The title of the film in question is " Tilly's Punctured Romance," and the blithesome story occupies five reels in the unfolding, and is said to be a "screamer." At the week-end patrons of this highly popular picture house are tu be given another rich treat .in the shape of a filmed version of Sir James M. Barrie's brilliant story, "The Little Minis- ter."

div.head: Latchford Baptist Sunday School.
div.p: Latchford Baptist Sunday School.

The Sunday school anniversary services in connection with the Latchford Baptist SI nday School were held on Sunday. The preacher for the day was Mr. A. E. Hoyle. In the afternoon a musical cantata was excellently rendered by the Sunday school and church joint choirs, under the leadership of Mr. F. W. Grounds. Solos, duets, &c., were given by the following: Mrs. J. Fairhurst, Mrs. J. Conway, Mrs. P. Grice, Miss D. Rigby, Miss H. Richardson, Miss P. Wootton, Mr. I. Wilkinson, Mr. J. Conway and Mr. P. Grice. The chair was taken by Mr. S. Albinson (the superintendent cf rite school) and Mr. W. T. Wilkinson, jun. , pr-sided at the piano. The collections for the day amounted to £8 Bs.

Motor Cyclist and Pedestrian.' A nasty accident occurred in Church-street at about 10.15 on Tuesday night, the victims being a motor cyclist and a pedestrian. The cyclist was Mr. Albert Hcrward, a metal broker, of Ivydene, Padgate-lane, and he was motoring home, when he collided with Robert Crook, a wiredrawer, of 2, Gold-street, who was in the act of crossing the road at the time. Mr. Howard was thrown from his machine and fractured his nose, whilst Crook was knocked down and rendered unconscious, in addition to receiving several cuts and bad bruises. P.C. McKenzie was soon on the scene and superin- tended the removal to the Infirmary of both men, who were promptly attended to by the home surgeon. Mr. Howard was detained, but Crook left after he had recovered consciousness and his hurts had been dressed.

div.head: Welsh Chapel Anniversary,
div.p: Welsh Chapel Anniversary,

Good attendances marked the anniversary services held on Saturday evening and Sunday, in connection with the Welsh Chapel. On Saturday evening, when the service was in Welsh, the preacher was the Rev. T. J. Row- lands, of Birkenhead. The Rev. W. Wynn Davies, of Rhos, who is well-known in War- rington owing to the prominent part he took in the eisteddfod formerly held in the Parr Hall, preached on Sunday, while at an English service held in the afternoon he gave a very interesting address, taking for his text "For Christ's. Sake." In the course of the address he welcomed the English friends present, and thanked thOm for their support.

div.head: Councillor Broadhurst ReMIMS From
div.p: Councillor Broadhurst ReMIMS From
a ,Committee.

The minutes of the Borough Gymnasium Committee, submitted to the Town Council at their meeting on Tuesday evening, contained the following :—"lt was resolved that the re- signation of Councillor Broadhurst as a mem- ber of ,the committee be accepted with regret, and that the best thanks of the committee be given to him for his services as their chair- man."—ln moving the passing of the minute, Alderman Tinnion said that the committee were losing a very efficient Chairman and a painstaking member, and all his colleagues on the committee regretted that he could not see his way to continue to find time for the wolk. —Councillor Dickenson seconded, and it was carried, Councillor Broadhurst briefly acknow- ledging the compliment paid him by Alderman Tinnion, and remarking that he thought it better to leave the post to a man who had more interest in sport; be, personally, being more accustomed to work.—Councillor Osborne has been appointed chairman of the committee in succession to. Councillor Broadhurst. /

div.head: Hold-Ups at the Wilderspool Railway
div.p: Hold-Ups at the Wilderspool Railway
Crossing.

At Tuesday evening's meeting of the Town Council, Councillor Hawthorn drew attention to a minute by the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee to the effect that complaint had been made to them of the delay caused at the Wilderspool railway crossing, and that they had given instructions that the attention of the London -and North-Western Railway Com- pany be called to the matter.—Councillor Hawthorn hoped that the matter would not merely 'end in the reception of the usual stereotyped reply from the company, but that it would receive serious attention. Lately the delays had been more frequent than usual owing to the abnormal length of some of the trains. When the engines were pulled up to take in water they were frequently so long that the rear portion of them extended over the crossing.—Councillor Pemberton suggested that one way out of the difficulty would be to remove the water standard further from the crossing so that the longer trains now in use could be drawn up without incommoding the public.—The Deputy-Mayor (Dr. Joseph) thought the best sway out of the difficulty would be to erect a bridge over the crossing.— The committee's minute was adopted.

Star Kinema's Help In A Good Cause. The recent matinee performance given at the Star Kinema in aid of the funds of the newly opened Auxiliary Military Hospital at Thel- wall Reyes realised the excellent tOtal of £l5 Is. Bd.

div.head: Served on the " Lusitania."
div.p: Served on the " Lusitania."

Mr. William Harding, of 21, St. Aiary-street. Latchford, was for two years a member of the crew of the ill-fated " Lusitania." He was transferred quite recently, however, to another boat belonging to the same owners.

div.head: War Causes Dearer Funerals.
div.p: War Causes Dearer Funerals.

Owing to the increased cost of horse-keeP, consequent upon the war, the Warrington Coach Proprietors' Association announce that they have been compelled to revise and slightly increase the charges for hiring funeral equip. ages, as from May 15th.

div.head: Cuckoo.
div.p: The Cuckoo.

The cuckoo has been heard frequently during the past week in the neighbourhood of the Cemetery. Those who experienced the delights of a walk in Cheshire last Sunday heard the welcome call from the Dingle. Swallows, too, had arrived in large numbers and formed one of the features in a very fair scene.

div.head: New Catholic Schools' Manager.
div.p: New Catholic Schools' Manager.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council, Mr. John Eckersley was, on the proposition of Councillor Roberts, seconded by Councillor Wilkinson, appointed a representa- tive manager of the St. Alban's, St. Benedict 's and St. Mary's Roman Catholic Schools.
Successes of Secondary School Pupils.

_ The Civil Service Commissioners have insti- tuted a new examination for clerkships to Surveyors of Income Tax and an examination for 390 vacancies has recently been held. In this examination three pupils of the Secondari School have been successful, viz., John B. KO (7th place on the list), Alfred T. Farrar (191st) and William C. Cookson (351st).
St. John's Sunday School Anniversary

As will be seen from our advertisement columns, the Sunday school anniversary ser- vices will be held at St. John's to-morrovi, when the preacher will be the Rev. Richard Downes, of Newcastle-on-Tyne. Special music will be rendered by the choir and Sunda)" school children at each service.

div.head: More Refugees Coming.
div.p: More Refugees Coming.

The local committee of the Warrington War Refugees' Fund are expecting a further parti of Belgian Refugeesi next week, and solicit gift! of clothing for men, women and children. Sim° gifts will be gratefully received at St. Austin 0, Bold-street.

div.head: Padgate Anniversary.
div.p: A Padgate Anniversary.

To-morrow special anniversary services are to be held in connection with the Wesley Sunday School-, Padgate, the Rev. Raby having promised to preach both in th,e morning and the evening and to give an ad dress at a flower service in the afternoon, when Dr. Bennett will preside.

div.head: Deserving Cause.
div.p: A Deserving Cause.

During next week a house-to-house collection, will be made in the town on behalf of the National Children's Home and Orphanag'e, which at present shelters and cares for no fevrer, than 2,250 children. The Home has receive many motherless children of reservists, is shel° tering Belgian Refugee children, and is P_Te" pared to receive the orphan children of soldiers and sailors who may fall in battle. div.head: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
div.p: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
PRIVATE PERCY BIBBY.
Fatal Shell-Wound.

The news that Private Percy Bibby—signallei; F Company, 4th South Lancashires, and the youngest son of Mrs. M. J. Bibby, of 15, Mill- street—had died at the Front from wounds, first came to his native town in a letter from Sergeant J. Stout. This ran :- 1 t is with very much regret that I have to write to inform you of your son's death. I have no doubt that his officer will also write you; but I feel it my duty as signalling ser- geant, and being in charge of the section of which Percy was a member, to offer you my greatest sympathy in your great loss. Percy had been sent out with a message by the Sergeant-Major to A Company, and
just as he Was about to reach their billets a

Shell came over and burst quite close to him, and a piece entered his thigh. We all thought at the time it was not serious, but I have just had the sad news conveyed to me that he died at five minutes past four yesterday (Wednes- day) morning. He was wounded on Tuesday evening about 6.30, and was taken straight to the hospital. I shall miss him very much, as

he was one of my best and most obedient lads. As I have no doubt you know when the Battalion went into the trenches Percy went in along with them to do duty as telephone operator; and when we were out of the trenches he acted as cyclist-orderly for the orderly room. It was while carrying out this part of his duty that he Met his death. You have a•great consolation in knowing that he died an honourable death whilst doing his duty for his King and country. The whole of the signalling section unite together, one and all, in sending you their greatest sympathy— as they all feel they have lost a good comrade and friend. Please accept the same from me. On April 30th (in a letter pissed by Colonel B. Fairelough) and signed "C. H. Mairs," to Miss A. Bunting, of St. Albans, it says: "Further to my letter of the 2,Bth, informing you that your nephew had been wounded, It is with my deepest sympathy that I now inform you that Percy has died, on the 28th, about 4.30 a.m. I-need not add how the news of his death affected me, as we had been pals since mobilisation. He was held in the highest esteem by the whole section, and was one of the most popular. . . . From his pal—Private Patrick Tiernane, of machine gun section—the following letter was recently received "April 28th. Sorry I have to write and tell you that your brother, Private Percyo Bibby, signaller, was wounded on Tues- day, April 27th. I was in the [base] hospital when he was brought in, and he gave me your address to write to you. His wounds are not serious, and you must not worry about him; he will be well looked after. His wounds were caused by shrapnel shell, sent by the Germans into the village where Private Bibby, along with his battalion, were having a rest after a long spell in the trenches. "He has a wound in the flesh on the left leg, and a slight one on the right hip. He suffered great pain at first, until he was dressed; but after that he told me he felt a little ease. He will, perhaps, be sent home shortly. We are all very sorry for him, and hope he will soon be well again. "He also told me to write to his mother— which I did immediately—and to his aunt. He said he would write himself in a few days. So when you hear from him please let me know how he is getting on; I shall be anxious to know, as he was such a nice chap. . . . I can assure you his wounds are not dangerous— as I saw them, and waited. with him until he was dressed. So don't worry !" This letter was passed by L. S. Henshall. At the same time Private Arthur Barker wrote: "Your son Percy . . . was wounded last night (27th). . . . We were all in the billet when a terrible shell came; and your son, along with two more, was hit—one being killed instantly. We all rushed out and three others with myself carried Percy to the hos- pital. . . . I shall never forget. It wa.l awful; shells were bursting round us while we carried him. . . ." Mrs. Bibby has received a kind letter of sym- pathy from the Mayor.
PRIVATE PERCY BIBBY.

div.head: SUNK.
div.p: SUNK.
The Latest German Infamy.
The Cunard liner " Lusitania " was tor- pedoed and sunk off the old head of Kinsale, eight miles out. The fate of 1,000 passengers and 900 crew was unknown last night.
A telephone message announced the landing of 300 passengers at Clonakilty. An unofficial message from Liverpool received as we go to press states that the whole of the passengers have been saved.

where Lce-Corpl. Knowles was standing, and a fragment of it struck hirg in the leg. His wound is severe, but I have every hope that your husband will recover, and that it will not be very long before he is back in England to con- valescence. I cannot tell you how grieved lam to send you this news, which I know will dis- tress you. Lance-Corporal Knowles has done so splendidly for the battalion since I came abroad that it is particularly unfortunate that he should now be numbered amongst the wounded. I shall miss him greatly. He has been of enormous assistance to me; and I shall have the greatest difficulty in finding a man to replace him. You have every reason to be very proud of him. He has been brave to a degree, which has gained him admiration from all; and to the wounded and sick he has been kindness itself. It is some consolation to you to know that he has received his wound whilst ozloing his duty, fearlessly. It is my most sincere hope that he will soon recover."

Operated Upon. Mrs. Knowles received a further letter on Mon- day from an Army Scripture Reader with the 11th General Hospital, Boulogne-sur-Mer, in which he stated that Lance-Corporal Knowles had undergone an operation.

Since going to the Front, Lance-Corporal Knowles has been acting as medical orderly to Lieutenant-Surgeon Law. Two years ago, Lance-Corporal Knowles rescued two children from a burning house at Latchford. for which gallant act he was publicly thankdd, and pre- sented with a certificate and medal.

A second letter, evidently written by a nurse, on behalf of the injured man, and bearing the date April 29th, ran : "I shall be coming home shortly, and will stay for good. I have been under an operation and have had my left leg taken off below the knee. Don't worry about me, I am going on as well as can be expected." Going for a Stretcher when it Happened. ; subsequent letter, written by Private Peacock himself, has been received, and in it he says:—

- "I write these few lines to lot you all know that I am improving fine, and expect to get to England before long. We had just come out of the trenches for a rest after six days in the firing line. Last Monday night they started shelling us and this is what they made of me! I was going for i stretcher for one of our lads, who had got badly hit, when they sent a shell and knocked me down, The Education Officer (Lance-Corporal Knowles) also got hit the same day." Private Peacock now lies in No. 2 Stationary Hospital at the base.

div.head: Keen Angler.
div.p: A Keen Angler.

Private Peacock, who is 20 years of age, was formerly employed in the warehouse at Messrs. Crosfield's. He was educated at Holy Trinity School, and for two years he attended an evening school. In politics he is a Liberal. He was a keen angler, spending much of his spare time engaT(ed in that sport. He joined the Terri- torials four years ago, and at the outbreak of war volunteered for active service and was drafted to Tunbridge Wells, where he under- went his war training, and from where he was drafted to the Front on February 16th.

div.head: War Service for Women.
div.p: War Service for Women.

The scheme by which women may be able to render valuable service to the country in the present troublous times is to be explained at a public meeting to be held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening next. The Mayor (Alder- man Peter Peacock) has consented to preside, and the gathering will be addressed by a num- ber of prominent speakers.

div.head: INFANTRYMEN WANTED
div.p: INFANTRYMEN WANTED
Writes Home That He Is "Lucky To Enlistments For Other Branches To Be Be Living." Curtailed.

News came to hand on Saturday that Private Joseph Howard, of the Warrington Terri- torials, who resides, in normal times, with his married brother, Mr. William Howard, at 18, Oxford-street, Latchford, had been wounded. "Stray Bullet" From Sniper.
The first notification came on a postcard, and was written for the injured man by a friend. The Card was dated 28th April. The message read as follows:
" This evening about eleven o'clock we were

trench-digging, and a stray bullet came from one of the snipers and caught me at the top of my left leg. The injury is nothing serious. I am feeling quite well in health. Don't get upset; I assure you I am quite lucky. Will write again shortly. Expect to be home soon."

A second postcard arrived on Monday, stat- ing that Private Howard was in hospital and doing well; and a third was received later in the day from a comrade named Jack Gannon, who wrote to say that Private Howard and Private Jack Smith, who was injured at the same time, were not dangerously wounded.

Men are still needed, not in thtir hundreds, but in their thousands, if the victory is to come speedily and to be of the decisive character that should crown the unparalleled outpour- ing of blood and treasure that has been going on this last nine months.

This week the local recruiting authorities make an earnest appeal to those of arm-bearing age and of the requisite degree of physical fit- ness to come forward and help in the achieve- ment of the glorious victory which must follow if the integrity of the great British Empire is to be preserved.

div.head: Shot Through The Groin.
div.p: Shot Through The Groin.

Yet a fourth communication reached 18, Oxford-street later in the week, in the shape of a letter from Private Howard to his brother. We quote from the missive :—" My turn Itas come at last. Our company were out trench- digging last Wednesday night, April 28th. We were digging a firing-trench three feet wide and three feet deep. I had only just commenced when I was caught by some sniper. The bullet has gone right through my left groin. It caught a bone and glanced off, coming out at the back. . . . . By the time you get this I shall be in England. .. . They tell me lam lucky to be living. The sisters out here look after us fins. I sail to-morrow (Sunday). I am writing this on my back, the best way I can.",
A Prize Winning Bowler.

Private Howard, who is a-brother of the well- known ex-Widnes half-back, joined the Terri- torials shortly after the outbreak of war. As a boy he a ttendPd the Silver-street School, and on leaving there he entered the service of Messrs.

div.head: MEN MOST NEEDED.
div.p: THE MEN MOST NEEDED.

Recruits are most needed for infantry regi- Iments ; indeed, with certain exceptions, enlist- ment will only be allowed for infantry of the line hnd not for other branches of the service. This regulation arises out of the present heavy demand for reinforcements for the infantry. Exception will be made in connection with certain locally-raised units and also in respect of artificer soldiers, for whom there are vacancies in such branches as the Engineers and the Artillery. Telegraphists and telephonists and smiths, ecc. may be enlisted in the Royal Engineers.

No men swill be accepted for direct enlistment i 4 cavalry of the line, the R.A.M.C: or the Army Veterinary Corps, save such as may be ineligible for the infantry. Men, hoNiever, will be accepted for the Army Service Corps Remount Section, if between the ages of 38 and

TRANSFERENCE IF AND AS REQUIRED. On enlistment in the infantry a recruit will be attested for general service and an entry will be made on his attestation form, should he wish to be " noted " for subsequent transference to any other branch for which his services might be both suitable and required. So far as the exigencies of the service permit preference will be given, when transferences are made, to men who have notified their wishes in that matter at the _time of enlistment.
The Public Schools Battalion of the Royal Fusiliers is still open for educated and selected men.

CHANCE FOR CHAUFFEURS. An officer of the Mechanical Transport branch of the A.S.C. will attend at the Recruiting Office at the Police Buildings on Friday, May 14th— between the hours of 10 a.m. and 6.30 p.m.—for the purnose of interviewing and approving men who wish to enlist as motor drivers—heavy, light and taxi—and drivers of steam-drawn vehicles. In the meantime particulars can be obtained on apnlieation at the Recruiting Office. The pay is 6s. a day, all found, and Separation allowances are granted.

div.head: SISTERS DIE TOGETHER.
div.p: SISTERS DIE TOGETHER.
Shock 01 Tragic News Proves Fatal

div.head: At Stretton.
div.p: At Stretton.
There was on Monday a singular and a melan- choly sequel to the attack of pneumonia which a fortnight or so ago laid low the postmistress at Stretton Sub-office, Miss M. Campbell.

ONE DEATH ,CAUSES ANOTHER. Miss Campbell was being nursed by her sister, Mrs. Dutton. The patient, who was attended by Dr. H. E. Bower, was in an improved con- dition on Monday, and sat up in bed during the morning. Her sister, meanwhile, was in another bedroom supposed to be sleeping, but about noon the tragic discovery was made that Mrs. Dutton was dead, having apparently passed away in her sleep. The news was conveyed to the patient, who suffered an immediate relapse and died two or three hours later. The cause of Miss Campbell's death was said to have been shock; Mrs. Dutton died from heart failure.

div.head: NATIVES OF THE HIGHLANDS.
div.p: NATIVES OF THE HIGHLANDS.

Both Miss Campbell and Mrs. Dutton were well-known in the locality, and enjoyed the general esteem and regard of the residents, amongst whom the news caused a feeling of deep gloom. The deceased came from the Highlands of Scotland.

Miss Campbell, who was 56 years of age, came from Glasgow three years ago to take over the office of postmistress at Stratton, commencing duties there on April 15th, 1912. Mrs. Dutton was formerly cook for the late Mr. Thos. Henry Lyon, of Appleton Hall. There was an unusually large attendance in Stretton Parish Church on Thursday afternoon, when the Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross (tha.vicar) conducted an impressive service. Interment followed in the churchyard, where a large num- ber of mourners were in attendsace. There were many beautiful floral tributes, including tokens from Colonel and Mrs. Lyon, Mrs. Henry Lyon and a number of local farmers.

div.head: FUNERAL OF LATE MRS. SHAW.
div.p: FUNERAL OF LATE MRS. SHAW.

The funeral of Mrs. Harriet Shaw, wife of Councillor James Shaw, whose dtkath was briefly recorded in our last issue, took place on Monday at the Warrington Cemetery, amid many tokens of affection and esteem.

Mrs. Shaw was born at Grappenhall in 1850 and her earliest years were spent at Walton. She came to Warrington in her youth and has spent her life in the neighbourhood of Brick- street and Lythgoe's-lane. She became a scholar of Brick-street Sunday School and a member of the Friars' Green Independent Methodist Church, afterwards becoming one of the first members of the new Mission Church at Brick-street. Her interests have centred here for many years, and tile church owes much to her constant attendance and labours. The affectionate regard in which she was held in the church and neighbourhood was evi- denced in the large assembly which gathered there at the funeral service on Monday after- noon, and subsequently at the interment at the Cemetery.

The services in the church and at the grave- side were conducted by Councillor R. Henshall and were marked by deep feeling. The coffin was carried to the church by six personal friends who are attached to the church. Among those who were, present were: Mr. James Shaw (husband), Mr. Henry Shaw (son), Mrs. " Herbert Jolley, Mrs. Appleton, Mrs. Chamberlain, Miss Eva Shaw (daughters), Mr. Herbert Jolley, Mr. George Appleton, Mr. George Chamberlain (sons-in-law), Miss Hilda Jolley, Misses May and Bessie Shaw (grand- children), Mr. and Mrs. Henshall, Mr. and Mrs. William Barton, Mr. and Mrs. William Wright, Mr. and Mrs. B. Warburton, Mr. and Mrs. Thorniley, Mr. and Mrs. James Harding, Mr. and Mrs. Hibbert, Mr. and Mrs. Dunkley, Mr. and Mrs. T. Bibby, Mr. J. H. Bibby, Mr. and Mrs. James Harding son., M. S. Gallop, Mr. Arthur Morris, Mr. and Mrs. A. Mounfield, Mr. and Mrs. James Hudson, Mr. and Mrs. James Birch, Mr. and Mrs. John Hudson, and many other members of the Friars' Green and Brick-street Mission Independent Methodist Churches.

Floral tributes were received from "Her hus- band and Eva," "Emily and Herbert," "Henry, Sarah, May and Bessie," "George and Har- riet," "James" (Canada), "George and "Bessie," "Hilda," Brick-street Mission, Brick- street Mission Sunday School, Friars' Green 'Church, The Neighbours, Mr. and Mrs. Hen- shall, Mr. and Mrs. Warburton and "May," Mr. and Mrs. William Barton; Mr. and Mrs. James Harding, Mr. and Mrs. T. G. Gallop, Mr. and Mrs. James Shaw (Battersby-lane), E. Sutton, J. H. Bibby, Mrs. M. E. Roberts, Mr. and Mrs. Taylor, Mr. and Mrs. Hibbert and family, Mrs. Sudlow and "Maggie," "William Henry and Polly Lewis," Miss Ethel Sankey, Mr. and Mrs. J. Thorniley, Miss Edith Davies and Sydney Greaves.

Mr. Shaw has received many messages of sympathy from the churches and public bodies with which he and his late wife have been associated as well as from the Mayor and members of the Corporation. A memorial service will be, held to-morrow evening at six o'clock at the Brick-street Mis- sion Church, conducted by Councillor R. Henshall.
The funeral arrangements were carried out by Messrs. J. Mounfield and Sons.
PRIVATE A. HERSCHELL 'Wounded.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
MERRY REVUE AT THE ROYAL COURT.

There is no lack of variety in the revue "What- Ho ! Tango" that is drawing good audiences tr the Royal Court Theatre this week. The pies!, is spiritedly presented by a capable companA The dancing in itself contains an indication ot the wide range of pleasurable possibilities covered by the revue. The terpsichorean features ran the gamut from the Tango, that far-famed product of the modern propensity towards eccentricity in entertainment, to graceful old English movements. Of the eight attractive scenes, perhaps the most effective in a general way is the Eastern Harem scene, the funniest is that outside the hotel, in which the admirable nonsense of Miss Eva Rosslyn and Mr. Tom Tufty causes the audiences fairly to hug itself with laughter. The theme of this mirth-manu- facturing episode is that of the invisible hus- band, extortionate, threatening; the distressed "wife," and her reluctant victim, who parts up with notes and personal valuables in response to the distracted lady's irresistible appeal for something with which to appease the unseen terror's wrath. Miss Rosslyn is as successful in her songs as in her comedy. The piece in- cludes delightful songs and such charming dances as the old English Gavotte, "The Death of the Swan," and the Persian Pastel Ballet. Miss Marie Annerbelle, Mr. Tony King, Miss Nini Pasionck, Mr. Bert Vernon and Mlle. Vivi, amongst others, contribute admirably to the enjoyment of the audiences.

div.head: Big Comedian and Company Next Week.
div.p: Big Comedian and Company Next Week.

Joe - O'Gorman, the well-known London comedian, and his company, which includes Norah O'Gorman, will present the all-Irish revue, "Irish and Proud of It!" at the Royal Court, twice nightly, next week. The show promises to be a rollicking one, the "book" being by, Fergus Hegarty, and the music by some of Ireland's standard composers, whilst the company will number about fifty artistes, including several who are well known as Irish vocalists and comediennes, amongst them Lily Edwards, the popular chorus comedienne

The revue, which Strikes a note all its own, is spoken of as quite one of the best on tour, and it is magnificently mounted, staged and dressed. It is permeated throughout with that blithe- some humour and tender melody which are SO typically Irish, and all in search of a merry two hours' entertainment may rely upon it to meet their requirements, most of those taking part being genuine colleens or "Paddies."
MISS NORAH O'GORMAN, In " Irish and Proud of It"

div.head: CLEVER PIANIST AT TIIE HIPPODROME.
div.p: CLEVER PIANIST AT TIIE HIPPODROME.

The outstanding turn in the excellent pro- gramme on offer twice nightly at the Hippo- drome this week is provided by Mdlle Chevalier and Captain Riego. The lady sings up-to-date songs, whilst the gentleman plays the piano with the touch of an expert; in fact, he plays two pianos simultaneously part of the time, and is quite one of the most facile "manipulators of the ivories" we have heard for a long while. His imitation of church bells is something worth going far to hear, and is absolutely unique. The Barnard Family revive the old-fashioned marionette show and give a really delightful entertainment, "working the dolls" with won- derful ingenuity. Another popular turn is that provided by Ted Le Roy and a clever troupe of juvenile artistes, who both dance and sing daintily. The English Proves are one of the cleverest troupes of trick cyclists that have visited Warrington for a long time, and Bart and Bart get through some slick acrobatic work, performed to an " accompaniment " of literally "quiet humour." There are other turns, and all of them were good, the pro- gramme, on the whole, being of a highly enter- taining order and fully up to the reputation of the house.

div.head: Attractive Fare Next Week.
div.p: Attractive Fare Next Week.

A fine bill of fare has been prepared for next week. It will be headed by Haley's Komets in "A Garden Revue," a turn overflowing with melodious music, catchy songs and delightful dancing; indeed, it is a turn which, in some respects, will prove the turn of the season. Another strong item in a strong programme will be provided by Arthur Melrose, the whist- ling-humorist, whose show is spoken of as a combination of refinement and humour. Mdlle. De Dio, in prismatic dances, will provide another feature, and all the other items engaged are fully up to the Macnaghten standard of excellence. A big treat is in store for the near future, Ernest Shand having been booked for a week and, as everybody who knows anything about music halls, is well aware, Ernest is "some goods."

div.head: NEW HIPPODROME MANAGER.
div.p: NEW HIPPODROME MANAGER.
One Of The Last Who Spoke To Captain Scott.

Mr. Will A. Jackson, the genial new manager of the Hippodrome, has spent a varied eighteen years as a theatrical manager. He comes here from Bradford with the reputation of being an admirable man for the job. One of the win- cipal factors in his success has been his unfail- ing tactfulness when that estimable quality was needed.

The new manager started at the Metropole, Glasgow, with Mr. Wm. Kelly, in "A Royal Divorce." For three or four years he ran his own companies, and at Hebburn-on-Tyne he managed his own theatre. He has been with the Macnaghten firm for the last eight years, first at Stalybridge and subsequently at Cardiff, Stoke-on-Trent and Bradford.

_ A native of Tyneside—" and proud of it " Mr. Jackson is a Glasgow University man.. He possesses a beautifully illuminated public testi- monial, signed by the Chief Constable and many of the most prominent public personages of Cardiff; and few theatrical managers can num- ber anything of this kind amongst their wall adornments.

Talking of Cardiff brings one to the interest- ing fact that Mr. Jackson was one of the last men to speak to Captain Scott, the famous Antarctic explorer, before he set sail on what proved to be his last voyage of discovery. He presented an entertainment to Captain Scott and his gallant crew on the night before they left Cardiff on the voyage.
VRESH ASPARAGUS every morning.—Hy. -11.: MILLING d; Co., LTD., Horsemarket-street.

div.head: IAYMM
div.p: IAYMM

" Brookfield" Re-decorated.--A large part of the Lymra Red Cross Hospital—which needed it —has just been handsomely, though economic- ally, re-decorated. Tribute to Private Peter Leigh.—" Our sym- pathies go out to Mr. and Mrs. Leigh on the death of their gallant min, Private Peter Leigh, of the sth Cheshires," writes the Rector in the May issue of the Lymm Parish Magazine. "His wounded companions, we are glad to learn, are making favourable progress." A Correction.—ln our Council report last week we stated that Councillor Holt, in seconding the proposition to elect Councillor Gotobed to the chair, said he did so" although he was often, an enemy of his (the speaker's)." We are in- formed that Councillor Holt really said: "Even if he had beea my greatest enemy, &c."

Many Burials.—In the current issue of the Parish Magazine, besides five burials already recorded in "The Examiner," appear those of: Harry Brazendale (Oughtrington), aged 32 years, on April sth; April 10th, Elizabeth Brazendale (Warrington), aged 68 years; April 13th, Sarah Guest, aged 85 years; April 23rd, Rose Hannah Hanapson (Oughtrington), aged FA years. The average age attained was 63. Four Marriages.—ln the May Parish Maga- zine are recorded four marriages: April 3rd, Joseph Hall (Parkfield, Middleton) to Ann Hayes (Lymm) ; April 3rd, Harold Hankinson (Thelwall) to Rosa Cash (Lymm); April 10th, James Sidley (Oughtrington) to Violet Pigott (Lymm); April 14th. John Henry Briars to Emma Ainsworth (both of Lymm). "Another Man Of Best Type."--Writing home to Lymm to say that the wounded Lance- Corporal E. Blease's section has been talcen over by his mate, Lance-Corporal F. Kay [whose home address is also Yew Tree-terrace, Rush Green], Sergeant H. Clare adds of the latter:— "He is another man of the best type. . . ." He also refers to him as f` one of our best men. . ." Local Pharmaceutical Success.—Mr. William Rigby, assistant to Mr. F. E. Evans, chemist, of The Cross, Lymm, has gained the prize in a competition inaugurated by the Manchester Pharmaceutical Association for chemist's assistants in the Manchester district. The com- petition, which had a large entry, was held in March. Mr. Rigby, who comes from West Houghton, has been assistant to Mr. Evans for two years.

Glowing Praise For Private H. Brooks.—ln a letter to Mr. and Mrs. E. Blease, telling them how their son was wounded at the Front, Sergeant H. 'Clare says that Private Harry Brooks dressed his wound. I may say here he is our stretcher-bearer, and does heroic work for the wounded. He is indeed a splendid man, and we were very fortunate to have him with us. I could fill -pages telling you of his noble work out here. . . ."

" Tommy's " Thoughts Of Spring.—"We must hope and trust in God for a speedy return," writes Private Ernest Hadden from the Front to his mother in Pepper-street., "I am glad to say I am enjoying good health, and the weather is simply glorious. It does seem a shame to think this awful war is happening while the country seems so beautiful with the woods, valleys,, and fields with the daisies

growing all over. . . ." Some relations " wit.nt to send me parcels: but we don't know where to put things—as we have not much room; and then we might move to another place. I am at present with the Major in some dug-outs behind the firing-line. . . ." Private Stanley Gibbs' word says: "At • times you would not think there was any War on, to hear the birds singing, and the quietness!"

"Charming and Touching Gift.'--After re- ferring, in the May Parish Yagazine, to the dedication of the new font at the Church of St. Mary the Virgin, the Rector adds: "There was a large congregation at the service, which con- cluded with the baptism of our little .son. All the day school children had a half holiday, and were entertained at a tea most kindly and efficiently catered for by the teachers and their friends. A great surprise to me at the close was a presentation to the baby of a beautiful isilver bowl and spoon, to which I_ was told all the children at Pepper-street and Statham Schools had subscribed. My wife and I are very much touched by the thoughts that must have prompted such a charming gift, and we trust and pray that the little boy will grow up a worthy son of the parish where I have lived and worked so long."

War Service Far Women.—lncluded with each copy of the Parish Magazine for May is a Government notice from the Board of Trade, headed "War Service for Women." It speaks plainly of the great emergency before the country and the necessity for men engaged in certain industries being set free and their place taken' by women. "The purpose of the circu- lar" says the Rector, "is summed up in one of the closing sentences thus: Any woman who by working helps to release a man or to equip a man for fighting does national war service.' This preliminary notification is given to _pre- pare the minds of all inhabitants in the district for a meeting which is contemplated at the Drill Hall 'towards the beginning of June, when the scheme will be fully explained, and those willing to serve invited to register their names. The necessity for men and equipment at the Front is greater than ever. In a letter from one of our men received the other day this need is thus expressed: 'I feel sure that if the young men of England only realised the great work the Army is doing they could not hesitate to join and thus help to bring this war to a speedy ending; there is no doubt we want more men. I am not complaining at all at the way our young men have come forward, but I'believe there are a great many more that are eligible.' It is difficult to turn a deaf ear to an appeal like this from those who are bearing the burden and heat of the day.'" •

Rector's Easter Greetings to "Tommy."—ln his letter in the May Lymm Parish Magazine the Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston) says: "/The beautiful weather on Easter Day helped to make up .for many disadvantages we are suffer- ing from this year. Most of the best of our younger men are away on service; I had the pleasure of sending Easter cards to no less than .fifty whose names appeared on the recent confirmation lists, those at the Front receiving a letter in addition. These cards, I have heard from many, were much appreciated, and formed a. link with us at home by turning their minds and thoughts towards us and our doings on that great day. Easter was early and public- schools had not broken up, but in spite of all draw- backs we had very bright and happy services, and very good congregations. The church was beautifully decorated by a band of ladies gath- ered together by the kind officesof Mrs. Callender to whom we are all greatly indebted. The sing- ing was good and "hearty. The communicants were less in number than usual, but this was only to be expected tinder the circumstances. with so many away.. I was much gratified and pleased at your generous Easter offerings. Personally. I was a little- in doubt as to whether it should be given this year, but the church- wardens. rightly as it turned out, decided other- wise. The amount, eighty pounds, was a sur- prise to them as well as to me. lam more than thankful that the important principle ,of the . offering has evidently taken so great a hold on the minds of the parishioners."

Football: Defeat and Victory.—The Wednes- day Football Club, at the Pepper-street 'ground on Wednesday afternoon, played a friendly match against Salford Wednesday— and contrived their defeat by seven goals to five.—The Lymm team was captained by F. Guest, and, winning the toss, elected to play uphill. By , half-time they had gained four goals against the visitors' three, the home scorers being Harry Holt (three) and H. Dodson (one). Lymm's form was by then shown superior to that of the visitors.—ln the second half the home team quickly re-com- menced scoring, for they had the sun in their favour in their down-hill tactics. H. Holt again led off in the seoring, his example shortly being followed by It. Dodson and Frank Guest. The opposing team gained two more goals.— Special mention is made of Oswald Garvey's splendid goalkeeping and of T. Hatton's fine display as left-wing forward.—The Lymm Wed- nesday visited Manchester on WednOsday of last week, when the Man Chester Post Office (in the final League game) defeated them by three goals to two, after a keen game. F. Guest captained the Lymmites, for whom the scorers were 11. Holt and IL Daniels.
LYMM TERRITORIALS' ROLL OF HONOUR.
_X NO'FIIER CASUALTY.
From the Front have arrived at Lymm this week particulars of still another casualty amongst the local Territorials :
WOUNDED. Lance-Corporal Edwin Blease.

The Lance-Corporal is the fifth Lymm " Terrier " to be wounded; there have, of course, also been one killed and one accidentally hurt. The casualties amongst local " Terriers " there- fore total seven. Writing of their fine work at the Eront, Sergeant Clare exclaims: "Really, Lymm has sent rare material to uphold the honour of old England!" Sergeant Harold Clare has had a narrow escape from being wounded. He is the third to experience such a "thrill." The Germans were firing rifle-grenades, and a splinter caught him just above the left eye—without, however, hurt- ing him! The " Terriers " are now serving in the trenches in a different series of periods. Hitherto they have " done " four days in, and four days out 'of the trenches. As we stated last-week, however, they were on one occasion not relieved for six days. Particulars of the new system upon which they have just entered we give below in Sergeant Clare's letter. The latest word available says they are in good health and excellent spirits, and have been lucky not to have more than one casualty. Another false rumour has this week gained considerable currency—in the village—that the" popular Captain Ridgway has been killed in the firing line. Inquiry utterly fails to verify the report. On Friday word was received from the Captain, in which he stated himself to be all right, and no bad news of him has reached his home. Natur- ally the report has cast quite a gloom over the district, and efforts are being made to trace the rumour to its source. It is sincerely to be hoped that the stupid and unpatriotic person or per- sons who originated this and other false news of the fate of the gallant Lymm "Terriers" will be discovered. In such case he or they will, of course, be liable to be heavily punished by law. Lance-Corporal Syd. Linley writes: "Is true? because I have not seen it in The Ex- aminer.' You know we chaps take no notice of rumours. We've had some; and the sooner you people at Lymm do the same, the better. . . . You know, Lymm people must not get down- hearted yet. Up to now the Lymm lads have been very fortunate, considering how many are out there. You 'can see by their letters the ' boys ' are not downhearted yet, so why should the people at home be? Keep on singing, for better days are coming soon ! . . ."

div.head: NEW REGULATIONS.
div.p: NEW REGULATIONS.

Sergeant Harold Clare's letter to Mr. F. E. Evans on Thursday morning, ran:—" Sunday, 2nd May,—We came out of the trenches last night; we were in two days this time. Now we are , occupying dug-outs in a beautiful valley half a mile from the trenches, in reserve. We shall probably be in these two days, and then two more in the trenches—and so on whilst in reserve.

div.head: Night Work Under Shell Fire.
div.p: Night Work Under Shell Fire.

"We carry out duties such as taking food and stores to the trenches and digging communica- tion trenches—for instance, to-night we com- mence digging at eleven and work until about two in the morning, under rifle and shell fire most of the time, for the Germans have recently taken a liking for shelling at night. Of course we have to be very careful; however, with our men being so steady and cheerful, and these excellent officers of ours, we never feel that we are in danger. "You will be pleased to know that we had not a single casualty in the trenches, and our boys are, as usual, in perfect health and spirits. Sergeant's " Near Squeak."

"I believe I was the only one to have a near squeak. The Germans were firing , rifle- grenades at us on the first days. A small splinter caught me just . above my left eye; happily I was not hurt—it just scratched me! All that I felt was a little headache, which soon worked off. I don't feel the slightest effect from it now, and am in my usual good health. . "

div.head: 28 LEFT OUT OF 50.
div.p: 28 LEFT OUT OF 50.

Private Henry Brooks, of 1, West Hyde, "Newfield," writes to a relation in the South: "You may be surprised to hear that we have only 28 left in our platoon; for when we came out we had 50 or more. This is a pretty hot shop. By the way, I saw a photograph of W. Milson [Warrington] in 'The Examiner last week, reported as being wounded. . . ."

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL E. BLEASE.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL E. BLEASE.
Slightly Wounded By Shell During

div.head: " Small Hours."
div.p: " Small Hours."
The news that Lance-Corporal Edwin Blease had been wounded first reached his native town- ship on Saturday morning—when his mother
LANCE-CORPORAL BLEASE. Wounded.

(Mrs. E. Blease, of Yew Tree-terrace, Rush Green) received a letter, dated Thursday, April 29th, and running as follows:— You will be surprised to hear that I am wounded. I got hit with a piece of shell about three o'clock yesterday morning. It caught me on my t6ft shOulder. It is not a

serious wound, only slight, but I have some- thing to be thankful to God for, as it might have been much more serious. I am writing this while on the boat crossing the Channei for England. I think lam being sent to a hospital in Manchester. Anyhow I will let
you know later. It is glorious sailing to-day, just like being on Blackpool pier. . . Now I don't want you to worry, as the wound is not serious.

The Lance-Corporal now sojourns in Netley Hospital, where he is making capital progress. On Monday morning Mr. and Mrs. -Blease received from Sergeant Clare the following:— , " I am very sorry to tell you \that your son lEddie unfortunately got wounded last night—or I should say early this morning; the time was 1.30 a.m.—by a piece of shrapnel. We were returning from the trenches, where we had been carrying stores. We commenced the work at 7.30 p.m., and the whole of the time we were under German shell-fire. It happened about half a mile from our destination, on our return; it was jolly hard luck. Lieutenant Walker (our platoon commander). and I were talking, at the time, of our good luck in accomplishing this dangerous task without a
