div.head: 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
div.p: THE 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.

single mishap. We had done a deal of manceuvr- ing to try to avoid it, when this shell burst and a piece struck Eddie's rifle, then his left shoulder. He was like he always has been— very brave and plucky whilst Private Harry Brooks dressed his wound. . . .

wanted one. We had just been in the trenches for six days, so you can tell what we looked like—no wash or shave for six days! "We are in a lively place. .. . I will .write again as soon as we are going to have another look at Kaiser Bill's men to see how they are getting on. You know we ask them—with a few bullets !"

div.head: " As !f Hit With Stone."
div.p: " As !f Hit With Stone."

"Now I know you are worrying and wonder- ing whether it is serious or not—which is quite natural; but take it from me .(I won't mislead you!) the wound is not serious. Far from it; his arm is just like it would be had someone hit him with a , stone. There is no shrapnel in. so I hope you will relieve your mind of all worry. He will be well looked after in hospital; then you will have him at home—in fact they may send him to England at once. He was quite cheerful when Lance-Corporal Kay took him to the Dressing Station. "I am sorry indeed to lose him, for he was along with Lance-Corporal Kay, one of the best men in my platoon. As you know, (Far officers realised this, and he was promoted to Lance- Corporal a fortnight ago. As a soldier, as al- - his work in private life, he had a brip. c future; and commanded a section long before he was promoted—a fact which speaks for itself as to his qualifications. I earnestly trust that he will have a speedy recovery, and once more return to us to continue the good work he has already done. He is exceedingly keen and in- terested in his work.
"His mate, Lance-Corporal F. Kay, has taken over his section. . . ."

Private H. Brooks, stretcher-bearer, describes their being shelled on their return to .the billets, and declares that they were very fortunate in having only one wounded! Private Percy Clare tells Master John Daniels that the wound, though not very bad, is "plenty bad enough." " Mending Nicely."

- On Tuesday morning the wounded Lance- Corporal wrote home again himself to say that his wound was not at all serious. He goes on to say that he spent a day and a half in bed, and is now looking after the other soldiers— bringing all they want and waiting on them generally. Netley, he adds, is a very nice place, and his arm and shoulder are " mending " quite nicely. The food at the hospital is ex- ceptionally good, and there is plenty of it.

div.head: STORY OF HIS LIFE.
div.p: STORY OF HIS LIFE.

Born in Rush Green twenty years ago, Lance- Corporal Blease is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Blease. Leaving the Oughtrington School (where he was taught under Mr. 0. G. Smith's' headmastership) at the age of fourteen, he worked for two years with Young's Paraffin and Mineral Oil Company, Manchester; after- wards leaving to take up the position of clerk in the offices of Messrs. Moore and Co., Lymm Salt Works. Here he remained until the out- break of hostilities.

In the meantime he had for a, year belonged to the sth Cheshire Territorials, and had at- tended a camp. Accordingly he was ealled up in August; and after training in Shrewsbury, Northampton, Stowemarket, Church-Stretton. Cambridge and other towns until February, he went out to the war zone.

In peace times he attends St. Peter's Parish Church, Oughtrington—of the choir of which he is a member. He also belongs there to Mr. Nash's Bible Class (out of which about thirty others have enlisted). Sports and Pastimes. •

He is a former member of the Heatley Boy Scouts; and has also in his day captained the 2nd Oughtrington Amateur, Football Club— being an enthusiast in the winter game. He is a member of the Oughtrington Men's Bowling Club.

Private Ernest Hadden writes home: "The Lymm lads went past the other night on their way to the ttenclies. One lad named Blease got wounded with shrapnel near this town, but I don't know if it is serious. I hope not !"

div.head: PRIVATE HENRY CADMAN.
div.p: PRIVATE HENRY CADMAN.
'Wailing To "6o lip Line" Again.

Private Henry Cadman, wounded, writes to his sister (Mrs. Sam Owen, Brookfield Cot- tages, Booth's Hill)/" I am in the best of health, and am now in the Base Camp, waiting to go up the line again to join my regiment—as this is where they send us from when we have got over our wounds. .. . It is really too hot for anything. . . .

div.head: Rather a Shock?
div.p: Rather a Shock?

"I expect it was rather a shock to .you when you heard about me being wounded. . . . But it does not give you much warning. I expect there will be some wounded home in Lymm now, but you see I had not the luck to come; I should have liked to come home for a day or two just to see you all once again. But we live in hopes. . . . So please remember me to all at Lymm. . . ."
Digging Party.

In word sent to another sister (Mrs. G. Rixon, of Pepper-street) a few days ago, the Private said: "I am out of the hospital now, and have been sent to the convalescent camp. .. . The night I got wounded we were going to be relieved; and I, with two or three others, went on a digging party. I had hardly got there when I was hit in the back. We were just work- ing in a ring—for we could see all the Germans' trenches right round us, and the fire from their guns.

div.head: " We Got Lost."
div.p: " We Got Lost."

"After I had got hit they dressed me to last until I could get down to the dressing station. We got lost, and it took vis about an hour to find our way again. And every time a German star light went up we had to get tight down flat on the ground—for wilien one goes ,up it makes night like day, and they can see you if , you do not get down right flat. "I can tell you when we did find our way it did not take us long to get tp the dressing station!
A card just received shows that Private Cad- man is not yet back in the trenches.

div.head: LANCUORPORAL S. LINLEV.
div.p: LANCUORPORAL S. LINLEV.
Keeps On Smiling—Ana Preaching.
Writing to his wife at Pepper-street from Hinton House, Hinton St. George, Crewkerne, the wounded Lance-Corporal Sydney Linley says :

"I am still doing well, as you will see by the photo I am sending you; you will see that I keep on smiling—for, as the song says, `We're not downhearted yet.' The photo where we are altogether was taken last Thursday afternoon on the bowling green. The others hre what one of our Sisters has taken; we think they are very good. What do you think? . . "This afternoon I have been for a motor ride -with two other of our chaps; our head Sister drives her own car. . . .

div.head: "Good Time on Sunday."
div.p: "Good Time on Sunday."
"I had a good time on Sunday. There were about twenty men in the afternoon, and at night the little chapel was well-nigh full—where of late they have only been having about ten or twelve.

"Next Sunday, if I am still here, I have been asked to go to the Wesleyan Sunday school at hiemott (about twenty minutes' walk) to give an address and present the prizes to the chil- al en; then at night to preach again in the vil- lage. So I am looking forward to another good week-end. . • •

"You will be glad to know that I have no dressing on my wound now, so you can take it that it is doing well. . I am happy here. . . . My chum's name is Jones. He comes from Lon- don, and we first met on board ship; we have been pals ever since. . . .

div.head: More About 100 Hymn-books.
div.p: More About 100 Hymn-books.

"I had a nice letter from Mr. Brown this morning. Enclosed was a letter he had had returned from the Front—one that had been sent along with the [IOO] hymn-books. He is wondering about the books, so you might let him see the postcard from H. Clare*; he will see then thiit they are all right. • • ." *The postcard sent by Sergeant Clare to Lance- Corporal Linley says: "24/4/15. I was very pleased to hear from you, and to know you were doing nicely. I passed both your letters to the boys, who wish. to be. remembered to you. The men of your section miss you, and hope you will be back soon. I gave each Lymm man one of those beautiful hymn-books that came for you; what were over I gave to the other men—l knew that would be your wish....•

div.head: PRIVATE RICHARD SHAW
div.p: PRIVATE RICHARD SHAW
Crosses Over To English Hospital.

Mrs. J. Shaw, Booth's Hill, received (p. Thurs- day morning a card to say : "British Red Cross Society,---I have just arrived at Southampton, and am going to 2nd Northern General Ham- ital R.A.M.C. (T.) Leeds; Ward Flo.—Priv ite Richard Shaw, sth Cheshires." A letter has also arrived to say he is going r.n all right, although unable to " put his toot dawn flat on the floor"—whica the (factor for- bids!
Private Shaw left the Versailles Hospital with many other• wounded warriors, tr, make way for three thousand new cases. PRIVATE JAMES TAYLOR.

div.head: Moved To Convalescent Home With Arm Still Useless.
div.p: Moved To Convalescent Home With Arm Still Useless.

To his mother at 1, West Hyde, Newfield, Lymm, the wounded Private James Taylor writes: "I have just arrived at the conv,ales- cent home [Red Cross Hospital, Grantham Bar- racks]. . . . This is a better place than the other one—although that was a good.one. We do as we like, and eat wlittit we like. . . ." "Let all friends have my address," adds the Private, "and then they can write a few lines. . . ."

Private Henry Brooks, stepbrother of the wounded Private, writes to him: "I am sorry to hear you have not yet regained the use of your fingers [left hand]. Of course, you must understand that the artery was severed; and, before you get the use of any part below where the wound is, a new artery has to be formed. which is made naturally. . . . You need have no fear. . . ."
Private Joseph Clare writes: "Has Jimmy Taylor got home yet? He will not half have a tale to tell if' he has! I believe his arm has been very bad...."

div.head: BEFORE HE WAS WOUNDED.
div.p: BEFORE HE WAS WOUNDED.
What Lance-Corporal S. Linley Wrote To Wesleyans.

The May issue of the "Warrington Wesleyan Record" contains the following letter, written from the Front by Lance-Corporal S. Linley, of C Company, sth Cheshires, and of Pepper- street, Lymm, to local Weskyans before he was wounded :

"March 17th,—Glad to say we are all well and happy. We are not downhearted yet, although we of course think of home and friends many a time." "March 20th,—I was stopped just when I had settled down to write. We have been in the trenches two days and nights. We came out again with one killed—a man from Runcorn. All our lads came out safe. When in the trenches, we feel the cold very much. Yester- day it snowed nearly all day. "Fancy standing stooping about all day so as to keep our heads down, or lying in our dug- outs. You would laugh to see us going in on our hands and knees under the earth.

div.head: "We Keep on Smiling."
div.p: "We Keep on Smiling."

"When we are in the trenches we have no sleep at night, but get a little as a rule in the day time. The thing we trouble about the most is how to keep warm. However, we are going on very nicely up to now. We keep on smiling and doing our best. I have not been able to get to many services lately. Hact not been to any for a fortnight till last Sunday night: You will be glad to know, though, that I have conducted two short services in our billet for our lads. They ask me to, and they want me to do so as often as I can. I am short of small hymn books. Would you send me about one hundred? [This has been done.] They will help to make the services brighter. "Pray for me that I may live and speak for our Master. Thankful to say lam keeping very well so far. I have had one or two near shaves. The night before last I went out of the trench with a party to bring food up to the trench. It was a very dark night, and we had to mind the 'Jack Johnson' holes. I was going through a gap when a flare light went up. We stopped dead, but somebody spotted us and let go. So we had to lie there for some minutes before we dare move again. One bullet hit 'a tree at the side of my head. However, it hit the tree—not me. That is one instance of the life we are living out here. Kind regards to all friends. I shall be glad to hear from any of them."

div.head: "A BIT OF SNIPING."
div.p: "A BIT OF SNIPING."
A War-Zone Diits Not Welcomed 113 Lymm "Terrier."

Private Stanley Gibbs, writing to his wife in Henry-street, early this week, says : "I have been doing a bit of sniping early this morning with a patent rifle—which is per- fectly safe to fire, as you have not to expose yourself when firing. We got one chap shot through the head this morning at about seven o'clock, and he passed away very quietly at 7.50. 'Poor chap! But he has gone to a better land.

div.head: Best Fighters In Big Battle."
div.p: Best Fighters In Big Battle."

"They call the Scotch out -here 'Jocks,' and my word! they can fight! I think they are the best fighters in the British Army. "We were engaged in that big battle a few days. . . . The Seotehmen have been in this big battle again. All that .you can hear is the roar of the big guns; this has been going on all the six days we have been un here. It does not quieten any yet; it's almost a fort- night since I took my boots. off. People in England don't realise what we have to go through. Comfortable Nights; Lovely Days. "We are sleeping out in a field, under a hedgeside—as the town gets shelled day and night. You would be surprised to know how warm we can make ourselves at night, and it's simply lovely through the day. All this morn- ing I have been sitting in the sun stripped, because it is so hot out here. We are going into the. trenches again to-night—for how long I don't know. .- ."

div.head: DIFFICULT RETREAT.
div.p: DIFFICULT RETREAT.
Germans Shell Lymm Men All Way
Out of Trenches.

Private Percy Clare—in a letter received by his mother, Mrs. G. Davies, of Booth's Hill, early this week—says: "April 26th. Thank you very much for the parcel, which I received all right this morning—the morning we came out of the trenches.

"We had six clays this time; we did not set relieved on the fourth day as we should have done, and .had a rum job to get away from the trenches—as the Germans were shelling us all the way to the place where we are spending our few days' rest. We are in the open fields. It is a nice morning, but I expect it will be cold at night sleeping in the open; but we will put up with that as long as we keep out of the way of the shells.

div.head: " Blown to Bits."
div.p: " Blown to Bits."

"It is a sad sight to see round here. There are very few houses or buildings of any sort standing, as the Germans are shelling the place night and day—and it is a fine place. Some of the finest buildings (churches, &c.) I ever saw are blown to bits.
Shot Through the Neck.

"All of us over here are in the best of health up to now, thank God. We all came out of the trenches all right—only one; and he got shot through the neck. But I think he will be all right, and get over it. (He is not a Lymm lad.) I received Mr. Daniels' kind letter while I was in the trenches. Will you please thank him for me? I will write to them soon. . . . Shells are flying round us while I write this letter. . ."

div.head: Very' Good Weather.
div.p: Very' Good Weather.
In word received on Monday morning, Private Clare said

"I would not mind if we were coming home this nice weather. But never mind! It can- not last for ever. . . . I have not much news this timel. only that E. Blease got wounded the other night. You-know him? I think he is the son of Mr. Blease from Brown's [the _grocers]."

div.head: TO WASH OR NOT TO WASH.
div.p: TO WASH OR NOT TO WASH.

To Master John Daniels, . Booth's Hill, the Private writes—to thank him for a fine parcel of towels, &c.: ."I was just going for a wash when I received your parcel: so I turned back, and when. I found the towels I threw my dirty one away and had g good 'do '—not before I

div.head: BOMBARDMENT.
div.p: THE BOMBARDMENT.
Local Corporal Shocked Al Hundreds
Of Guns.

Corporal J. Moston, in a letter (principally of thanks) just received by Mr. D. Daniels, con- fectioner, Booths Hill, says.: "I am writing this in the trenches, so don't feel in a good humour for writing. The Germans are sending shells over our trench; they are dropping near the support,. and are awful things to put up with. 1 hope they dop't drop a few in ours! "I suppose you have read a good deal just lately in the papers about the bombardment which took place last week-end? It was simply awful to hear hundreds of guns going off at once; I am sure the damage .must have been terrible.

div.head: shelling the Town.
div.p: shelling the Town.

"We are at a beautiful town at present, with some of the nicest buildings I have ever seen; but I am sorry to say the Germans have started to shell it this last night. We can see it burn- ing away out of thQ'trenches. . . . It does seem a shame. . .."

div.head: LYMM REGULAR KILLED IN ACTION.
div.p: LYMM REGULAR KILLED IN ACTION.
Private Walter Jackson Shot Through
The Head.

April 23rd.—It is with a very sad heart that I am writing this short note to tell you that your husband, Private Walter Jackson, was killed in action this evening about 6.30. His death was instantaneous, a bullet passing right through his head. It will be some consolation to you to know he has been buried very respectably near where he fell; a large wooden cress, bearing his name and number, company and regiment, has been erected over his grave. The service was read over him by an officer of his own company, and everything possible to be done has been done. Although your husband had only been with us for a short time he made himself well liked by everybody by his willingness and application to duty. In closing I can assure you of the deepest sympathy of all ranks in your sad loss. If you think I can be of any assistance to you I shall be only too willing to do all I can."

In this, pathetic letter, Sergeant-Major E. Owens, of the Ist Cheshires, on Saturday broke to Mrs. Jackson, of Newfield, Lymm, the news that her husband-r--Private Walter Jack- son—had been killed in action. The dead soldier also leaves four little children. A son of Mrs. Peter John Jackson, of Mos- ton-street, Newfield—whose husband (himself

div.head: PRIVATE WALTER JACKSON.
div.p: PRIVATE WALTER JACKSON.

well-known and respected) passed away some time ago—Private Jackson's age was 32 years. In November he enlisted, and having under- gone four months' training, he, on March 24th, left for the Front with a draft of the Ist Cheshires. Thus his service in the acttial war- theatre was of but a month's duration. His Last Letter Home.

The private's last letter to his wife was en- closed in Sergeant-Major Owens's letter an- nouncing his death. It Pis .dated April 19th, and runs :—" Just a few lines, hoping to find you and all the. children in the best of health —as it leaves me very well at present We are having grand weather over here, and killing Germans and taking them prisoners. I am quite all right at present. Ido hope that God will spare me to come to you all again when this great conflict is over. I think it will not be long. I had a nice letter from the Rev. Horace Gray, and also one from my brother Sam; at Garston.

"I am writing this letter .to you in the trenches. -I am sitting down, and you would be surprised to see us. I am always thinking about the children; God bless them all Kiss them for me. Well, I have not seen the ' Terriers ' this week, but I will let you know when I see any of them. I should like to see Willie [his brother]."

div.head: Council's Condolences.
div.p: Council's Condolences.

Jackson was, until his enlistment, employed at the Lymm Gas Works, and at a meeting of the Council held on Monday evening a sincere vote of condolence was passed to his widow. Accordingly the following letter has been sent to Mrs. Jackson

"May 4th, 1915.—Dear Madam,—At a meet- ing of the Urban District Council held last evening a resolution of sympathy and condolence was passed by the Coun- cil to you and your family circle on the death of your gallant, husband, who has fallen in action, with the fervent hope that you will have strength to bear up in your most terrible trial.—l should very much like to associate myself with the above.—l remain, yours-faith- fully, W. 11.1IILLARD, Clerk." Lance-Corporal S. Linley writes to his wife: "I am sorry to hear about Owen's death [fully reported in our last issue] and W. Jack- son's. . . . Please extend my sympathy to both of their families. . . ."

div.head: Patriotic Family.
div.p: Patriotic Family.

Formerly Private Jackson belonged to the Lymm Volunteers—under Company-Sergeant C. E. Ardern. His aim in joining the Cheshires, he told his wife after saying how proud he/felt to be off to the Front, was "to help to defend his country, so that it should not be over-run like Belgium." _ _
One brother of the dead private is now serv- ing on the Continent with the Lymm "Terriers," whilst another (Fred) is in train- ing as a unit in Kitchener's Army.

div.head: Fumous, BUT FUTILE.
div.p: Fumous, BUT FUTILE.
" Allemans" " Attempts To Break Through Lymm "Terriers" Line.

Yesterday morning Private Joseph , Clare's word to his mother said "I never was in better condition. . . . It is awful at present in this place, for they are blowing it to atoms all the day and night over. But as long as We are only getting them wounded it is not so bad. . . . I think that before long we shall be having a good rest—and not before we need it, either; for we have not had a proper rest for this last month, working night and day at the trenches. However, it is for our own benefit, so there is no use grumbling. We shall be in the trenches again_ by you get this." _

Writing on Monday, the 3rd. the'Priv-ate said: " We are in dug-outs only a few hundred yards behind the firing line. We are safer here than in the town. They don't give us much peace But keep on smiling! We are going through it
very nicely. Everything is beginning to look lovely—only this war; that does not look so bright. But it will end sooner or later. It is difficult to get letters off at present. . . ."

div.head: Soon Be Getting Sunburnt.
div.p: Soon Be Getting Sunburnt.

On Saturday morning a-communication from the Private said they would soon be getting sun- burnt, but they must expect that, as it would soon be getting at its highest pitch—for it was either now or never with the " Allemans." "They are trying their hardest to break through," he declared, "but have got a busier task on than they expect. . . . We have just been talking of what we §hall do when we get back. We don't often. . . . All of us are merry and bright. . . ."

div.head: LYMM LABOURER'S REMARKABLE
div.p: LYMM LABOURER'S REMARKABLE
DEATH
After Walking Home With Fractured
Skull.
FELL OFF TRAMCAR.

A remarkable feature of a fatal tramcar acci- dent, investigated by the Manchester District Coroner (Mr. Sellars) at Old Trafford on Thurs- day, was that the victim, Joe Marsden (58), a fitter's labourer, lodging in Fourth-street, Trafford Park, walked home and went to bed with a fractured skull. Marsden's home is at Rush Green, Lymm— and he formerly had been employed as a flatman on the Manchester Ship Canal.

div.head: Somersault Into Roadway.
div.p: Somersault Into Roadway.

• At the inquest it was given in evidence that on Monday night last Marsden fell off the plat- form of a car near Longford Bridge, Stretford, in attempting to alight when the car was in motion. A fellow passenger said he turned almost a complete somersault into the roadway, and probably alighted on his head. The car had not slowed up, as there was no stopping place there. According to other evidence, Marsden ap- peared shaken, but not much hurt. He was accompanied home by a constable, and went to bed after saying that the accident had given him a headache. He could not be roused next morning, and a doctor pronounced him dead. The post-mortem revealed a three-inch fracture of the base of the skull. and there were wounds on the left shoulder and elbow. " Most Unusual."
The Coroner remarked that he would not say that such a case had never been heard of before, but it was most unusual. A verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned. _ _
Only on Saturday Marsden was in Lymm village. Talking to a friend, he then remarked how splendidly he was getting along with his work. He leaves a widow to mourn his loss.
To " Cross " and Back.—A detachment of " Tommies " in the making on Tuesday after- noon marched from Altrincham to Lvmm Cross, when they returned after a brief halt.

div.head: INCREASED RATE.
div.p: INCREASED RATE.
Urban Council's Important AVar-Time
Decision:

A special meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Lymm Urban District Council was held on Monday evening, when two hours were spent in discussion of the new rate. Having arrived at their decision,

The committee formed themselves into open Council to approve (or otherwise) the recom- mendation arrived at in committee. There were present: Councillors Gotobed (in the chair), Bolt, Cowper, Groves, Ingham, Mac- Intyre, Barker and Warburton; and the officials, Messrs. W. Mullard (clerk), W. Tim- perley (assistant clerk) and D. Mort (surveyor).

div.head: PROPOSAL APPROVED.
div.p: PROPOSAL APPROVED.

The rate recommended to be fixed to meet current expenses was 3s. 3d. in the Z. Last half-year's rate was 2s. 10d. The new rate pro- posed was unanimously agreed to on the motion of Councillor Parker, seconded by Councillor Cowper.

div.head: TRADESMEN'S DECISIONS.
div.p: TRADESMEN'S DECISIONS.
Lengthy Discussions On Important Questions At Quarterly Meetimi.

A fairly well-attended meeting of the Lymm Tradesmen's Association, held in Hirst's Pavilion on Tuesday evening, discussed at length many important questions. Dir. David Daniels (president) occupied the chair.

It was ;Wed that the ?` M.C." had found the secretary's proposed programme for Citizens' Sunday unworkable, and Mr. Odber said he thought the committee were to blame.—The Chairman thought "it had been done to avoid friction."
It was unanimously decided (on the motion of Messrs. F. E. Evans and 11. S. Saville) that no picnic be held this year.
Public Bodies' Support.

Much argument arose from -a- complaint made by Mr. H. E. Odber, who had been reported to have supported the secretary's remarks, at the last Association meeting, anent the lack of opportunity extended to Lymm traders by local public bodies spending public money. It was admitted that Mr. Odber made it quite clear at the time that he had no comploint to make. _ .
The Tradesmen desire now to make no com- plaint anent lack of public bodies' support.
Earlier Closing, &c.

A letter of 'hearty thanks from the Rector, for congratulation upon the birth of his son, was noted with pleasure. Attention was drawn to the fact that Some members of the Association were, and had for some time, been trading with an institution whose aims were in opposition to the private tradesmen's interests.—Several strong opinions were expressed, and the defaulters are tst .be acquainted that the Association has noted theii actions.
Whit-week holidays were fixed : Monday, all day; Wednesday, close at one; and Thursday, close at one—as usual.

Councillor Gotobed raised the question of still earlier closing on account of " war " direct and indirect. It was decided unanimously that from the first Thursday in June shops close at seven o'clock.

div.head: Council Chairman Congratulated.
div.p: Council Chairman Congratulated.

The Chairman spoke of the great honour paid to the association by the election of one of its members to the Council (chairmanship. Mr. Allman supported, and Councillor Goto- bed made suitable acknowledgment of the compliment.

div.head: PEN K Erni.
div.p: PEN K Erni.

The New Flates.—Messrs. James B. Aitken and Charles E. Parker (two of His Majesty's justices of the peace for the county) have just allowed the application of the overseers to levy a peer rate of 3s. in the £ for the half-year ending September 30th next. This is 4d. increase, and is caused by the larger calls upon the overseers, viz: The County Council, £722; the Warring- ton Union, £366; the Rural District Council, £238. These items total £270 more than for the corresponding period last year. The call for special expenses is £l2O, and the rate of 4d. in• the £ tepresents no change.

div.head: SANKEY.
div.p: SANKEY.

Football Club Whist Drive.—On Friday last week the Sankey Football Club held their annual whist drive tind dance in the Sankey School- room. There were about 90 visitors. Dancing was indulged in from 8 to 1.30, Messrs. Ray Brothers, of Sankey, providing the music. There were nine tables of whist, and the prizes, which were presented by Mrs. T. Cook, were won by Ladies: 1, Miss E. Jones; 2, Miss M. Gough; 3, Mrs. J. Wilkinson. Gentlemen: 1, Mr. F. Illidge ; 2, Mr. L. Davies; 3, Mr. J. Wilkinson.

Intercesrvion.—lnstead of the usual quarterly C.E. Men'A Society service, a special war inter- cession service was held in Sankey Church last Sunday afternoon. There was an excellent at- tendance. The sermon was preached by the , Rev. J. Martin, St. Peter's, Warrington, who. in the course of an earnest address, said if out of the present discord a perfect harmony is to be evolved and the nations are in the future to dwell together as one family, it can only be accomplished by the strong hand of God. Thig must be ever sought by the diligent and faith- ful prayers of His Church.

div.head: S "CULTURED WARRINGTON."
div.p: S "CULTURED WARRINGTON."

Sir,—ln your report of the recent visit of the North-Western Branch of the Library Association you quote me as having said that, "taking size into consideration, and exCepting the University towns, I ' doubt if there is any town in the country that is in front of Warrington in the number of people who are interested in the higher things of life —in literature, and in culture in general." Alas, the is should have been was! I was talk- ing of the Warrington of one hundred and fifty years ago! And it was of the "poetical works of" An Letitia Aikin (Mrs. Barbauld), not of " MisF, Lucy Aikin," that I "spoke in terms of high appreciation." Miss Lucy Aikin was a niece of Mrs. Barbauld, was born in Warrington in the house which stands at the corner of Orford - street and Buttermarket-street, and was an eminent writer and historian, and she well deserves remembrance on her own accord; but I do not think she claimed to be a poet, and it was Mrs. Barbauld who learned in Warring- ton the charm
"Of poetry's divine first finger-touch," and left to her adopted town the lasting laurels of mellifluous song.
ARTHUR BENNETT.
The Old Academy, 4th May, 1915.

div.head: "SOBRIETY
div.p: "SOBRIETY
AND ABSTINENCE."
Spirit That Should Assuredly Be
Manifest To-day.

Writing in the current issue of the S!. James' (Latchford) Parish Magazine, the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Firth) Says:—" At last it seems as if the country is realising that England is at war and that issues of unspeakable import- ance are at stake. Recruiting has become brisker, many of our own friends are at the Front, the Government have admitted the people to a greater share of their confidence. The English people have been told some un- pleasant truths. which have not been too well received, and one member of the Cabinet has had the courage to say that excessive drinking has played a part in delaying the output of the munitions of war which are so urgently re- quired.. An appeal has been made to the nation to show its sense of the gravity of the position by a general abstinence from alcoholic bever- ages during the time of war. Among the first to declare that he would forego such luxuries was our beloved King. and his example has been widely followed. The Archbishop of Canterburl had, some months before, urged the same course being taken, and now we have the happy com- bination of Church and State in an endeavour to promote that spirit of sobriety and abstin- ence which should assuredly be manifest in se critical a time as-this. I venture to hope that the examnle set by the King will be wide', copied by his loyal subjects who are parishioner° of St. James', Latchford."

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
A Striking Surname.

have long • been interested in surname origins, and have written much on the sub- ject in at least two papers while serving as editor. I was sorry to note that a Fleming bad figured discreditably in Warrington Police Court. I wondered if it occurred to many readers that the somewhat violent and excitable prisoner in that case, probably with- out herself knowing or caring anything about it, comes of a remote ancestry that, perse- cuted for their Protestantism in their own native Flanders, accepted the hospitality of Sympathetic co-religionists here, and, settling in this land of religious freedom and intel- lectual liberty, materially and permanently Contributed by peculiar industrial knowledge and skill to the commercial supremacy which We have for so many years enjoyed.

History Repeats Itself. The 'recent influx of Belgian refugees, and Our ready. recognition of their claims .upon our gratitude may thus fairly be said to mark a revival of the cordial relationship ex- isting between their and our forefathers, being in a very real, sense a repetition of their mutual experiences. Since I left the West Riding I have made a point of revisiting Hardcastle Crags each summer, and have never failed to climb the adjoining hill to the interesting old village of Heptonstail, with its ruined church and historic God's acre. I 011) just fresh from this yearly pilgrimage, and as usual it has added to my stock of reminiscences. In the churchyard I came unon the newly-made grave of a Belgian baby, the child of refugee parents whom it was the Pleasure of the villagers to entertain; and within a few feet lay the remains of some of 41; e Flemings of old whose trials in similar e'relunstances I have recalled. Anotlier fact arisin,, out of .the considera- ;lon of this fruitful theme may just be men- welled before I change the subject. On the advent of the earlier batches of Belgian exiles, Berne of us began to rub up our French in anticipation of usefulness as interpretators, and were naturally disappointed on learning that not a few of the refugees, being of the halmbler classes of Antwerp and thereabout, IPoke only Flemish. This variety of the -eirisian Low German, dialect, while nearly akin to the basis of our own language, has not been cultivated among us, and is familiar to very few of our people. This is t'ogrettable. One may well marvel at it, too, in view of the late Victorian revival of the glories of Flemish through the powerful n°vels of Hendrik Conscience and the works of the historian Blommaert, to say nothing the great merits and extreme local popu- aritY of the seventeenth century. poet Cats, who likewise wrcite in Flemish. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.
THE GERMAN MIND AND THE AMERICAN,

By the courtesy of friends in America I am able to read the articles through which tal- ented Germans are striving week by week to influence American opinion, and the words which they are addressing in their own lan- guage to the ,German-speaking population. Nothing reveals more completely the in- vincible stupidity of the Fatherland than this attempt to represent the war as a piece of philanthropy and Germany's contribution to- wards the progress of the race.

A number of these articles for American consumption have been quoted for the advan- tage of the readers of "The Examiner." In curious contrast are some voices that are be- ginning to be heard, and which will fall curi- ously upon the ears of Americans who have been assured a hundred times that Germany was innocent of any thought of war. We quote from "Der Tag," a German news- paper Of considerable standing.
"WE MADE OUR PLANS." •

" So =Old our calculations have deceived us. We expected that British India would rise when the first shot was fired in Europe, .but in reality thousands of Indians came to fight with the British against us. We antici- pated that the whole British Empire would be torn to pieces, but the Colonies appear to be closer than ever united with the Mother Country.

" We expected a triumphant rebellion in South Africa, yet it turned out nothing but a failure. -We expected trouble in Ireland, but instead she sent her _best soldiers against us. We anticipated that the party of peace at any price' would be dominant in England, but it melted away in the ardour to fight against Germany: We reckoned that England was degenerate and incapable of placing any weight in the scale, yet she seems to be our principal enemy. "The same has. been the case with France and Russia. We thought that France was depraved and divided, and we find that they are formidable opponents. We believed that the Russian people were far too discontented to fight for their_ Government, and we made our plans on the supposition of a rapid col- lapse of Russia, but, instead, she mobilised her millions quickly and well, and her people are full of enthusiasm and their power is crushing. " Those who.led us into all those 'mistakes and miscalculations have laid upon themselves a heavy responsibility."
AN EMINENT JURIST ON REPRISALS.
As an example of the working of the mind of the German intellectual, our readers may
Scathing Criticisms of the Pariah Amongst Nations.
like to weigh the words of Dr. Sieveking, a well-known writer and authority on interna- tional law : •

"Any infraction of the law of nations de- mands reprisals. As a reprisal it is, of course, permissible to visit undefended towns with bombs. Reprisal is punishment, and the more it is felt the better.

"The question of the possibility of combin- ing with it strategic or tactical results is quite a secondary matter. " We should, for example, be perfectly jus- tified, as a punishment for. Russian. maraud- ing raids, in showering bombs on Oxford or Cambridge, or imposing a high fine on French towns.

" From the juristic point of view our enemies, so far as they are Allies, form one entity, and the idea naturally occurs to make the civilised nations,' England and France, feel what kind of creatures their brothers in arms are."

div.head: MANY MISNOMERS.
div.p: MANY MISNOMERS.
Nanws Which In Certain Departments Of Science Are Misleading.

There are terms in certain departments of science that positively misname the products to which they are applied. The word " oil " in its more comprehensive and indiscriminate uses is made to include hydro-carbons, like petroleum, and also many other. substances that have an oily appear- ance, like " oil ot vitriol," which is not oil at all, but sulphuric acid. Strictly speaking, the mineral oils, includ- ing all petroleum products, are not oil, although .we speak of " coal oil" and " kero- sene oil." The best classifications of oils do not include mineral hydro-carbons, like naphtha, paraffin and petroleum, but treat only the two well- defined groups—fixed oils and fats, nfl the essential or T Ola!;;Ie oils.
" Copperas " is not copper, but sulphite of iron. • " Salt of lemon " has nothing to do with the fruit of the lemon tree, but is potas- sium binoxalate, or potash treated with oxalic acid.

• "Carbolic acid" is not an acid, but a phenol. In structure it is allied to the alco- hols, and has only slight acid properties. "Soda water" has no trace of soda. "Sul- phuric acid" contains no sulphur. " Sugar of lead " is innocent of sugar.

" Cream of tartar" has nothing to do with cream, nor " milk of lime " with milk. "Ger- man silver" is a stranger to silver, and " black lead" is not lead at all, but graphite. " Mesaic gold " is a ,sulphide of tin. These misleading names have come down from the vocabulary of an early and inexact chemistry. As popular science extends the old terms are yielding to the more scientific nomenclature.

div.head: MANY MORE MALES
div.p: MANY MORE MALES
Than Females in Russia and a
Premium oil Brides.

So far as • the, returns of the nry census show, Russia, unlike every other European country, has a male population far outnum- bering the female. Indeed, in certain dis- tricts an actual bonnnercial value is set upon marriageable women, and a profitable "com- merce in brides " is being carried on by en- terprising peasants. These matrimonial in- termediaries bring a number of marriageable girls from European Russia, obtaining cheap tickets for them on some pretext or another, and play the part of father or guardian in the ensuing negotiations with the settlers. Their average cash profit on each bride is ,between 40 and 100 roubles, and in addition to this they get presents and vodka, according to the means 'of the bridegrooms. ‘The new census shows that the male in- habitants of Petrograd outnumber the female by 124,000. The total population of the capital is now 1,454.704, showing an in- crease of 230,000, or nearly 19 per cent., as compared with the census of 1900. There are 315,632 children between the ages of 1 and 15., and of these 163,476, are boys and 152,158 are girls.

div.head: PARIAH AMONG NATIONS.
div.p: A PARIAH AMONG NATIONS.
America does not lack journalists' who can say the right word in reply to German cant and apply the right adjective to her barbarity. The " New York World " deals this sledge- hammer blow :

" There is no parallel in all history to this super-stupidity. "Every blunder that diplomacy could com- mit was committed by the time the war was fairly under way. Every blunder that a mili- tary autocracy could commit in the name of ruthless war ' is well on the way to be com- mitted. The ability of the German Govern- ment to inflame the public opinion of other countries against Germany and the German cause seems to know no limits.

" The" situation is .so grotesque that • it would be humorous if it were not so ghastli tragical. • "To be defeated in war is Unfortunate, but it is not necessarily fatal. Many great nations have survived such defeats, made an honour- able peace, bound up their wounds,. and gone forward to new greatness. But to become a pariah among nations is a calamity that no nation could survive, and that is the grave danger that now menaces Germany. It is a danger from which her worst enemy would wish to spare her. "When Germany was weak and divided, Bismarck's genius welded it into a mighty empire that ought under wise government to have endured for centuries. Genius. passes away, but the folly Of fools is into everlast- ing." A.M.

div.head: AN EDUCATION PROBLEM.
div.p: AN EDUCATION PROBLEM.
No Room For Collage Homes' Children At Paduate.
NI, WHIM. ON'S OFFER.
A matter affecting the education of the children in the Warrington Guardians' Cottage Homes was discussed at Wednesday's meeting of the Board. Mr. A. J. Jolley presided.

div.head: MINUTE MATTER.
div.p: A MINUTE MATTER.

The Rev. .1. M. Mtchell, after the minutes had been read, raised a question on the matter of a recent election to a vacancy on the Assess- ment Committee. The contest between himself (as representing Burtonwood) and a Warring- ton representative resulted in favour of the latter by reason of the Chairman giving his casting vote to the Warrington representative, after voting, in the first instance, for him (Mr. Mitchell). It was. merely recorded on the min- utes that the election had taken place. Nothing was said about the contest, and he thought it ought to be recorded that a contest took place. lie bad no personal animus in the matter, but he thought that Burtonwood was entitled to the representation, and that mention should be made of the contest.
The Chairman: You don't question the accu- racy of the minute, but the fullness? ' The Clerk said that. no record was taken of the vote because it was taken on a show of hands.
The Rev. A: M. Mitchell commented that whether a record Of the actual vdting were in- cluded or, not, it ought to be mentioned that there was a contest.
Mr. , Wle asked Whether there was any rule with regard to the order of taking Totes in such matters.
The Chairman replied in the negative, adding that it saved time to take a show of hands.
NURSES' SUCCESS.

Dr. Bowden reported that two of the Board's probationer nurses had just passed their final examination, with 91 and 90 per cent. of marks, respectively, in the practical work. This was.a reflection of the excellent training they had had whilst in the Board's employ.

div.head: TRANSFERENCE OF CHILDREN.
div.p: TRANSFERENCE OF CHILDREN.

The Homes Committee reported that a letter was read froMthe.Director of Education, County Offices, Preston, enclosing a copy of a letter received by him from Mr. H. Denham, corre- spondent to the Church of England 'School, Padgate, relative to the proposed transference of children from the Cottage Homes to the Church of England School, Padgate, for educa- tional purposes. The recognised ' accommoda- tion of the school was 326, and the number of children at present on the register ,was 300; the number of children from the borough of War- rington who were attending the school was 72. During the past few years over £l,OOO had been raised by voluntary effort and expended in the enlargement of the school, which would now satisfy the requirements of the township, under normal conditions, for many years to come. the children from the Cottage Homes were transferred to the school, an enlargement would be necessary at a very early date, and such enlargement would have to be done by volun- tary effort. If voluntary effort should not be forthcoming—which was very likely—then, it would necessitate an expenditure of some £lO,OOO, and mean a heavy increase in the rates of the township, and money already spent on the existing accgmmodation at the Cottage Homes would be wasted. The nuinagers were of opinion that it ivas not possible to find accom- modation at the school, and that to attempt to do so would involve unnecessary expenditure, in view of the provision for the efficient teaching of the children already existing At the Cottage Homes.

ACCOMMODATION AT OAKWOOD SCHOOL. The report further stated that a letter was also 1.11(1 from the ,Director of Educatton at Warrington, stating that that authority was Quite willing ,to permit the children from the Cottage homes to attend the, Oakwood Council School when it was completed, if the Guardians were prepared to make, under Section 2 of the Education Act, 1900, a maintenance contribu- tion according to the net cost per head in. re- spect to the average attendance of the children. The Clerk was instructed to ascertain the amount the Guardians would be called upon to pay, if the terms of the Warrington Education Committee were agreed to.

div.head: STEADY IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: STEADY IMPROVEMENT.

Mr. F. 0. Mann, L.G.B. Inspector, reported having visited the Padgate Homes. The steady improvement started by • the new master had been continued, and it was gratifying to see that there were growing signs of interest and responsiveness amongst the children.

div.head: RURAL MATTERS.
div.p: RURAL MATTERS.
Ilr. AV. Furness Re-elected Chairman Of 'the i‘arritioton.ll.D.(:.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S SERIOUS ILLNESS.
Mr. W. Furness was re-elected chairman of the Warrington Rural District Council 'at the annual meeting of that body, held in Bewsey Chambers, Warrington,- on Wednesday after- noon.

div.head: Could Not Have A Better Chairman
div.p: Could Not Have A Better Chairman

The re-election of Mr. Furness was proposed by Mr. J. Ball, who.said that the Council could not be better suited in the matter of a chair- man; they could not have a better man for the post, or one who took more interest in his work.

Mr. G. Mather seconded, and the proposition was carried unanimously, it being made clear that the re-election was for the remainder of the period during which the Council might sit, before the next elections of members, assum- ing that the war again interferes with them. Returning' thanks, the Chairmtan expressed himself as much, obliged for the ebnfidence the Council had again reposed in him., It had been a pleasure to preside over the council meetings during the past twelve months, for he had had the entire support of the.members, all working together in harmony for the com- mon interests of the ratepayers.

div.head: "The Right Vice-Chairman."
div.p: "The Right Vice-Chairman."

Mr. Mather proposed Iho re-election. of Mr. P. Lougton as vice-chairman, ,the Rev. A. M. Mitchell seconding and remarking that during the coming period, however long it might be, the Council would be served by the right chair- man and the right vice-chairman. (Applause.) Mr. Longton had conducted the meetings over which be had been called to preside in a most business-like manner.

The proposition having been carried, Mr. Longton briefly acknowledged the compliment paid him by his re-election. • The various committees of the Council were re-elected en bloc. • Lowest Death-rate on Record.

Dr. Sephton, jun., attended, and explained that .his father, the medical officer of health to the Council was seriously ill and unable to be present and. make his usual report. In con- sequence, he was deputisingv for his father in the matter, and desired to report that, among other things, the monthly rnedical report showed that the death-rate. (3.2 per 1,000 of the Population) was the • smallest on record, the Chairman adding: "'that speaks volumes for the district."

div.head: Sympathy With The Medical Officer.
div.p: Sympathy With The Medical Officer.

Mr. G. Mather moved that a vote of sym- pathy, be accorded the Medical Officer in his illness, and said that it was more than half a century since he first became acquainted with Dr. Sephton, sea. During that time he had found the Doctor among the first of all men; full of everything that could make a man a real man in this world. (Hear, hear.) The Doctor had never Spared himself, night or day, when sick people required his services, and he had 'not merely given those services for the sake of half-crown fees, but for the love of his neighbours and 'of suffering humanity in general. In Dr.. Sephtan, sen., the Council had one of the best and most conscientious officers that could be wished for; a man who always studied the good of the district before everything else. When the time came and they must lase his services they would find it difficult to get anybody to adequately fill his place. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Ball seconded the proposition. The Chairman, in supporting, added his tri- bute to the worth of the services of Dr. Seph- ton, sen. The Doctor had, said the Chairman, not only been a genial presence at ..the Council meetings, but lie had, time to time, given abundant proof that he had the best interests of the public at heart. He was no mere time- server. (Hear, bear.) There were times when be could have made recommendations that would have put•money in his own pockets and those of the medical profession in the district, but he always looked to the interests of the ratepayers first; indeed, lie was ever ready to sacrifice himself in the interests of the people whom he was called upon to serve. (Hear, hear.)

The Vif:T-Chairman (Mr. P. Longton), the Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Mr. J. Backhouse added their tributes to the worth of Dr. Sephton, sen., as medical officer of health for the district, and the proposition was carried unanimously. Dr. Sephton, jun., expressed thanks, on be- half .of his father and family, and said that anything that the Medical Officer of . Health had done he would only be too pleased to do again if health were given him. However, when one reached the age of 88 life hung by a very slender thread and his father's illness was a really serious matter, though, of course, his family hoped for the best. His father had been in practice since 1857.
An Acquisition.

It was reported that at a meeting of the General Purposes and Finance Committee the Clerk again produced the draft Provisional Order altering the county boundary. Upon examination of the plan, and, explanation by the Surveyor,, it was found that a small por- tion of land was 'added to the Council's dis- trict at Rixton-with-Glazebrook, and the com- mittee recommended that the Clerk inform the, Local Government' Board that the Clerk had no observations to make on the matter.
The recommendation was adopted. New Road for Old.

The Surveyor reported with regard to the Council's claim in respect to the repairing of the Burtonwood roads—necessitated by the extra traffic consequent upon the diversion of the main route through Warrington to Man- chester and Liverpool, owing to .the re-build- ing of Sankey Bridge—that the County Coun- cil, through. their Surveyor (Mr. Schofield), had offered to allow the Rural District Coun- cil threequaTters of the sum expended by them on the work, up to a maximum for the county of .1610 10s. That would mean that the Rural District Council would be called -upon to pay a sum of £203 .10s., whilst the county found £6lO 10s..

•In answer to a Member, the Surveyor added that the question which naturally occurred was as to whether they should spend £203 10s. on behalf of the County Council in. Burton- Wood? Up till recently, however, the District Council had failed to get a better offer from, the County Council than the payment of three- quarters of the cost. They had hoped to have had an offer which would have covered any outlay that had been required. , The Rev. A. Mitchell asked the Surveyor whether he considered the County Council's offer a • remarkable one, and one that they ought to accept. The Surveyor (Mr. B. S. Newcombe) replied that there Were two points of view, .and, look- ing at it from one of those standpoints, he did not 'consider it reasonable to accept less than the full cost of the work. On the ether hand, however, the District Council would certainly derive some. slight .advantage from the fact of the work having been done by the County Council. • The Chairman. suggested that. the Council should accept the contribution offered by • the County Council, for, after all, the Rural Coun- cil must remember that the County Council were_going to make a-much more permanent job of the roadway than had ever been made before. In the long run the Rural. District Council would probably find that.a.saving had been effected, for as time went on they might not find themselves face to face. with the same amount of expenditure on the roads in ques- tion as previously. Therefore, although they were spending a large percentage of the total sum expended on the making up of the stretch of roadway concerned, it behoved them to bear in mind that they were getting a more permanent and lasting surface and one that should prove more satisfactory than it had ever proved before. He thought the Council owed a satisfactory road to Burtonwood, for the district had been suffering in the matter of its principal road for many years. It was decided to accept the County 'Council's terms, and, immediately the bridge is opened up, to take steps to get the roads concerned into a proper condition as soon as possible.
Vocal or Instrumental?
It has never yet been decided by competent authorities whether snoring is vocal or instru- mental music. Calling it "sheet music" dcmszet settle the matter at all.

div.head: DESPITE THE WAR.
div.p: DESPITE THE WAR.

The captain of the Warrington Cycling Club, Mr. J. B. Poole, took the chair at the annual meeting, held at the Patten Arms, on Monday evening. He was supported by the Hon. Sec- retary (Mr. C. A. Berry) and Hon. Treasurer (Mr. A. G. Robertson). There was a fair attendance.

div.head: CLUB AS STRONG AS EVER.
div.p: CLUB AS STRONG AS EVER.

The lion. Secretary presented the 29f1i annual report, which showed that on the whole the past season had been a successful one. While attendances at club runs showed only a .moder- ate improvement, the .social and bowling fix- tures had again been well supported. The club was numerically as strong at present as it had been at any period, the membership standing at 110, a figure which represented a slght increase on the previous year. The earlier fixtures of the past season were excep- tionally well attended, and everything augured well for one -of the most successful seasons of recent years. The falling off occurred early in August at the. time of the outbreak of war. Fifteen Saturday afternoon. fixtures were car- ried out, the attendance averaging fourteen. "kbe prizes for run attendances were won by Mr. J. 13 Poole, Mr. H. W. Whittle and Mr. C. A. Berry. Reviewing the bowling side of the club's activities during the past season, it could again he placed, on record that interest in the Wednesday evening. Sankey meetings bad been well sustained throughout the season. Members who had long ago renounced the .heel retained their interest in the club and its doings by attending the many congenial meetings at the Chapel Hoye. The average attendance at the Wednesday evening bowling meetings was 20. The series of knock-out bowling competitions were , well supported. There were 33 entries for the main proper, and the 'winners of prizes in the principal and consolation handicaps were :—Principal handi- cap: 1 and " Watkin's "Cup, A. 0. Robertson; 2, A. Kenyon; 3, C. A. Berry. First consola- tion handicap: 1, J. Houghton; 2, G. Steeples. Second consolation handicap: 1, A. Beddard ; 2, L. C. Daintith. Third consolation handi- cap: 1, A. N. Chester; 2, W. P. Ashton. Fourth consolation handicap: • 1,. 11. Rush- worth; 2, J. Emmett. Owing to the national crisis, the usual winter programme in con- nection with the club was dropped. The cancelled winter programme, however, had, to a considerable extent, been replaced by the shooting meetings at the Whitecross Works' range. In the earlier stages 'those meetings were well attended, but latterly the members had somewhat fallen off, due, no doubt, to the fact that many of the members had joined the Preparatory Training Corps. Several shoot- ing competitions had been carried out, and it had been demonstrated that the club num- bered amongst its members a few very excel- lent shots'.

div.head: CLUB'S ROLL OF HONOUR.
div.p: CLUB'S ROLL OF HONOUR.

. . Tte following memberhe s, t report continued, had responded e to the call to arms and were serving in the Army: Messrs. AV. H. Bellian, L. C. Daintith, F. Greenwood, H. Hayes, T. Hewitt, S. Partridge, H. Rushworth, R. Park- inson, E. Stirrup, H. Law, A. Spinks, and R. Davies. •

The report concluded with an intimation of the Secretary's intention of -resigning. Mr. C. Houghton, in proposing the adoption of the report, commented on its excellence and expressed the hope that Mr. Berry would see his way to "remain in office and so tide the club over an anxious time. If the club were to lose his 4rvices as secretary it would suffer considerably.

Mr. T R. Critchley seconded and also paid a tribute to the work Mr. Berry had done for the club—work which he (the speaker) felt the whole of the members would regret to see him give up. The report was adopted.

div.head: CLUB'S FINANCES.
div.p: THE CLUB'S FINANCES.

, The Hon. Treasurer (Mr. A. G. Robertson) submitted a satisfactory statement of accounts disclosing the fact that the club was worth .L 29 9s. 6-Id. A donation of .L 5 it was stated, was made to the Prince of Wales' Fund. The accounts were passed.

div.head: AN EXCELLENT CAPTAIN.
div.p: AN EXCELLENT CAPTAIN.

A vote of thanks was accorded the Captain (Mr. J. B. Poole), on the proposition of the Hon. Secretary, who observed that the success of most of the functions that had been held dur- ing Mr. Poole's captaincy had been largely due to his geniality.
i Mr. G. F. Freeman seconded this proposition, which was carried.
The Captain, replying, said that some of the best times of his life had been spent with the members of the Club, than whom he wished to meet no more congenial set of men.

div.head: AN OLD MEMBER AND SUB-CAPTAIN.
div.p: AN OLD MEMBER AND SUB-CAPTAIN.

Before resuming his seat, Mr. Poole proposed a vote of thanks to the Sub-Captain (Mr. H. W. Whittle), who, he said, had -helped him a great deal. Incidentally, he mentioned that Mr. Whittle's membership of the club was of longer -standing than that of the majority of their number.
Mr. Critehley seconded, and the motion hav- ing been endorsed, Mr. Whittle replied in a few apt words.
"AN INIMITABLE SECRETARY."

Mr. George Newburn, in proposing a vote of thanks to the lion. • Secretary, described Mr. Berry as an inimitable secretary, and warmly eulogised the services he bad rendered. His loss at such . a time was more than the club could afford.
Mr. .T. Houghton seconded, and, in doing so, made reference to the Secretary's excellent work as the representative of the Club on the infirmary Committee.

div.head: ,Secretary's "Sporting Offer "-
div.p: The ,Secretary's "Sporting Offer "-

• The lion. Se. cretary, in the course of his response, said that he had rendered the club such services as he had been able out of love of the club. Consisting of the members it had, he felt he could not but do his utmost in their interests. At the same time there were cer- tain other calls that ,were often rather pressing and that claimed a good deal of time; and, again, lie had found himself wondering whe- ther he was not becoming a trifle stale. Hav- ing alluded to the work the club was doing in helping the Infirmary and other charities, the Hon. Secretary thanked the members for ,the kind remarks that had been made, and stated that lie had no .wish to leave the club in the lurch and was prepared to continue in office providing no one else came forward to fill the post. (Applause.)

- Votes Of thanks were accorded to the Hon. Treasurer, the committee, aml the honorary auditors, on the proposition of Mr. J. Critch- ley, seconded by Mr. G. Newburn. The Chairman proposed the election of Mr. W. H. Whittle to the captaincy, and this was seconded by Mr. A. Beddard and carried un- animously. 'Mr, T. Berry was elected sub-captain. •

Is Accepted. Advantage was taken of Mr. C. A. Berry's pffer to continue in the office of secretary, pro- vided nobody else could be found, and he was enthusiastically re-elected, on the proposition of Mr. G. Bowman, seconded by Mr. H. W. Whittle.
The Treasurer (Mr. A. G. Robertson) was also re-elected.

The following w6re electefl to constitute the committee: Messrs. J. B. Poole, F. Garnett, C. E. Houghton, F. Fieldhouse, J. L. Emmett, G. H. .Anderton, and P. 0. Bailey. The Hon. Auditors (Messrs. G. F. Freeman ad W. Litton) were re-elected.
, Mr. James Critchley, with the Hon. Secretary and the captain, were elected the club's repre- sentatives on .the National Cyclists' Union.
VOTES OF THANKS.

Mr. and Mrs. Burley, the manager and manageress of the Patttn Arms Hotel, and Mrs. Unsworth, of the Sankey Chapel House, were accorded a vote of thanks for the manner in which they had catered for the members of the club during the past season.

div.head: CYCLE AS A TIME SAVER.
div.p: THE CYCLE AS A TIME SAVER.

Quo reason why a larger number of i.e.sple do not live Out in the country, away front the Uirt and noise of the cities and towns where they have perforce to work, is that the time taken, and the unpleasantness experienced by making the journey by train, does not appear to com- pensate them for the benefits they would attain by living in the country. It is tiring to have to wait for train, and then to make the trip in an overcrowded carriage. This, twice a day, is sufficient to deter many. If the cycle is made to take the place of the train, however, the disadvantages are all done away with. A ten or twelve mile spin into town .in the morn- ing is invigorating, and fits one for the work of the day. The return journey at night enables one to throw off the worries of the day, The fresh air, instead of a stuffy compartment, the exercise instead of being packed like sardines in a box, and the saving of time, makes cycling a pleasure as well as a convenience.

div.head: WHAT SIZE IN'BICYCLES.
div.p: WHAT SIZE IN'BICYCLES.

This is a question that the dealer seldom thinks of asking, yet it is equally important to have a cycle to fit, as it is to have one's wearing apparel made to measure. Most people imagine that it is quite sufficient if they can manipulate the: saddle pillar and the handle-bars, so as to enable them to reach the pedals without an effort. This is not correct. To enjoy cycling to the full the balance of the machine must be maintained. A good machine must be well balanced, in the same way as a gun. As a general rule, each cycle is turned out with the saddle and the handle-bars the correct height. True, in all probability they may have to be altered slightly to suit the rider, but this adap- tation, should not amount to much. To obtain the maximum amount of power with a mini- mum expenditure of energy, the saddle should sbe of such a height that when the pedal is at its lowest the leg should be just comfortably stretched. Have the machine that fits you if you desire comfort.

div.head: CARE OF THE BICYCLE.
div.p: THE CARE OF THE BICYCLE.

If smoothness of running is desired, as is certainly the ease if the full pleasure of cycling is to be experienced, a few minutes should be devoted occasionally to looking over the work- ing parts of the machine. This. will only occupy a short time, but every second so spent will repay the rider. There are so many little things that can get out of order—a thing which usually happens when least expected or wanted. Nuts, cotter-pins, &c., should be tightened, and, if on the point of giving, out, renewed. The bearings, brake-blocks and the valve-tubing should be, inspected. The tyres should' also cdme in for their share of attention. It is wonderful how the value of a .tyre can be in- creased by the aid of a little stout canvas, Or a band fixed On the cover. The alignment of the wheels should also be noted. If out of the true, the fault should be rectified. The effect of a wheel running out of track is to strain the machine, and very probably cause more rapid tyre wear.

div.head: DANGER OF " TINKERIMG."
div.p: THE DANGER OF " TINKERIMG."

A very large number of people are taking up the pastime of motor-cycling for the first time this season, and therefore I want to give them a little bit of advice before they run into error. It is on the question of "tinkering." Every rider shOuld take a big interest in his mount, learning all he can about its mechanism. He will find the whole field of motor-cycle engineer- ing•a most fascinating one. But this may prove his undoing. One frequently hears ,a motor- cyclist says he has done so and so to increase the speed of his mount, or something else to make it a better hill-climber. If he is an ex- pert, all well and good. If he is not, it won't be long before his machine has to go back to the makers for a general overhaul. There are many jobs that an amateur can tackle success- fully, but all big things should be left to the professional man. This will be found to be good advice in the long run.

THE STANDARDISATION OF RIMS. At last this subject is receiving the attention that it undoubtedly deserves. Why the question has not been tackled before is a mystery. The standardisation of motor-cycle rims and tyres is a necessity. I am glad to hear that things are now moving rapidly, and it should not be long before the question is settled in a satisfactory
en

manner. When the official sanction of the engineering standards committee of the Cycle and Motor-cycle Manufacturers' and Traders' Union has been received, the type committee will be able to go ahead. They have evolved a number of different rim standards for 'certain sizes of tyres. It is not expected that there will be any difficulty experienced in getting makers, both at home and abroad, to adopt the stand- ards. This is really good news. The grumbles we have indulged in, owing to the non-inter- changeability of tyres, will then happily become a thing of the past.

div.head: ST. LUKE'S CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: ST. LUKE'S CYCLING CLUB.

div.head: ACCUMULATOR CAPACITY.
div.p: ACCUMULATOR CAPACITY.

Those who make use of accumulators for light- ing purposes, instead of an ordinary dynamo set, would do well to work out the number of hours' light that can be expected from them when 'fully. charged. If the lights fail when out on the road, it is often extremely difficult to rig up something to enable one to reach home. Ti. lighting capacity of the accumulators can be worked out quite easily .by, the following method: The voltage of the system is divided into the total candle-power of the lamps, and ;the answer is then divided into the ampere hours of the accumulators. The final result will give the number of hours the lamps will burn, given that the wiring is in good order and the accumulators fully charged. As an example take the case\of a set of three lights, each of four candle-power, or four volts with two 40 ampere hour accumulators. The total candle-power of the lamp is 12. This divided by four volts gives three amperes. This again divided into the 80 ampere hours of the accumu- lators shows thaethe lights will burn for 26 2-3 hours.

div.head: SPARE SPARKING PLUGS.
div.p: SPARE SPARKING PLUGS.

It is of no use advising motorists to carry a, spare sparking plug in their kit, since practi- cally everybody does so. All, however, are not as careful as they might be in looking after them. To carry them loose in the box contain- ing the small spares, means. that they may be destroyed. Yet very many motorists do this. A simple device will prevent damage. I use the metal box in which shaving soap is purchasvd. A small wad of felt or cotton wool, at either end, will hinder injury, and the plug cart be relied upon to keep in good working condition. In the garage at home one usually has a few extra sparking plugs, and these require look- ing after as well. For storing them I hays a piece of soft wood a foot long, and about two inches away from the next. The plugs sire in- serted in the holes, and, by turning them rnana, they make a thread for themselves. This I have found to be a convenient way for storing tbens in the garage.

div.head: HUB. TESTING A CYCLE'S COMFORT.
div.p: THE HUB. TESTING A CYCLE'S COMFORT.

The famous Old Kent-road, of London, has the reputation of being a perfect testing-ground for cycles; its natural condition being such that all wheelmen who have ridden over it will agree that it has "knocked 'em" in a way never con- sidered by Chevalier. But a cycle that will make even the Old Kent-road endurable must be well designed as well as properly saddled, and therefore the testimony Mr. E. Henson, of 23, Maryon-road, Old 'Charlton, gives to his Raleigh is Of quite special interest. "The springing is so excellent," he states, "that after five years' ,use I can ride at a real good pace along the Old Kent-road, which is no mean testi- monial I can assure you, and would not be pos- sible on many makes. All my friends who have tried the Raleigh say that they have never been on such a smooth and easy-running machine." The secret lies, of course, in the design as much as in the saddle, for the design of the Raleigh gives rigidity under driving stress, but resilience where it is needed to ensure comfort. It is the perfect combination of the two faculties which constitute the charm of the all-steel bicycle.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

The Princess Juliana of Holland., The little Princess Juliana of Hol- land. the only child of Queen Wilhel- mina, is- now :approaching the comple- tion A her sixth year, consequently her education is about to be seriously begun, and a governess has been engaged for her. This lady is said to be an American, but as she bears the name of Stewart, it is just possible that she may be of British nationality. The majority of European Court and minor Royal Families, show a preference for English teachers and nurses, even when they themselves are little in sympathy with the British people, and their in- stitutions. Queen Wilhelmina was educated by an English lady, who resided for many years at the Dutch Court. The little Princess will, for some time to come, receive all religious instruc- tion from her mother only.
" Our Own Princess" and The Guild of The
Brave Poor Things.

The many efforts made on behalf of the Belgians, and of our soldiers, the sailors, and their wives and families, all deserving the utmost we .can do for them, overshadow many admirable institutions founded in happier days. A pathetic interest attaches to the Heritage Craft Schools, founded by Mrs. C. W. Kimmins, at Chailey, Sussex, for crippled boys and girls. The schools are the outcome of Mrs. Ewing's "„Story ;of a ,Short Life." princess .Louise, Duchess. of Argyle, is the patron, and tenderly she watches over and helps the brave cripples who call her "Our Own Princess." Many lame boys and girls have been completely cured after a longer or shortef residence, and of the former no fewer than six are now in the Army. The nui•ses have lately given up their room, and the children their library, in order to accom- modate a number of wounded soldiers, who are being nursed back to health in this delightful Sussex home and village.

Rice and Lentil Savoury. A teacupful each of rice and lentils, three onions chopped, pepper and salt. Cover them with water and cook slowly, adding more water ' as required. A double saucepan (or a jar stood in a saucepan of water) is best, to avoid burning.

Cheese and Potato Pie. Put Ilb. of peeled potatoes and 2oz. rice on to cook. (irate ilb. cheese. Mash potatoes, and mix one-third of them with the cooked rice, the cheese, lb. bread-crumbs, 10z. margarine, one egg and some pepper and salt. Add some gravy, if mixture is not moist enough. Put in a pie dish and cover the rest with potatoes. Put some margarine in 'small pieces over top of pie. Bake a golden brown colour in quick oven.

Flowers. • To keep cut flowers so they will not wither and die quickly, insert their stems in water in: which 25 grains of ammopia chloride have been dissolved. Flowers can be preserved in this way for two or three weeks. To preserve them per- manently for several months dip them into per- fectly limpid gum water and then allow them to drain. The gum forms a complete coating on the stems and petals and preserves their shape and colour long after they have become dry. Any kind of flowers can be well preserved for at least two weeks by putting a little saltpeter or carbonate of soda in the water in which the flowers are left standing.

Spring Cleaning. Spr;ng . cleaning season has been called the "time of a woman's life." Personally, says Maud in "Farm and, Home," I cannot agree with that, as no one can really enjoy having the house at sixes and sevens while this mysterious performance "spring cleaning" is going on. Now that women have other interests besides housework, spring cleaning is usually so arranged that it does not interfere at all with the comfort of the home, only one room being undertaken, and finished right off, before another is commenced. But whether you go in for this method, or for the old way of having the whole house under process at the same time, you will certainly require a suitable overall for the 'work, and if you purchase double width casement cloth you can by folding it over cross- wise, and then lengthwise, cut yourself an over- all with sleeves cut in with the garment, so that you have but the underarm and sleeve seams to sew. It can be round or square in neck finish and slipped over the head, as no opening is really required at back or front, but it is newer and, in my opinion, more dressy to have the front cut down and finished with press studs or buttons and buttonholes. In cellars, and among the ruins of their once com- fortable and happy homes—for Belgium was one of the most prosperous cduntries in the world— these women are still keeping their flag flying. Some of their lace, made under the most trying circumstances, has been smuggled over here, and was shown lately at an exhibition held at the International Women's Art Club. At the opening ceremony M. Lambotte. who had suc- ceeded in bringing over the greater part of the pieces and specimens, pointed out that if Englishwomen bought hand-made lave for their lingerie, the women of Belgium would be helped to a very large extent. It is possible that Belgian lace will be made permanently in this country. as a number of workrooms have been established for those refugees who are with us, and the art is being taught to English girls.
The New Corsets.

The change in' the silhouette this season may be described as an evolution rather than a revo- lution, therefore the alteration in the shape of corsets is by .no means as drastic as in skirts and coats. The chief features to be noted are higher busts. A suggestion of curtves at the sides and fronts, a " nip " at the waist, and a shorter skirt. The new models follow strictly the natural curves of the body, and mould the figure into graceful lines. The slight curve at the front and sides gives that suggestion of roundness which rightfully belongs to the -feminine figure. Many delightful 'models are shown in silk .baptiste, silk-finished suede, and handsome brocades. Every type of figure hits been studied most carefully by manufacturers, who predict great success for the corset that laces in front. Few women comprehend the im- portance of properly lacing their corsets, and many disappointing results may be attributed to ignorance on this apparently trivial point.

Three-quarter Coats. Moire has heretofore been considered the special privilege of the elderly woman, but this year's coats are so youthful in design and detail, that the gin of seventeen will find models of moire as suitable to her Wage, as to that of her grandmother. , Such a model has a wide sash belt, caught with long buckles of moire. and 'flutings gave fullness to the back. The skirts are always wide, and flare at the sides. Covert coating is almost an obsession at the present moment. It is worn indiscriminately over afternoon or morning dresses, and is par- ticularly suited to the three-quarter overcoat. In the prettier shades of khaki, this material makes charming suits or coats, trimmed with steel buttons. Blue serge ranks next in favour, the darker shades being preferred, and these are often trinimed with black patent leather. This modish trimming is used now on colours, more particularly in red, by milliners and by tailors.

div.head: Summer. Capes.
div.p: Summer. Capes.

Parisian dressmakers are adding the quaintest of capes as a finish or ornament—for they can- pot be said to have any use—to afternoon and evening dresses. Frequently they are of the some material as the dresses, or they may be of taffetas in the same shade, but are at their best in tulle, or laces, of the filmiest makes. These little capes fly from the shoulders, and do not cover the arms. they are very full, and often fall below the waist. From the shoulders the fullness is gathered into a stand-up collar, the cape suggesting wings rather than anything else. At several recent fashionable weddings
