div.head: " Worse Than The Disease."
div.p: " Worse Than The Disease."
"According to this recipe," said Mrs. Biffing- ham, "sliced onions scattered about a room will absorb the odour of fresh paint."
"I guess that's right," rejoined Biffingham. "Likewise, also, a broken neck will relieve a man of a cold."
Easily Destroyed.

The pearl is nothing but carbonate of lime, and vinegar or any other acid will eat away the polished surface in a few moments. As for the opal, hot water is fatal to it, destroying its fire, and sometimes causing it to crack. Soap is a deadly enemy to the turquoise. If a tur- quoise ring is kept on the hand while washing, in a short time the blue stones will turn to a dingy green.

National Opinions on Woman. " The Greeks say love is blind, but marriage is clear-sighted enough, and they add that after three 'days the most troublesome things in the world are rain, a guest and a wife." The Persians say "Always consult your wife, and then do as you please." They say, too, "Many wives are a good thing, for while they quarrel you are left in peace." A German will tell you that a woman and a stove ought not to stir out of the house. The Indian says that you test gold by apply- ing acid, the strength of a camel by loading it, a man's character by listening to him, and a woman's thoughts—" By Allah," they break off, "it cannot be done."

"I cannot say, darling; but it is wonderful did not care for these delights, liked to bring their chairs and sit under the pleasant shade. But best of all were the rooks which built there, giving the children constant delight to watch and to learn all they could of the habits and customs of the birds. Every spring they would spend hours staring up among the branches at the birds as they flew to and fro, building their nests, and, later on, feeding the young and teaching them to fly. One very old tree was a particular favourite with the little Morleys, because there were so many nests in it, and year after year it was the nursery and home of young rooks. The chil- dren called it the "Rook Town," and gave it their chief attention.

div.head: Mystery of the Old Tree.
div.p: Mystery of the Old Tree.

But one year there was a change. "I can't think why the rooks do not seem to be going to the old tree," said Alice, sadly; "I have watched ever so many times, and I have not seen a single one go to any of the nests there."
"Perhaps they .are tired of the 'Town,'" said little Dick; "they want change of air, just as we do in summer."

"Oh, Dicky, I don't think it can be .that," said Alice, laughing; "all the trees are so close together. But perhaps it is, not too late yet." "Well, they'll have to be quick," said Tom, "for I climbed up the tree the other day and the nests are getting very ragged! 1 don't be- lieve the birds will go there at all now." • Just at this time a heavy gale of rain and wind set in, and as the elms were some little distance from the house, the 'children were not able to watch their beloved ropks- for some time.

div.head: After the Gale.
div.p: After the Gale.

On the first fine morning of a stormy week, as the children were sitting with their mother in the nursery, Tom burst into the room. '" Oh, I say, what do you think ?" he cried breathlessly: "the old elm-tree has been blown down! , You can see it was ever so rotten!" "The old tree?" "The Rook Town '!"

"Oh, the.poor birds; I am sorry!" "Why, Mother," cried Alice, "did you not know? The rooks did not go to that tree at all this year. Oh, I wonder if they knew it was not safe; do you think so, Mother dear ?"

div.head: Women Workers.
div.p: Women Workers.

Recent investigations show that a high per- centage of working women support relatives as well as themselves. Taking laundresses, nurses. domestic servants, and Post Office" women workers, more than half the total number engaged in these occupations contribute help in one way or another to the needs of their parents or other relatives. The number of women bread-winners is ever increasing, and the Labour Exchanges will be glad of the names and par- ticular:4 of any who are prepared to fill positions vacated by men. In many towns emnloyers cannot obtain workmen, or even errand boys, and the farmers in some diseects are allowing I?nd to go out of cultivation for want of labour. The charge that there has been an increase of drinking since the outbreak of war, has been made against women workers as well as men, but investigations do not bear out this allega- tion. Inquiries by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, tend to show that in nearly every case where there has been excess, the woman had been of drinking habits before the war.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information in Popular Lanuuage.

Don't Eat Quickly • Rapid 'eating is a common means of encourag- ing dyspepsia, which would be impossible if people took pains to masticate their 400 d as Nature intended. Efficient mastication brings out the delicate flavours of the food and makes the use of condiments superfluous. Careful chewing. of the food is one of the best means of preventing indigestion and dyspepsia, and such a practice also helps to preserve the teeth by putting them to their natural use. •Or Too Much

To eat to repletion is a mistake. It is always better to leave the table before the' appetite is satiated. Ovtreating brings un- comfortable feelings in the region of the stomach, if not actual pain, and makes one drowsy and 'lethargic and ready to have a good sleep. Such feelings after a meal are positive evidence of over eating. Between Meals.

No food of any kind should be taken between meals. The common habit of .taking sweets, cakes, pastries and fruit at any and all times is not conducive to good digestion and sooner or later brings trouble. Adults as well as children very often give way to this habit but always suffer in consequence sooner or later. Nothing but water or lemonade or some similar drink should be taken between meals.

Neuralgia. Cold and damp are especially prone to aggra- vate a neuralgic condition. The lack of certain elements in the food may also be a factor, the nerve not receiving the right kind of nutriment. Pressure along a nerve-trunk due to new growths or inflammation of the surrounding tissues is sometimes responsible. Perhaps it would be safe to 'say that the most frequent of all causes is the consumption of tea and coffee, the caffeine in these acting as a nerve-poison. The use of flesh meats, containing as they do uric acid, may be another factor in the causa- tion of this disease. Nicotine, the poison pre- sent in tobacco, must receive its share of blame. In all cases, it is a good plan to ascertain, if possible, the cause of the trouble and have this removed. Fomentations, a hot water bag, electric light applications, gentle massage, and the galvanic current, are amongst some simple home, remedies which give relief. Decayed teeth should receive the attention of .a skilful dentist. Thought should be given towards supplying the system with a pure, wholesome, nutritious dietary and an abundance of fresh air. Daily exercises out of doors is one of the best remedies, not only for restoring diseased nerves, but also for maintaining the health of the body. An abundance of pure, soft water taken one or two hours before meals will greatly aid in thq elimination of-toxic substance.—"ooo4 Health."

div.head: GUARDIANS AND GIRLS
div.p: GUARDIANS AND GIRLS
Undesirable Environment Of Licensed
Premises.

div.head: 3IXITER OF PRINCIPLE.
div.p: A 3IXITER OF PRINCIPLE.

No matter how great the care that may be exercised by a licensee, it is inevitable—they would be amongst the first to admit it—that the environment of a public-house should be unde- sirable for a young girl starting on life.. It is calculated to create a certain attitude. . , .

These words of the Rev. A. M. Mitchell's were spoken at Wednesday's meeting of the Warring- ton Board of Guardians, in the course of a dis- cussion arising out of a report to the effect that a girl in one of the Guardians' homes was about to be placed put in a situation on licensed premises.

div.head: WANTED TO KNOW.
div.p: WANTED TO KNOW.

Mr. Dale wanted to know whether it was not a rule -of that Board not to send any girl from their Homes into; service on licensed premises. If such a rule -existed, it ()fight not to b 3 de- parted from. -
- The Chairman said that such an .understand- ing had existed for many years.. Mr. %Dale inquired whether he would ho in order in moving that the matter be referred back.' '

The Chairman replied affirmatively, and said that he presumed Mr. Dale moved his amend- ment on a point of principle and ,without any intention of casting a reflection on the person to whom it had been arranged the girl should
pe sent. Mr. Dale concurred. EFFECT OF ENVIRONMENT.

The liev. A. Al. Mitchell said he thought it his duty to second the amendment. • It was a matter of principle. 'There were most excellent people engaged in the licensed trade, lie had known such and could mention several at that moment—people who had brought up children in most exemplary fashion—but he thought they (the Guardians) ought to hold to their tradi- tions. It was not a light matter to step .aside

from a tradition simply because. some case was put forward which claimed &lie special merit. No matter how great the care that might be exercised by a licensee, it was inevitable—they (the licensees) would be amongst the first to admit it—that thp environment of a public- house should be Undesirable for a young girl starting ok_life. It was calculated to create a certain attitude of mind which was not at all desirable. He was not suggesting for one moment that the lady in the particular case under notice was not an admirable person—he believed she was—but, as be had said before, it was a question of principle.

div.head: PRECEDENT.
div.p: A PRECEDENT.

Mr. McKinley objected to the amendment. lie said that he knew of a case in which a girl was sent by the Board to a situation on licensed premises, some years ago. She was very hap- pily placed, and married well whilst in the same situation.

The Chairman questioned the statement that the girl was sent by the Guardians to the situa- tion. He thought she went to the situation Mr. McKinley referred to from the Post found her by the Guardians.

Mr. Bent confirmed Mr. McKinley's state- ment as to a precedent, and added that be understood that, in the case under notice, the proposed situation was. on off-licensed premises —not at a public-house. Be_ supported the
amendment because he knew there- were cases where it wonld be objectionable to send a girl to licensed premises.
UNIVERSALLY ADMITTED SOUND.
The Chairman said that the Clerk though
there was a resolution passed forbidding .the

sending of girls to licensed premises, but that he was unable to place his hand on it for the timo being; If it transpired that there was such a resolution, then the minute under dis- cussion was out of order, lie was entirely in

agreement with the principle, and he thought that public bodies should be chary of departing from a principle that was admitted by every- body to be sound. The matter was referred back for re-considera- tion.

div.head: TRE MEANING OF ROGATION-
div.p: TRE MEANING OF ROGATION-
TIDE.

In the current issue of the St. 'James' (Latch- ford) .Parish Magazine, the Vicar (the Rev. 11. B. Firth) writes :-,--"The Rogation days were set apart A.D. 452 at a time of great calamity when Litanies and Processions of supplication were solemnly sung and the people exhorted to pray that God would grant peace and quiet to a distracted world. Almost fifteen hundred years have passed since then and once again the world is plunged in strife and misery. It would be well if this year special use were made of the Rogation days which should be observed like Lent, as a time of abstinence, and a great volume of prayer went up from the hearts of Christians that peace may be speedily restored and that good may come out of this terrible evil."

div.head: GALLANT DEAD.
div.p: THE GALLANT DEAD.
?resbyterian Memorial Seniee For
Fallen Heroes.

It St. John's Church on Sunday evening an impressive memorial service for men who have fallen in the present war was held. His Wor- ship the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and the Mayoress very kindly lent their support and were present at the service. The preacher was the Rev. William Reid, and the Mayor occupied a seat beside him at the communion table and read the lessons. The service opened by the congregation standing and singing the first verse of the National -Anthem, while suit- able hymns were rendered, led by the choir under the.leadership of'Mr. A. G. Lewsey, Who is also the church organist.

div.head: Time for Pocketing Scruples.
div.p: A Time for Pocketing Scruples.

Speaking from the text " Greater love hath no man than this, that he should lay down his life for•his.friend," the preacher touched upon the conscientious scruples to be: met, with in different •quarters in regard .to the war, but said that while such scruples could not be brushed aside, those who held them were reasonably expected, while under no obligation to relinquish them, to do all in their power in the direction in which, according to the views of the majority, lay the best interests of the national life. Ile also laid emphasis on the value of the sacrifice made by the soldier and sailor, which he declared lay in the fact that their men were not conscripts, but had. the power to lay down their lives; and in their act of self- sacrifice, rendered not under compulsion, but willingly, lay the efficacy, even as in the great Atonement, which constituted them the saviours of the nation. The preacher closed with an appeal to his hearers to emulate the soldiers and sailors by placing themselves under discipline, in regard to pleasure, and, as the King had done, in regard to drink.
Mayor Hopes St. John's Example Will Be Copied.

Towards the close of the service it was an- nounced that the collection was in aid of the local war fund, and Mr. Reid asked the Mayor to say a few words before, the offertory was taken. His Worship said he was pleased that-it had been decided to take the collection in connection with that service for the local war fund, which, he explained, was for meeting cases not coming within the Category of those that could be helped from the National Fund. That was the first service of the kind which he had attended, and he hoped other congregatidns would follow the example set them at St. John's. He kleew the claims that they and other churches had upon them, but he hoped that their efforts in this direction would meet with a great response. The service closed With the playing of the Dead March in "Saul," the congregation stand- ing.

div.head: INDIA'S CRIMINALS.
div.p: INDIA'S CRIMINALS.
What 'the Salvation Arin;% Is I)oing
For Them.

The criminals of India are born criminals— criminals by caste. They think there's no other prospect but a life of crime before them. When tackled on the subject they say " But it's my Kismet; my ancestors have always lieen thieves, and therefore I must be a thief also."

The above lines are quoted from an address given in the Warrington Salvation Army Hall. Academy-street, 'on Sunday afternoon, by Colonel Sowton (late Chief Secretary for. India). The subject was "India; its people and customs, and the Salvation Army's work there." Colonel Sowton has a .racy delivery and, draw- ing from the wealth of his twenty-five years' experience of India, he succeeded in giving a hall full of hearers an extremely interesting hour. The chair was ocCupied by Mr. Benjamin Farrar. During the afternoon Bandmaster Lee and his splendid band contributed materially to the enjoyment of the gathering.

div.head: Caste and Custom.
div.p: Caste and Custom.

Colonel Sowton divided his address into two parts. In the first, he dealt with the people and their customs, leaving the ,work of the.- Salva- tion Army for treatment in the second. Out of the 315,000,000 people in India, he said, only 3,000,000 were Christians. That seemed a very insignificant percentage, but the Christian religion was making more progress in propor- tion to its. numbers than any other religion in the land. The barriers, of caste and. super- stition were being gradually undermined, and there • were Millions of people in India .to-day who, while convinced that Christianity was the best religion, yet lacked the hardihood to openly proclaim themselves' adherents of that faith and join the Christian ranks. There Were in India two thousand distinctions and shades of caste. It was thought that a man of 'the lowest caste .could not become of -the highest caste--a Brahmin—without passing through a process of a thousand re-incarnations. very high caste Indian was walking along ,the street and saw a very low caste native approach- ing in the opposite direction he would call out and the low caste man would clear off into a side street while the high caste person .went by, lest the low caste Ma 11'S shadow should fall on the high caste man and pollute him. The religion of the Indian people was a religion of fear. They feared their idols, and they feared the evil spirits with which they. imagined themselves to be surrounded. Only two out of every hundred people in India could read.

div.head: Love of Religious Argument.
div.p: Love of Religious Argument.

The Salvation Army, said the Colonel, open- ing the second .portion of his address, had 2,700 stations in India. For the most part the meet- ings 'were held in the open-air, as the people, as a rule, could not be persuaded to enter a build- ing for the purvose of hearing what they had to

say. Of course, that was in the initial stage; later on, when they had agreed to drop all their idolatry and embrace ,the Christian faith, they. assembled in the various Meeting places to be taught. There was nothing an Indian liked so 'much as a religious argument—a dis- eusSion of the respective merits of the various religions. An Indian did not, as a rule, become converted alone; he waited till there were others ready to be converted, and then they all accepted the new faith together. Ten or twenty heads of famine:4 would go to see a •mission- ary and say that they wanted to become Christians. They were not called Christians at once—they ,were styled adherents; they had centuries of superstition and heathenism be- hind them, and it was not worn down in a moment. The reason the joined in bodies *as that if they joined separately' thy persecution they would have to undergo would be too much for them. The Salvation Army had three main hospitals in India and a number of branch , hospitals and dispensaries in various .parts of I the country;

div.head: Criminal Colonies.
div.p: Criminal Colonies.

Having alluded to the Naval and Military Homes and the Rescue Homes of the Army in India, Colonel Sowton went on to speak of the colonies the Army had established for the criminals of the land, and made,the statement quoted in the ,first paragraph. !The criminals of India wandered .over the country doing a great deal of harm. The 'police had done all they could in the matter. of segregating them,

but without very much success; and then they (the police) turned to the Salvation Army and asked them if they could do anything. The Army consented to see what they could do, and had met with gratifying success. A great deal of the degradation amongst these people was due to the opium habit; a traffic in opium was carried on, very much to the disgrace of the
British Government, who had forced it from the Chinese. A.t last, however, it had, been stopped. This had left a number of ..buildings on the Government's hands, and those buildings had

been havled over to the Salvation Army or use as centres of Criminal settlements. The natives who came there were taught to try to earn an honest living, and the products of their labour were sold by the Army to help to maintain the settlement. As they were accustomed to live by crime and had never done any work, it was no easy matter to help them to the new life, but
)y the exercise of patience and perseverance, he Army missionaries had been able to train hem to honesty and usefulness, and to, get ,
llem to realise how much better such a life' was
han the old one. The Colonel also addressed devotional meet- vs at the Army's Academy-street head- uarters, on Saturday and Sunday.

Mr. lorris asked whether the wall that had been mentioned at the last meeting had been repaired, in accordance with the instructions given a fortnight ago. The Superintendent said that nothing had been done.

Mr. Morris: It's a most -serious matter. If the wall fell down on some of the children, what would be our position if an inquiry were held? The Clerk promised to call the attention of the agent for the property concerned ,to the matter.

BOYS' BRIGADE.
First Warring lon Company Enrolled
Wycliffe Church.

div.head: CHAPLAIN'S COUNSEL.
div.p: CHAPLAIN'S COUNSEL.

The Christian is like a soldier because he is always ready to go to battle; always fighting —or getting rcady to fight. And none of you is so young that he has not discovered already that for everybody life is a battle against evil and wrong.

So spoke the Rev. T. T. James at the Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday morning. The occasion was one unique in local history— the enrolment of the Ist Warrington Company of the. Boys' Brigade. Of both congregation and boys there was a good assembly, although the company is not yet a complete one. The youthful recruits were officered by Mr. T. F. Wallington (captain) and Messrs. E. Jeffery and 11. Eccles (lieutenants).

A NEW OPPORTUNITY. After the officers and boys had taken the oath of allegiance to all Christian aims and principles, The Chaplain ((lie Rev. T. T. James) ad- dresscd them from 2 Timothy ii. 3: ". . . good soldier of Jesus Christ." Mr. James said he wished to speak a woad of congratulcion to them. TO the officers .he addressed his iwords of congratulation because they had entered upon an opportunity of Christian service such as they had not had before. As sfar as they Were concerned at Wycliffe this was a new movement, although it was in -itself an old one—having been in existence since 1883; and, in the past, many people had been struck by its possibilities, includin,g "-Henry Drummond. An old movement got traditions and associa- tions and memories ; and if traditions could IK, lived up to they were a good thing, but if they had to be lived down it Was a had thing. The Officers of that company had a great op- portunity of making traditions, and the corn - pan's tone, spirit and power were bound up with their work. Might God make them wise in doing the work they had been called to! •

What St. Paul Meant. The boys he would exhort to be ." good sol- diers of Jesus Christ '.'—the text was .out of the New Testament; the most wonderful book in the world; and the Bible Class was the chief thing in the Boys' Brigade. Si. Paul wrote the text, and knew what he. was talking about. Of course, there were a great ninny people talking in this world, and some of them -- were worth listening to; the .Apostle Paul was, one of those.- Re knew -what soliiier like, because he had been arrested by thew, and as a prisoner lived with them. What, then, did he, mean? He meant that the Christian life demanded discipline and vigilance and watchfulness, obedience, loyalty—and things like that, juSt as they were demanded of a soldier. And the objects of the Boys' Brigade were to promote honour, discipline, obedience and self-respect : by practising them continually they were to follow Jesus Christ. Paul also believed the Christian was like a soldier because he loved the fight. There were evils against which they would have to fight and root out of their own lives. Until they had done that they were not going to go far. There was an evil side; there was the good side: they could not learn too soon to take the side of Jesus Christ;

Manliness v. Boyishness. He thought it magnificent that those- lads right at the ,beginning had made up their minds about this Christian life of manliness. It seemed a very strange thing to talk about a boy being a Man, but they had no word " boyliness," and "boyishness" was not tho thing. It was right to begin early, because the things they learnt at the beginning were the things they were going to carry with then). into later days. Let. them "Play up, PlaY up; and Play the game !" SPECIAL MUSIC AND PARADE.
The many rousing Boys' • Brigade hymns which were sung .throughout the service Wern accompanied on the Organ by Mr. W. IL Payton. .
After the service, a fine parade was held out- side the church.
The initial costs of the company (which reaclt a considerable sum) are generously to be Paid by Mr. Ziba Armitage.

How One Affects Many. div.head: " MORE SERIOUS CASE."
div.p: " MORE SERIOUS CASE."

f "-Jae second case was that of Michael Virai.d, roller and leading contractor, of 19, Pj•nester-street. lie also was summoned for hay- g absented himself from the service of the vearson and Knowles' Company, pre- -1"s17 entered in% avolitraCt of -K6 riic
them—on Tuesday, Apia 27th. The damages claimed amounted to RS 10s. Defendant pleaded not guilty.

The (Unwashed) Face At The Window. Mr. Steel said his clients regarded this case as more serious than the previous one. Defend- ant should have started work at 6 a.m., but did not appear. At twenty minutes past six, the _ _ .

foreman of the rolling shop (Mr. Algie) went to Ward's house and found that he was not up. After considerable knocking, Ward came to the bedroom window; he had not been washed after the previous day's work. He said he would go to work immediately. He did not do so; and half an hour later Mr. Griffiths, the forge manager, went to the house. Defendant— still unwashed—came downstairs and promised to go to work at once. Mr. Griffiths then went back, but defendant never turned up. The result was that for twenty minutes the forge was completely stopped, and the iron—which was ready for working in ten separate furnaces —damaged and to a considerable extent wasted, for about an hour whilst a suitable man was being found. The extent of the damage was really more than the amount claimed—and the other workmen also sustained loss. Defendant held rather an important position. Mr. Algie corroborated.

div.head: Increased Work and Bad Steam.
div.p: Increased Work and Bad Steam.
Defendant: If I had been there that morning was the steam very "bad?" Witness: Well, it wasn't too good; that is true.
Defendant: Have I practically been doing two men's work since October?
Witness: Well, yes: about.. The Chairman: When did you get to know about the steam?

Defendant: On the Wednesday. The Chairman: It wasn't on account of the steam that you stayed away? Defendant: Well, the steam had been rather bad on the Monday. Mr. Griffiths also bore out Mr. Steel's remarks, and said that Ward has been in an unwashed condition. The damages were really £3 us. 2d-30cwt. of iron was spoilt. He acknowledged that the steam was more or less "bad," and said Ward was a good worker, although the amount of work turned out lately had not been as much as at first. " I Felt Worn Out."

Defendant: I meant to go to work right enough, but I felt worn out. He went on to ;-ay that he had done five turns the week before, "on nights." He finished at 4.30 on Saturday morning, turned out again at Saturday noon, worked all day Sunday and on Monday, and felt a bit worn out on Tuesday morning. He admitted that he should ,have gone to work when he had promised. He had been working for the firm 20 years, and that was the first ease brought against him. _

The Chairman: Why did you not turn ,up when you promised? Defendant: Mr. Griffiths told me they had a man working there, so I thought I would have a day's rest. I have been working ever since. Mr. Griffiths denied that he told defendant that a substitute had been obtained. What he did say was that one was being sought. The Chairman (to defendant) : Did you tell either Mr. Algie or Mr. Griffiths you wefe done up? Defendant: No.

div.head: Extraordinary Labour Conditions,
div.p: Extraordinary Labour Conditions,

The Chairman pointed out that it was strange as this was Ward's only excuse that he did not mention it 'to either Mr. Algie or Mr. Griffiths. "If you had only said" continued Councillor Roberts, "to either of them what YOU say now, it wotild have been a reasonable excuse to offer. You let them both go back, believing you would follow in a few minutes. The conditions to-day are not ordinary, they are extraordinary; and whilst I personally wish to give you every credit for the way in which you have, admittedly, worked, we have all got to put in a bit more than the ordinary, and the sooner we realise this' fact—and it applies to every one, man and master alike—this country will be in a safer position than it is to-day." Mr. Steel said that had defendant tendered his present excuse at the time, steps would at once have been taken to procure a man to fill the vacancy.

The Chairman said one could quite understand when that kind of excuse was put forth— although it was not proved—that the Bench did not want to appear to press a man beyond his capacity. He thought in view of the circum- stances and facts of *ie case—if the firm did not press the matter strongly—the magistrates would be disposed to treat it as a first offence. Mr. Steel said he would leave the case entirely in the hands of the Bench. His clients' one desire was to keep the men at their work. and they would be quite prepared to accept nominal damages.

div.head: Lenient View.
div.p: A Lenient View.

The Chairman accordingly announced that in all the circumstances. the Bench would take a lenient view of the offence. The case had been undoubtedly proved, and it was not so much q question, of monetary damage as the disorganisa- tion entailed for the tine being. Defendant must pay 20s. He was getting Off very, very "I am quite sure," concluded Coun- cillor Roberts, addressing defendant. "that Pearson and Knowles will meet you in the mat- ter of paying."

div.head: E-20NEST TRADESMEN.
div.p: E-20NEST TRADESMEN.

The public of Warrington may be congratuH lated upon the fact that the amount of adulteration of foodstuffs practised by the local tradespeople is practically a negligible! quantity.

So said the Deputy-Mayor (Dr. Joseph) -at Tuesday night's meeting of the Warrington Town Council. The Doctor was referring to the annual report of .the Public Analyst, which, it was reported, had been laid 'before the Health Committee. That report, he said, was of an eminently satisfactory nature and must be gratifying not only to the committee and to the Council, but also to the community at large. Last year, it might be remembered, he called attention to the question' of the adulter- ation of coffee, which had become rather a serious matter, many of the samples obtained showing signs of serious adulteration. Indeed, in one case, the adulteration was so bad that 51 per cent. of extvaneou wetter Was intro- duced.
Important From the Hearth Point of View.

This question of the adulteration of coffee was a very important one from the health point of view, because, if it were tampered with, in,s.tead of being a tonic or a nourishing beverage, Coffee might easily become an article of food that was at once depressing and dan- gerous to people in the best of health, and more particularly so to people suffering from heart disease. He felt that on the whole the shopkeepers of Warrington -were to -be con- gratulated upon having conducted their busi- nesses honourably during the past year, and he hoped that his few complimentary words might have the effect of causing them to do, if possible, even better in the future than they had done in the past.

div.head: Why Worry About Meals?
div.p: Why Worry About Meals?

Through the inefficient working of the stomach, liver, and bowels, which pre. vents the thorough digestion of food, your body, if you, are a sufferer, becomes badly nourished. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY.. MAY 8, 1915. FRUITS OF THE WAR Archdeacon Spooner Tells Of Coming Brotherhood. CAPITAL AND LABOUR.

To thc; Wiarington Parish Church on Wed- nesday morning, Archdeacon Spooner paid the archdeaconal visit for the Purpose of ;giving the charge to the clergy—of whom, in addition to church officers, there was a large attendance. The Rector (Canon Willis) conducted the prayers.

div.head: PRUSSIA'S ACCURSED SYSTEM.
div.p: PRUSSIA'S ACCURSED SYSTEM.

The Archdeacon, referring to the war, said it was evident that Austria's primary object was to crush Servia, and that of Germany to obtain possession of the colonies of France, and so to cripple her as to render her impotent and use- less as an ally of Russia. Beyond that our own country—her commerce and supremacy—had been the ultimate objective,, and the intention had clearly been to grasp such a hold on the harbours of Western Europe as would be a perpetual menace to our shores, and would endanger, if not actually wresting from us, that sea supremacy which, owing to the insular position of Great Britain, was essential to the commerce, industry and the very livelihood of our people. The Most signfficant Witness to the soundness of our momentous decision had been found in the unanimity of feeling and co-operative action at home, in the Colonies, and our great Indian dependency, and amongst the people with whom .they had been brought in contact on the frontiers of our Empire. He endorsed the recent utterance of one of Our prelates. "Peace at the moment on uncertain terms, leaving still living the bare ideals of the worst influence of Prussia, would be as un- Christian as it would be unworthy. Germany had been the blind folloiver of an accursed system foisted .upon her by an unworthy caste, and they could only show by conquest that-peace meant the possibility of the full power o,f Christ in international life.

Was it true that- for forty-three years the German people "had maintained peace," and that whenever a danger of war arose they exerted themselves to assist in removing or diminishing it, that she "had not dreamed of depriving others of light and air," and that that war "had been wantonly thrust upon her people?" Was it true that it was a war of Slav against Teuton—" Asiatic barbarism" against "German culture "; that it was a war against Protestantism, limited on the one side to Christian combatants, while on the other the assistance of non-Christian people was sought and welcomed?

From different points of view the aerman peoples had been worshippers and apostles of power; the gospel of militarism and force had been preached without intermission, taking its stand upon the old, naked, immoral doctrine that might wds right. Bernhardt had plainly stated that "in one way or another they must settle accounts with France if they were to gain elbow- room for their own world-policy." Englishmen. therefore, ought not to have been surprised at their attack on Fronce, nor at the violation of Belgian neutrality; nor had they appreciated till quite lately the ties which bound them to Belgium.

div.head: Christianity's Violated Traditions.
div.p: Christianity's Violated Traditions.

With regard to the conduct of the campaign on the part. of Germany—after fully allowing for exaggeration—there still remained an ap- palling residium of barbarity, proofs of which had been gathered from every quarter. The crime against the civilisation of the world fore- shadowed in the horrible words "France is to be crushed," was before a high tribunal. The experience of the last few weeks had taught them that neither Christian tradition possessed any sacredness, nor supreme beauty in art any charm, nor historical records any value. Should the fortunes of war bring the tide of invasion in our own land, where would be Westminster Abbey, St. Paul's, the British Museum, and the Bodelian Library or Oxford? God alone knew when this war, deliberately planned, would come to an end.

div.head: Clergy's Golden Opportunity.
div.p: Clergy's Golden Opportunity.

The issues and character: of the future they must leave in His hands. The clergy, as well as citizens generally, had an immediate duty. A golden opportunity opened out for ministerial activity. The attitude of men's minds was favourable; their hearts were softened, and in many case there was a yearning for gilidance, comfort and sympathy. Let each and all of them redeem the time.

As to some of the fruits which they might hope to reap from the war when it was over and victory—as they trusted and s hoped—had de- clared itself on the side of the Allies—the effect upon the consolidation and unity of Our Empire would be immense. There would be a quicken- ing of imperial thought, of imperial feeling, and of imperial action. A blow would have been struck—severe and wholesome—at the spirit of luxurious self-indulgence, of selfishness and separation. The poor would perceive that the rich were their friends, not their foes; the chasm between Capital and Labour .would be largely bridged over; and "from the wings of the Angel of _Death were even now dropping the dews of a new life for human brotherhood."

div.head: Even Germany to Benefit.
div.p: Even Germany to Benefit.

Our unhappy division; were being healed IT p by the blood flowing from the wounds of wta... The spirit of the speech of Mr. Redmond in the House of Commons—a splendid page in both English and Irish history—would, if translated into, or reproduced in action; inaugurate a new and happier era. The great • German people might largely benefit in the obtaining of free representation and full power as a condition of taxation in the overthrow of the oligarchy of military autocrats, and the day might not be far distant when they would rise up and bless England and her Allies for their intervention in this war, if it finally delivered them from the yoke and bondage of Prussian militarism. The war had produced acts of heroism, and they all prayed that it would warn them all in the beneficent discipline of self-denial and self- sacrifice, and would revive our own national recognition of God. "Up Against Eternity."_ . _

"Our soldiers and sailors at the Front," said the Archdeacon, in conclusion, * "are up against eternity. We all stand at a crisis in our history, nationally, ecclesiastically, per- sonally. We cannot forecast the future. We cannot foresee the Issues of this tremendous conflict, which, is fraught with destiny for the whole of God's world. It is a time for prayer, thought, action. For the moment it is our duty to strike our hardest to'break away at any cost and sacrifice the sanguinary foes of mili- tarism which aim at nothing less than sub- jugating the world. It will be our wisdom to listen humbly to that voice which pleads with us as we pass through the furnace of our tr)al to learn the lessons God would teach us, and to make a new acknowledgment of' Him. Changes in Local Clergy.
Alluding to focal matters, the - Archdeacon

said the fate Vicar of Earlestown (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) passed away at a ripe old age, his interest in his church remaining unabated to the end. They welcomed his successor, the Rev. H. C. Moor, and • wished him God-speed.
The late Vicar of GlazeburT (the Rev.,,,G. Feather) was respected and beloved, and the'dis- trict had gained by the appointment of the Rev. S. E. Dymott. The death of the Rev. G. W. Dickinson, vicar

of Padgate, had been a great shock. He liter- ally "died in harness," after a short but faith- ful service. His successor, the Rev. H. F. S. Collier, was well-known throughout the diocese as a doughty champion of the cause of the waifs and strays. God had spared to them the venerated and venerable Rector of Winwick (the Rev. Canon Penrhyn). Might his • declining
years be rendered ever increasingly happy and peaceful by the knowledge that his Lord and Master had abundantly blessed his ministry,
and that among the clergy and laity of the diocese his name was honoured, his influence felt to be a power for good, and he himself universally beloved.

He congratulated the Rector of Warrington (Canon Willis) upon his commodious and well- designed new vestry; the Rector of Winwick upon having so successfully met the demands of the Board of Education by providing ,well- planned and up-to-date additions to his schools, thus setting a splendid example to the Churches; the Rev . J. Ryder, vicar of St. Peter's, Newton; his indefatigable colleague. the Rev. B. E. Taylor, mad their lay supporters„ upon the completion, dedication and opening for divine worship of the admirably designed. well-constructed and ecclesiastically furnished Church of All Saints', round which useful or- ganisation was growing up, and which was a living centre of zealous and successful ministra- tions.

div.head: FAIRFIELD UNITED CYMYLPIONS.
div.p: FAIRFIELD UNITED CYMYLPIONS.
Longford United Take The " Starkey " Cup

div.head: AFTER AN EVEN CONTEST.
div.p: AFTER AN EVEN CONTEST.

On Saturday the football season for 1914-15 was brought to a close by two very important matches being decided in the competitions conducted by the Warrington and District League officials. One was the final tie for the " Starkey " Cup Competition, and the second the deciding match for the Championship for the League. • The weather during the week

had been- of the best, but unfortunately on the Saturday Jupiter Pluvius decided to attend, and the conditions were rather unpleasant from a spectator's point of view. nut in spite of these conditions a very good crowd assembled at the King and Queen ground to witness the final for the cup. The contesting teams were Longford United and Paddington United, both of which had had the novel experience of jap- Pearing in the final after being previously defeated in the competition, but gaining the verdict in their favour against their respective opponents on protests for playing ineligible men.

The game opened very tamely, but gradually became very keen and exciting as each team scored, the interval arriving with the score one goal each. During the second portion each side scored again, making it necessary to play extra time before definite issue could be arrived at, and it was during the first quar- ter of an hour that the Longford team gained the lead, during an attack on the Paddington goal, when the ball rebounded through the goal off Bramhall, which was indeed *very un- fortunate for the Paddingtonians, as a similar result had occurred when the Longford team secured their first point. On. the run -of the game, however, the Longford team just de- served the verdict. It was in their lhalfback line that they proved to be the 4.trongest, Smart doing a great amount of work and being' ably supported .by Fearnley and Sherratt; whilst Hughes was the most dangerous for- ward. The Paddington forwards were smarter on the ball and combined more effectively until they came near to goal; then they were over- powered by their opponents' height and weight, Taylor being their most prominent forward, whilst Marsh and Pritchard were good at half- back. Holmes was the pick of the backs and Harrison could not be blamed for the goals scored against him.

The match for the League championship, which was played at Earlestown between the Mission and Fairfield United, was a very im- portant affair for the latter, because having failed to travel the previous week, the United decided to play on thesis opponents' ground for four points, in order to make a definite issue for the championship. Both teams -were strongly represented, and no goals were scored in the first half. In the second portion the United quickly asserted themselves, and Put on two goals, after which the interest in the game deteriorated, and the United scored two more goals before the call of time, having scored three _ _ _

times from penalty kicks, and ran out winners by four goals to none, thus securing the championship over their keen rivals, the Orford White Star, by two points. The United having played a match more than the Star, head the table by four points.
The Longford team are to be congratulated on

the success they they have achieved by winning the "Starkey" Cup, as they have only had twenty players registered during the season, of which six have joined the Army, and nine are working on Government work at the present time. Two of their best players were unable to 'turn out in the final, owing to injuries received during the week. ;As the team were in the running for the League it was necessary for them to play four League games in seven days to complete their fixtures before playing in the final for the cup. On their return to their headquarters at the Unicorn Hotet,,'Winwick-Street, the players

met with a grand reception from the supporters, and at a committee meeting, held later in the evening it was decided to hold smoking con- cert at an early date to celebrate the team's success in the final for the " Starkey " Cup.

The Walton Club were unable to fulfil their fixtures on the Thursday evening with the Fair- field United team and on the Saturday with the Orford White Star team, owing to the greater portion of their members being engaged on Government work; they are working overtime at nights and they also had to work last Satur- day afternoon.
Hollins Green were treated, in rather a shabby mar.ner by the Warrington Central team last week. They travelled to town, but the Central players failed to put in an appearance.

The Offord White Star team are to be con- gratulated on the splendid fight they have made in the League. They lost their first two games at the commencement of the seasou, hut after settling on their team they have played very consistently, and have given the Fairfield United a very good race for the championship. Their half-hack line has been their strongest line, and in Gifford, Denny and Caldwell they had players who have had evperience in a higher class of the Association game than at present is attained in Warrington and district. A few weeks ago Denny and Caldwell deserted the football area and joined the Army, to take part in the sterner battle that is at present raging.
Notes by " Linesman."

citadel, when the ball was handled by one of the backs in the penalty area. The kick was taken by Millward, who placed the ball safely past Wallis and gave the United the lead. From the centre-kick the home team could not beat the visitors' half-backs and were soon on the defensive again, but the ball was sent wide of the goal. Following the goal-kick one of the home backs picked the ball up inside the penalty area. Ditchfield took the kick and registered' the second goal. After this reverse there was not much interesting play, the home forwards only passing the half-way line on two or three occasions. Further goals were scored for the visitors by Long and Bebbington from another penalty kick. Time was called with the result :—Fairfield, 4 goals; Earlestown Mission, nil.

div.head: FAIRFIELD
div.p: FAIRFIELD
EARLESTOWN MISSION v. UNITED.

On Saturday the above clubs met on the ground of the former club to decide the cham- pionship of the League, both teams being strongly represented with the following ' players:— Mission: Wallis; Winders and Eaton; Theo- bald, Eaton and Taylor; Wallis, Taylor, Roth- well, Sherlock and Plumpton. Fairfield United: Potter; Bebbington and Kelly; Gleave, Ditchfield and Payne; Long, Whitfield, Millward, Lewis and Taylor. Referee, Mr. S. C. EsSenhigh. The home team won the toss and Millward set the ball rolling against the wind. The visitors quickly advanced, only to be sent back by the home backs and a visit was paid to the visitors' lines, where Bebbington and Kelly defended well. From a free-kick the United goal was in danger, but Kelly cleared, and then another good movement was spoiled by Wallis getting offside. This relieved the visitors and from the free-kick Millward shot over the bar and a few minutes later Whitfield' sent just wide of the uprights. Following some even play in mid-field, the home for- wards again attacked, but Potter cleared just on time. The visitors' defence gradually gained the upper hand and forced the home team back, and Whitfield was tripped up when attempting to go through. The free-kick was not improved upon, and the interval was called, neither 'team having scored. - •

On resuming, the visitors-, showing much On- provement in their display, were soon testing the home defence, when Ditchfield shot over the bar. After a brief visit to the United goal .the visitors returned to the attack on the hone

div.head: " STARKEY " CUP.
div.p: " STARKEY " CUP.
FINAL TIE.
LONGFORD UNITED v. PADDINGTON UNITED.
On Saturday the above teams met on the King and Queen ground in the final tie for the above cup competition, before-a very good crowd of spectators, when the following players faced each other :

Longford United: Stui-gess ; Mason- and Holden; Fearnley, Smart and Sherratt; Finch, Eccleston, Hands, Bennett and Hughes. Paddington United: Harrison; Bramhall and Holmes; Pritchard, Marsh and Griffiths; Gar- nett, Derbyshire, Taylor, Warren and Scans- brick.

Linesmen, Messrs. Smith and Tidwell; referee, Mr. E. Aldred. The Paddington captain won the toss and played up the slope with the wind in his favour. Hands set the ball in motion, and the game opened with even exchanges in midfield. As th,e players settled down to their game the Padding- tonians were the first to attack, and Sturgess was called upon to save several easy shots. Then the Longford forwards tried to get into their opponents' half, but met a strong opposition in the opposing half-backs, Marsh driving them back. From Garnett's centre Holden made a big clearance, and Smart transferred to Hughes, who raced along the touch-line and passed to Bennett. The latter shot high over the bar. From the goal kick the Paddington forwards, by neat combination, transferred play to the opposite end, and a. clearance by Smart was returned by Marsh to Garnett, and the latter passed to Derbyshire, and hesitation by Mason and Holden allowed the former to get through I and open the score after fifteen minutes' play. After this reverse some keen play was witnessed, and both teams played strenuously, and after a visit to the Longford end their half-backs played the stronger game, and play was carried into the Paddington area, and several shots were sent wide. A corner kick was not im- proved upon. The Paddington team, respond- ing to .the calls of their supporters, made another attack on the. Longford goal, but their attack failed at the critical moment, their final shots being weak. A goal kick followed, from which Smart set his forwards going, and they made a strong raid- into their opponent,' quarters. Bramhall and Holmes cleared well, as also did Harrison from a centre by Hughes, and the latter shortly after hit the foot of the upright on the wrong side. The Longford team were now' having the best of the play, and Smart was very much in evidence. It was from , a centre of his that Holmes, in trying to clear, ! had the misfortune to put through his own goal, thus making the scores equal after twenty-five minutes' play. The players were now fairly on their mettle, and played in ding-dong fashion. Eccleiton, receiving from Finch. shOt over the bar. The Longford defence was next very hard ' Pressed, but the backs Played a strong game, and succeeded in clearing their lines, and after some even play in midfield, where both Smart and Marsh were very prominent, the Padding- ton goal was attacked, and Harrison cleared twice in quick succession. Later, offside against Hands spoiled a good opening. This gave relief to the Paddington defence, and very soon the Longford defence had their work cut out to (keep their goal intact, Sturgess making several smart clearances. Anther . visit to each end was made without success. :When the interval was called the score was one goal each. On resuming, the Paddingtonians again made the first attack, and for several minutes play was around the Longford goal, without Sturgess being called upon, Smart and his colleagues dealing successfully with the opposition, of whom Marsh and Taylor were the Most dan- gerous. By the aid of several throws-in, play was grodually worked towards the opposite end, and following individual efforts by the Long- ford forward, which were continually driven back by Pritchard and Bramhall, Longford suc- ceeded in gaining the lead, Hands shooting through at close range. This reverse caused the Paddington players to put more energy into their play, and mud] of their work was spoiled by the ball being placed in touch, but they stuck to their task in determined fashion, and were ayiarded a free kick in the Longford half. This was nicely placed to Taylor, who beat the oppesing backs, and sent the ball just inside the post, Sturgess failing to touch the sphere. The scores being equal again, .the players became rather excited, and too flinch long kicking was indulged in. Smart and Veamley on the one side, and Marsh and Pritchard on the other, played keen football in the half-back lines. The play now appeared to deteriorate somewhat, and neither side' played as if capable of gain- ing the lead, the Paddington forwards being too light and small to force the opposing defence. whilst the Longford forwards made several good 'attempt A on their left wing, but their final shots . were easily cleared. When the final whistle was blown, the score was 2 goals each.

div.head: Extra Time.
div.p: Extra Time.

"r --Extra time was decided upon, and Longford played uphill, and with renewed energy.. Both ends were quickly visited, the Paddington for- wards failing to take advantage of a good open- ing. Play was transferred to their defensive lines, and after several low shots had been re- pulsed the ball rebounded through the posts off Bramhall, the latter being in an unfortunate position. Half-time: Longford, 1 goal; Pad- dington, nil.
After changing ends play opened evenly, and
the .defence on -both_ sides were hard pressed,
several corner kicks being taken without effect. At the call of time the final score was: Long- ford, 1 goal; Paddington, nil.
CUP PRESENTATION.

At the close of the game, Mr. Brandreth, the hon. secretary of the League, in a few well- chosen words, asked Mr. Starkey to present the cup to the Longford team as winners of the final tie, which had just been decided after 125 minutes' play, the Longford team winning by 3 goals against 2 goals. Mr. Starkey had a hearty reception, and ex- pressed great pleasure in presenting the cup to the Longford team as winners. He also sym- pathised with the Paddington team in being de- feated, after a.•Fery hard game, and hoped they would be successful in their endeavours to win the cup next season. He also went on to say that now the football season was over he would like to see all the eligible .young men present offer themselves for service in the Army or Navy and help to inflict on the Germans a much heavier defeat than what had been witnessed that afternoon on' the football field.
Mr. Holden, the captain of the Longford team, accepted the cup from Mr. Starkey and made a brief and suitable reply.

div.head: WITH THE WOODS.
div.p: WITH THE WOODS.
" FINLAYSON CUP COMPETITION. First Round Fixtures Played Despite Rain.

Although Saturday afternoon was far from ideal for outdoor pastimes, rain descending more or less steadily during the major portion of the time, a large number of bowlers made their way to the local greens and, "in between the drops" as one of them expressed it, /managed to complete a number of games, those of chiefest general interest being in the first round of the " Finlayson " Cup Competition, in connection with the Warrington Works' Amateur Association. Five pairs of teams did battle, out of the twenty or more entered for the tourney, the other-pair having brought off their fixture a day or two earlier. Saturday's games produced some interesting bowling, and three close results, only two points separating winners and losers in one tourney, whilst in two others victory was only secured by the narrow margins of five and seven points.

div.head: RESULTS UP TO DATE.
div.p: THE RESULTS UP TO DATE.

Briefly stated, the results of Saturday's tourneys were as follows : Grappenhall Tannery, 166; Randall Bros.' Tannery, 159; a win for Grappenhall by 7 points.
