div.head: WAR ITEMS.
div.p: WAR ITEMS.

PRISONERS OF WAR IN GERMANY ALLOWED TO WRITE OFTENER. Writing to his sister, Mrs. A. Smith, of 11, Hopwood-street, Warrington, Private J. Harrop, of the Cheshire Regiment, who is at present a prisoner of war in the hands of the Germans, and is quartered at Sennelager, near Paderborn, Germany, says that prisoners are now allowed to write a bit oftener. "OWNED UP." William Hartley "owned up" both to the policeman who arrested him and to the Bench before whom he was brought on Wednesday morning, that he had been an absentee from the 4th Battalion of the 19th Fusiliers since Mgy 3rd.—He was arrested at 12, Melville-street, at 3.15 on Tuesday afternoon, and was ordered to be handed over to an escort upon its arrival.

FOR "TOMMY." During the month of April the scholars at the Fairfield Day School contributed the sum of .28 16s. 6d. to the Y.M.C.A. fund for providing recreation huts-for " Tommies " in training. The sum of £5 has also been collected from the teachers and ctildren of the mixed and infants' departments of the day school towards the scheme. These huts are greatly appreciated by the men, for in them not only can they obtain recreation and refreshment, but, in addition, facilities are given for writing letters to their friends at home.

WHY "TOMMY" WAS UNHAPPY. Writing to his Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Firth) at Eastertide, an old chorister at St. James' Church, Latchford, now serving at the Front. said: "I was very unhappy here, for I only came out of the trenches the night before Good Friday and couldn't find out if there was a service for us, but my thoughts were in the same place as if I had been in my usual place in the church. I don't know how long it is since I missed the Good Friday service." COMMISSION FOR CORPORAL WADSWORTH.

Corporal W. H. Wadsworth, T.A.S.C., son of Mr. T. C. Wadsworth, of Church-street, War- rington, has been gazetted a second-lieutenant in the Royal Field (County Palatine) Artillery. At the time of his enlistment Second-Lieuten- ant Wadsworth was engaged as committee clerk in the Town Clerk's office. The fact that he had obtained his commission was mentioned by the Mayor at Tuesday evening's meeting of the Town Council, the announcement being received with much satisfaction.

div.head: TWO PATRIOTIC SONS.
div.p: TWO PATRIOTIC SONS.
Warringtonian Who Paid !are From U.S.A. To
"Join Up."

Mr. W. J. Scragg, of 17, Myrtle-grove, Latch- ford, has two sons serving with the Army, one at the Front and the other undergoing his final training at a big Lancashire camp. The .son at the Front is Sapper F. Scragg (27144), and he is attached to the Ist Army Signal Section, Royal Engineers. He was amongst the first to cross to France after the declaration of war, sailing from England on August sth. When last heard of by his father, on Easter Monday, he was in good health. Mr. Scragg's other soldier son is Private Rennie Scragg, and he is at present training with the E Company of the 4th South Lancs., having "joined up" on December 7th last. He came over from Newark. 0.. -U.S.A., on Decem- ber 3rd, specially to offer his services to his country, and, as further proof of his patriotism, paid his own fare.
=WE
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1915.

div.head: LICENSEES' LOSSES.
div.p: LICENSEES' LOSSES.
How The War Has Affected The Liquor Trade. , REDUCTIONS OF FIFTY PER CENT.

In view of the loss of custom resultant from the early closing and late opening of their premises, from the increased beer duty, and from the absence at the Front of thousands of erstwhile customers, a number of War- rington publicans have appealed for reduc- tions in the assessments of their houses. The appeals were submitted at the monthly meet- ing of the Warrington Assessment Commit- tee, held at the Workhouse yesterday, when consideration of the matter was adjourned for two months, in order to give the licensees the opportunity of placing themselves in the strongest possible position to support their claims. It was suggested that they might apply, with reasonable hope of success, to the owners of the houses for reduction in rent. Thirty-one appeals were made in respect of fully-licensed houses, and four in regard to off-licence premises. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Furness, and there were also present: Messrs. G. Mather, R. Lee, W. C. Brooks, J. Billinge, E. L. Bent, A. J. Jolley, W. J. Shaw, J. Robinson, J. W. Knowles, A. Bottomley (clerk), E. Gun- son (valuer), and W. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer for Warrington). The Chairman said there was no need to go over the whole list; a representative of the whole of the appellants would state the case in general. Messrs. W. J. Shaw and W. C. Brooks elected to retire from the meeting, as their names figured on the list. It was suggested to Mr. Bent by the Chairman that it might be as well for him to withdraw also, but Mr. Bent chose to remain, unless it were the wish of the meeting that he should retire. His personal interest in the decision of the committee was only indirect.

div.head: AVERAGE REDUCTION-35 PER CENT.
div.p: AVERAGE REDUCTION-35 PER CENT.

Air. D. P. Davis stated the case for the apel- lants. He wanted, he said, to .convince the committee that it was only fair to make a re- duction and that it was possible to arrive at a round figure for the whole lot, instead of taking each case individually. Ten thousand men had gone from Warrington to the Front— and more would be going—and a large number of them were customers of his clients, speak- ing generally. Then, many hitherto customers had followed the King's lead in the matter of abstinence. There was an increase in the beer duty in November, which resulted in a reduc- tion of trade of 26 per cent., as compared with the previous twelve months. In some cases in Warrington there had been a reduction of quite 50 per cent. in the turn over. Thirty-five per cent. would be a fair figure for a reduction of assessment all round. On top of the handi- caps already mentioned there was the limita- tion of hours. By being open only from 10.30 to 10, the licensees lost a great deal of cus- tom that would otherwise be forthcoming from the men who were working On alternate night and day shifts. If the committee saw its way to make any reduction in the assessments, the licensees would be quite willing to revert to the old rates as soon as the war ended.

WHAT MR. LLOYD GEORGE PROMISED. - Mr. Mather asked whether it was' not a fact that the Chancellor of the Exchequer distinctly said that compensation would be paid to the licensees who suffered by the reduced hours. Mr. Davis: Yes! Under the Defence of the Realm Act. But that will not come into force until October.

The Chairman, before asking Air. Davis to withdraw, while the committee considered the question, said that they knew the special con- ditions prevailing must have caused the trade to suffer, and they were desirous of doing justice to all the appeals. Some discussion ensued.

The Clerk suggested that the best plan to adopt would be to postpone consideration of the whole of the appeals, so as to give the appellants the opportunity of applying to the landlords for reductions in the rents of their houses. If they were good landlords they would surely make reductions to compensate for losses sustained through the war.

div.head: RATEPAYERS' VIEWPOINT.
div.p: THE RATEPAYERS' VIEWPOINT.

Mr. Woodeoc'k put the point of view of the average ratepayer. The publicans were not the only class of people that had suffered by the war. Shopkeepers had suffered, and, indeed, the majority of the ratepayers already had sufficient burdens to bear.

Mr. Knowles proposed that consideration of the appeal be adjourned for two raonths, as that NV ould give the licensees the chance of placing themselves in a strong position, if it were pos- sible to do so.
This motion was seconded by Mr. Robert Lee, and carried.

The Chairman informed Mr. Davis, on his return to the room, of the decision of the com- mittee. and the reasons for that decision. He pointed out that, in any case, the appeals would be considered separately, as that was the only way to ensure that each was dealt with according to its merits.

div.head: ABSENTEES.
div.p: ABSENTEES.

"OUGHT TO MAKE A GOOD SOLDIER." At Wednesday's Police Court, before Mr. J. W. Hayward and other magistrate, John White, a well-built young man, admitted being an absentee from the 3rd Battalion of the Che- shire Regiment since May 4th.—The evidence showed that a police officer saw the defendant drop off the rear of a motor waggon in Sankey- street, and, upon challenging him, found that he had no pass. He said that a "pal" who had remained on the -waggon had it.—lnforming him that he would be remanded to await an escort, the Chairman told the youth that it was a pity to see him trying to run away, as, judging from his appearance, he ought to make a good soldier.

div.head: AN OFT-TOLD TALE.
div.p: AN OFT-TOLD TALE.

At the same Court, Abel Booth pleaded guilty to being an absentee from the Royal Field Artillery, and Detective-Sergeant Reddington described how he arrested the man as he was coming out of a public-house in Norfolk-lane. The man's explanation was that he had been fo on leave, and met his wife in Liverpool, nd, instead of re-joining his regiment at the p r time, came over to Warrington with her.. e now told ;the Bench that he was just in the act of making his way back to his regiment when he was arrested.—Supt. Williamson: They are nearly all doing that when we catch them.— The man was ordered to await the arrival of an escort.
"SLOPED" WITHOUT TRAIN TICKETS.

When stopped at Bank Quay Station and asked for their tickets, John Johnson and John McEwan, both of the 9th Battalion of the Rifle Brigade, stationed at Aldershot, admitted that they had travelled without any, and when a policeman was called to them he found that they were absentees to boot. They stated that they had travelled from London to Warrington, via Liverpool, and they supplemented that statement by telling the magistrates that they "lost their corporal at Sheerness," and being 'stranded there thought it best to -come home to Warrington, and, from there, get into commu- nication with their C.O.—They were remanded pending the C.O.'s instructions. DEAFENED BY THE BIG GUNS.

A grey-headed soldier stood in the dock at the Police Court on Wednesday to explain • why he had absented himself from his regiment—the Royal Field Artillery—without leave, and in order to catch what was said to him he had tg put his hand to his ear, explaining that he had been to the Front and had been deafened by the noise of the big guns. By his side in the dock stood a Comrade, charged with the same offence against military and civil law. The names of the men were given as John Hurley and Edmund Casey, and the excuse of the first-named was that he had slipped over to see his wife, who lives in Warrington, whilst the second said that he had accompanied his friend, both adding that had they not been arrested they could have been in barracks that morning and nothing would have been said to them. "Men home from the Front," one of them explained to the Bench, "are allowed out in the Nnornings, and if they are in the next morning nothing is said to them, and we should have been in." The sneaker added that he had been sixteen years in the sell- vice and had never been in a Police Court before.—The men were remanded to await in- structions from the officer commanding their &pot at Preston,

div.head: DRUBBING THE TURKS.
div.p: DRUBBING THE TURKS.
"Like Being In Hell Alive," Says An
Orfordian.
DARDANELLES DASII 'DESCRIBED.

The Vicar of Orford (the Rev. G. Vale-Owen) publishes in the current issue of his Parish Magazine a highly interesting series of, letters received from a parishioner who served on one of the battleships engaged in the recent dash on the Dardanelles.

"We have," says the writer in his first letter, "been under heavy fire for three days, and for four hours during that period we were under 'particularly heavy fire before we could silence the enemy's fire, from one of their big batteries. We have been very busy bombard- ing the most strongly fortified and dangerous place in the world. But we mean to capture or smash every fort in the Dardanelles before we give over. The other morning, while under heavy fire and still bombardipg, we had shells bursting all around us, which gave us a very anxious time of it. But we kept at it until 'they. gave up firing. During the action one of the enemy's shells-exploded ten yards from my gun. It struck the fore part of our ship and caused a lot of damage. How my gun's crew escaped' I do not know.

div.head: Hottest Time Of His Life.
div.p: The Hottest Time Of His Life.

"Thank God for guiding. us 'safely through that day's work, for it was the hottest time of my life. I shall never forget it. One piece of the shell just missed one of my gun's crew and dropped alongside of him. I picked it up and put it in my pocket for a souvenir. You can guess what a hot time we were hav- ing, for we took no notice of it, but still stuck to our guns and carried on the bombarding as if nothing had happened. The Turks and Ger- mans who are up here are not such good shots, for they only hit us once out of about 300 shots; but, so how many they fire, we will face them. We all thank our Captain and Gunnery Officer for the way they mancenvred the ship and. conducted the firing through the heavy hail of shot and shell."

Ina later letter the same writer refers to a second experience under fire. "It was like being in Hell alive—please excuse my re- mark," he says. "We were among shot and shell for six and a half hours. I am sorry to say that we had three ships sunk by mines, two British and one French. It was a pitiful sight to see the French battleship (the Bouvet) sinking, for when she struck the mine she sank in less than four minutes, and there was a great loss of life. Owing to her Sinking so quickly the crew had no chance of escape. lam ,glad to say that our life-boats were the first to the rescue, and we saved be- tween 60 and 70 of her crew. Over 500 got drowned.

div.head: On A Lucky Ship.
div.p: On A Lucky Ship.

"I must congratulate myself upon being on a lucky ship, for we were only 100 yards from the French ship when she struck the mine and sank. It made us all feel a bit sorrowful, for the time, to think of the poor fellows who were down the 'stoke-hole and engine-room, for they had no chance of escape whatever. A second sight was the poor chaps waiting to be rescued, for, ;while our life-boats were picking up the survivors, the Turks were firing shrap- nel shells at them in the water. Don't you think we are lucky? After we had been firing for six hours we were relieved by the Irre- sistible, and she had not relieved us more than an hour when she struck a mine. But I am glad to say there was not what you may say a heavy loss of life considering the number of men she Carried. There were about 200 killed by shells from the enemy's forts while she was sinking. Well, lam glad to say that everything was very satisfactory, for we smashel up three or 'four of the 'enemy's larg- est forts and some field batteries. You should have seen one of the 15-inch shells from the Queen Elizabeth dropping in the forts. One of them dropped straight inside one of the fort's magazines and blew it sky-high. The flames rose about 200 feet high in the air—just nice for toasting bread. I'll bet the Turks didn't half scatter. From district reports we learn that there were over 6,000 Turks and Germans slaughtered. So we got the best of it.

div.head: Food for Those at Home.
div.p: Food for Those at Home.

"I assure you that we are going straight through to Constantinople, never mind what comes or goes, for Britain has never yet failed to do anything she has undertaken to do; for we never let any obstacles stop our advance. There are tons of wheat and corn up here, and we intend to have it out at all costs, and then the people of England, who are ignorant of what our Navy is doing, can thank the Boy in Blue for the cheapness of food again. I see by the papers which were sent to me that it has dropped a little in price since we started blowing up the Dardanelles, and it will go cheaper still. before we finish. If we only had the forts and guns to face we would not mind so much; ,but there are mines of all descrip- tions, torpedoes and submarines -

The Z has been sunk for the third time since the war started, • according to the Ger- man Press news. It's very interesting to pick up 'news' like that by wireless, then to have a stretch along the upper deck and dis- cover that we're very much on top. That's the best of these cork ships, they always come to the top, no matter how they're pushed down by a Press not particularly noted for its veracity.

div.head: Shell Through the Front Door.
div.p: A Shell Through the Front Door.

"You will, no doubt, have read of our, so far, successful operations in the Dardanelles. I think it's safe to say that the back of the place is broken now, in spite of difficulties and the continual resistance offered. We no small undertaking, I can assure you, for even after the big forts are silenced, our ships are con- tinually harassed by hidden and movable field batteries, floating mines which come down with the current, and other difficulties, not to mention the delays through bad weather, which give the enemy time to recuperate. It was the sight of a lifetime, on our first day in the Straits, to see the forts on either side and three large villages all masses of flame and dense smoke. The villages were packed with Turkish and German soldiers firing on our landing partiee. I watched the destruc- tion of these villages through a telescope. On the sea-front was one large white house stand- ing high above the others. I saw several shells drop near it, so kept my glass on it. Presently one went through the front door, and the back of the house fell out. The enemy's losses must have been appalling that day, hut their reports only said 'one killed and three wounded.' That's how they give themselves away, because 12-inch lyddites, at very close range, usually do more than kill one man in a crowded village."

div.head: "TRUSTING AS THE MOMENTS FLY."
div.p: "TRUSTING AS THE MOMENTS FLY."
" Terrier " From St. Peter's Church Writes Home.

In the current issue of the St. Peter's Parish Magazine appears the following letter from an old Sunday school and Bible Class lad, now serving with the " Terriers " at the Front, to his parents :—" I often wonder how you all are going on. Although lam a distance away from the old home lam with you all in prayer. As the days roll on we are nearing our turn to face the foe which our dear Christian country has set herself to wipe out. I shall go out fully trusting to my Heavenly Father to guide me and protect me from all harm; but if it is His wish that we should be drawn to His fold we shall enter in fighting for a Christian and good cause. . . . They are rigging us out with bits of our kit nearly every day, trying to get us fully equipped as soon as possible. I have had a hard day of it I can tell you. I've been out twice with the horses to-day, and I have plenty to do after I come in." The letter is signed Edwin. and concludes with the quotation from the well-known hymn: Trusting as the moments fly, Trusting as the days go by.

div.head: SENT BACK "ON HIS OWN."
div.p: SENT BACK "ON HIS OWN."

"I missed my train on Monday night," was the excuse tendered to the magistrates on Wednesday morning by James Billington, when he was charged with being an absentee from the 2/4th South Lancashire Regiment.—He was arrested at his house in Bewsey-street on Tues- day, and, as a return half of a ticket to the place where his regiment is stationed was found 'on him, it was decided that a policeman should see him safely off by the 11.58 train that morn- ing.

div.head: STORIES FROM niE TRENCHES
div.p: STORIES FROM niE TRENCHES
"NOT L\ YS LUCK."
Scout " Climatised To Bullets"
Of Narrow Escapes.

Scout Joseph V. Podmore, of the 4th South Lancashire Signalling Section (whose home address is 6. Golborne-street, Warrington, and who recently had at the Front three hairbreadth escapes—as reported at the time in our columns)—writes to thank a Warrington gentle- man for a letter and parcel of tobacco, cigarettes, cake, &c. Writing under date Monday, April 26th, he says :—" We were relieved from the firing line yesterday, and the parcel came just in time— after my roughing it for six days. I am going to have a rattling good feed as soon as I have written this letter to you, and will let you know how the cakes went down. "A God-send."

"Thank you ever so much for the cigarettes also. Whilst up at the firing line I had run out of them. . . . It will be a pleasure to have a decent good smoke. . . . "Both parcels and cigarettes are a God-send out here; and every time we come out of the firing line they are eagerly sought for. We do six days in the trenches, and then come out for six days' rest. We go back again, on the first of May. . .

div.head: SEVENTEEN-INCH SHELL.
div.p: SEVENTEEN-INCH SHELL.
Territorials Make Their First Acquaintance With It.

div.head: SHRAPNEL AMONG FOOTBALLERS.
div.p: SHRAPNEL AMONG FOOTBALLERS.

A Warrington Territorial officer writing home. says : The terrible fighting Of the last week still continues to rage in this part of the line, and has drawn into its terrible maw large masses of troops behind us, and included in these is an Indian division of native troops. It appears that a series of hand-to-hand fights have engaged. To-day at 2 p.m. our troops made a further attack, in which the Indians took part, and the sights one's eyes gazed upon were horrible to behold.

- 'Without exaggeration we saw . hundreds of wounded. Those who could amble along must do so; those who could not were being conveyed in a continuous stream of amublance motors. In one batch of about 150 Indians, all appeared to be wounded in the band, and from what 1 could learn when they get to close quarters they seize the German bayonet with one hand and deliver their own bayonet thrust with the other.

Heavy Casualties. Appearances indicate total casualties far in excess of Neuve Chapelle, and the move still continues. Shells are bursting everywhere, and our billet rattles as I write, though some dis- tance away. We saw the country swarming with troops, all on the move—Cavalry with little of the panoply of parade; armoured motor- cars, motor machine-guns and a continuous stream of transport, both mechanical and horse- drawn; and, though it looked a medley of dis- order, there was a wonderful organised contrdl of it all. The Indians were interesting. Those not actually fighting could be seen preparing their native dishes in comical fashion, for although they mingle happily and fraternise with " Tommy " they still adhere to their own customs.

The beautiful clear sky has hummed all day with aeroplanes, and has been dotted with the white clouds of the bursting shells fired at the hostile aircraft. Just to the rear of our billet are two of these anti-aircraft guns mounted on motor-lorries. They boom intermittently throughout the day. We have experienced for the first time what the German heavy 17in. siege guns are like. They appear to have one operating against Ypres, and although we are some four kilos away, when they do send one of these shells we know it here. These shells are sft. long, and their passage through the air resembles an electric car running at full speed. When they burst it is like a gasworks explosion. They belch clouds of smoke and dust, and these soar up into the air. The de4sity is comparable with some of the forge chimneys. It is now 9.30 p.m. At six I had just picked up my writing block to start this, when with- out warning two 6in. shrapnel shells burst ,over this billet. Pieces came into the room in which we were. Some of our men were playing foot- ball in front, of the house, and had miraculous escapes. Happily none of them were touched. Several °their' shells broke near, and again none at our men were injured, but something like twenty cases of other regiments were treated in hospital-12 cases in the H.A.C., three of which were fatal. One civilian was killed and two badly wounded.

div.head: Civilian Population Agitated:
div.p: Civilian Population Agitated:

Since the opening Of these recent activities the civilian population has become very restive and frightened, and it is a sad sight to see whole families with their scanty belonging tramping along the roads. Whenever the Germans com- mence to bombard, the people clear out and curiously return when they cease, often to find very little of their homes remaining. We hear heartrending tales of German brutality to the civilians, and the despair of the people at the thought of the Germans over-running the country again. 'Here most civilians are refugees who fled before the advancing Germans, the original populace apparently being' either out of the country or further back in France. - -
The parcels you send come through regularly, their contents are always very acceptable.
Accounted for a German.

I am as fit as ever personally, but I have seen enough of this game, and don't care how soon it is all over. Some of the work is enjoy- able, but other is not only dangerous but dis- agreeable. I must not forget to record I can account for at least one German. I got him when he was looking through a loop-hole early one morning last week.

The garden at home is sure to be nice and green, with the spring blooms at their best. Would \I were amongst it all. Here of course everything suffers as the result of the war. Beautiful big trees will break into leaf no more; hundreds, yes, thousands, have had the barks gnawed by tethered horses and, of course, ruined.
Well, it is "good morning," and when I think it I wish I was off to catch the ten to nine.

div.head: " TOMMY'S ". TRIBUTE TO THE "TERRIERS."
div.p: " TOMMY'S ". TRIBUTE TO THE "TERRIERS."
"Doing Just As Much As Any Line
Battalion."

Writing from "Belgium," on April 25th, to Mr. M. Burke, of the Mersey Hotel, Warring- ton, Private J. Wilcock, who is on active ser- vice with the 2nd Battalion of the South Lancs. Regiment, and who was formerly employed at the Corporation electricity works, acknowledges with gratitude the receipt of a parcel of good things forwarded him by old friends using the hotel. He adds This has been a beautiful eountry, but now it is a collection of ruins. Every place one comes to has, suffered, even if it is not completely ruined. . . . I have now got used to the shells. We take very little notice unless they come very near, and then we do a run, for apart from the damage they do to you, if you happen to be close enough at hand, they make holes in the ground about as big as the backyards at home. 'lt's the bits as does the damage' to the boYs. . . . To-night we go into the trenches to relieve the 4th Battalion (the Warrington Territorials.) I am quite proud to think that I come from the same town as the 'Terriers.' They are doing just as much as any line battalion, but, I am sorry to say, they seem to have bad luck. I have met a lot of them. One night, when we were changing over, it fell to my lot to have to relieve my brother, Frank. Warrington Boys Festivate Together. _

Yesterday tom Guest and I had a- refresher ' together, and Wallace, from Forshaw's Works, was one of the little company. I only hope I meet Mr. Melia out here. . . . I hope the boys at the Mersey and myself will live to have another bowling handicap together; in fact, I would suggest that the boys who have been out should play those who have had to stay at home."

The writer adds an expression of his apprecia- tion of "The Examiner," which is sent out to him and, quaintly remarks that he has dupli- cated the advertisement for old scrap iron appearing therein, and stuck it up in one or two places "as there is plenty of that sort of com- modity out 'here !" In conclusion, he begs the recipient to excuse his handwriting, as "the top of a cap does not make the best kind of table to write at."

div.head: FAMILY PRIDE.
div.p: FAMILY PRIDE.
Hopes Brother AVill Be Out Before It
Is All Over.

Mr. M. Chambers, 10, Bowes-street, who is in the service of the Provident Clothing and Supply Co., and formerly worked as a foreman at the Pearson and Knowles' forges, has received a letter from his son, John Joseph Chambers, King's (Liverpool) Regiment, in which he says: "I am very glad to hear of Brother Michael serving his King and country. I am at present in the trenches not 200 yards away from the Germans. Hurry him up and tell him to be quick before it is all over, as it cannot last any longer than August, in my estimation. I am also proud of Liza's husband coming out, too. So you can tell Jim to get his gun ready for home defence.
"It is rather quiet round here, except for the blowing up of two mines by lyddite, in which I think we did great damage to their front line of trenches.
"I was 30 years of age yesterday, April 30th."

div.head: Sniping in the Moonlight.
div.p: Sniping in the Moonlight.

"Well, you want to know if it is 'luck' when you have narrow escapes. It is in one way, and not in another. Being a scout, I have got' climatised 'to bullets—what with going out to the trenches at night-time, &c. If it is a moonlight night a sniper. may see you and let drive; but they are chiefly stray bullets which come our way, and a good many of our chaps have been hit through stray shots. I have had one or two more narrow escapes, but have got that used to the bangs of them that I walk on and take no notice. .. . I shall be home soon. . . ."

div.head: " TERRIERS " CHEERFUL AND HAPPY.
div.p: " TERRIERS " CHEERFUL AND HAPPY.
Another " Terrier " hailing from Orford. writes to the Rev. G. Vale Owen to say:—

"Our Battalion are again taking their turn in the trenches, and it is a pleasure to see the boys going to , them all cheerful and happy and ready to pass a joke on whatever comes along. We are shortly to go back for a few weeks for another rest, and then back again to the trenches. We have had the misfortune to lose one of our officers since being here, Lieutenant Jones. He was a very decent officer indeed, and very much respected by all the men. He had the mis- fortune to get hit by a bullet in the head. We have also lost other men, both killed and wounded. But still we mustn't let that droop our spirits; it is only what we can expect out here. I could not imagine before coming out here the wanton damage that has been done to the towns and villages here in Belgium; and the further we move on the more we see— churches, houses. and all buildings are alike, nothing but walls left standing. I am writing this in the open. and from where I sit I can see two villages that are nothing but a mass of ruins, and one church, which seems to have had a lovely tower at one time, is simply and solely a mass of fallen bricks and stone."

div.head: "MAKES US SAY OUR PRAYERS."
div.p: "MAKES US SAY OUR PRAYERS."
"Terrier's" Vivid Deseriptiou Of The
Perils Of AVar.

Writing under date April 28th to an old friend (Mr. F. Gibson, of Sandy-lane, Orford), Private W. Swinton, who is serving "some- where in France" with the Machine. Gun Section of the Warrington Territorials, says:— "We have had quite a lively time in the trenches the last six days. The first night we were in we spotted a working party of the Germans, repairing their barbed-wire entangle- ments. As, perhaps, you know, we use what are called to locate the enemy. They are fired- in the air from an apparatus which resembles a pistol and when in the air they light up the place for a good half-mile round.

div.head: " Spotted " and Peppered.
div.p: " Spotted " and Peppered.

"On this particular night we were in a trench only about a hundred yards away from the enemy, and our 100k-out thought he could hear the sound of knocking. Our officer sent up one of the lights and by its aid we could see the Germans busy .at work. We opened a rapid fire on them and scattered them; in fact, they scuttled off like rabbits. How many we accounted for I could not say, for they had shifted their casualties before morn- ing Our chance with the machine gun comes when the enemy are in a . large body. Generally speaking, I have no need to use my rifle, being with the gun, but when that light showed us the beggars at work on their wire, I had to have 'a packet' at them. I got on top of the traverse and did not get down again until I had emptied my pouches of over a hundred rounds of cartridges. I can. tell you, we had quite .a 'beano.' Of course, the enemy fire 4 back, but they did not hit any of us.
The Officer's Little Joke.

"I made the officer laugh at the 'slick' way I ripped off my rounds. He asked me if I were game shooting. You would have laughed, too, if you had seen our lads the next day, for the word came down .the line that we were ex- pecting 'bother'; otherwise an attack. There- upon our lads fell to sharpening their bayon- ets, and we were soon quite ready for the foe.

. . . . . At preset we are out of the trenches for a rest, after six days in them, for we now do six in and six out. Sometimes when we are out we wish we were in, for they shell our billets every day we are out. When in the trenches we,are more in the open and stand a better chance. A Bad Time!

"Yesterday (April 27th) we had a had time, for there were at least Ave casualties that I know of. The worst of it is that when they start shelling our billets we have hardly any protection, and the shells come not only from the front, but also from both sides of us. So we have to trust to Providence. One poor chap, out of ' A ' Company, ran right into a shell and was blown to pieces. I helped the doctor to ,dress • another who was badly wounded. . . . . . We have been just on the right of the place where the big light has been going on By Jove! this war- fare makes a good many of us say our prayers; even those who have not said them since childhood. It will be a lifelong lesson to a good many."

div.head: IN "DEATH VALLEY."
div.p: IN "DEATH VALLEY."
Ambulance Man's Experiences In Shell-Sept Zone.

"I have just come back for a rest after seven days in the ' dug-outs,' " writes Private Stanley Furness, son of Mr. Cornelius Furness, of 117, Gorsey-lane, Warrington, to his sister. Private Furness is serving at the Front with the R.A.M.C., Field Ambulance Section, and his letter was penned on April 26th.

div.head: " On The _Go Day and Night."
div.p: " On The _Go Day and Night."

The " dug-outs " to which he refers, he goes on to explain, ,were just behind the firing trenches. "We were rushed up there in motors" he adds, "and we were on the go night and day all the time we were there. I have never bad such an exciting time of it before. We had some hot hours on the Marne and the Aisne, but this particular battle is the worst I have experienced. To collect the wounded we had to go along a railway line—which was being shelled night and day—up to a cutting which we christened Death Valley.' A party of us went up one morning at about three o'clock, and were waiting in the 'Valley' for the wounded to be brought in by the stretcher- bearers, when the Germans sent over two shells from their trench mortars which killed 20 and wounded sixty of the Regiment, who were waiting to relieve another regiment in the trenches.

The news reached Mr. and Mrs. T. Frank more, of of 4, Steel-street, on Saturday morning; " that their son—Rifleman Stanley Podmore, the 3rd King's Royal Rifles—had been wounden• , Sent apparently by one of his companions. the - letter conveying the tidings stated that the gallant rifleman was at the base hospital at the Front, wounded in the mouth and shoulder. -0 the end of the letter the rifleman himself wrote: "Don't worry; getting better." _

On Wednesday morning arrived from th? Rifle Record Office, Winchester, the Army notv fication of the casualty, and from it were crosseJ all three descriptions, "Dangerously, sever& and slightly." Further Ninformation is not yet to hand.

WOUNDED MAN'S CAREER. Born in Warrington 9.4 years ago, Riflenl Podmore till aged 13 years attended the Hairgl" ton-street School. For eight years then 11° served in Messrs. Rylands Bros.' barb mon, afterwards going as a box-maker at MessTl' Crosfield's.

fn September he enlisted, and had been at the Front since early in December. Formerly he. attended Cockhedge Mission. 111 also for many years played for Padgate-Uniteu Football Club, and has taken instruction, too' in boxing and fencing. - He has a brother [Percy] in the Queen's 010 Cameron Highlanders—now training in Scot' laud.

LANCE-CORPORAL J. RILEY. Writes That He Is "Doing As Well As Can Be Expected." Lance-Corporal Joseph Riley, of the 4th South Lancashires—whose home is itith his wife and three little children at 133, Willis- street—wrote on board ship, coming back to England, to say he had been wounded on the
LANCE-CORPORAL J. RILEY. Wounded.
PRIVATE J. SMITH. Wounded.

27th April in the left side. No further infor- mation was given. The first news, however, was contained in a letter received on Saturday morning by his father, Mr. Thomas Riley, of 137, Willis-street. The Lance-Corporal is now at Netley Hos- pital, whence he wrote on Wednesday morning to say he is doing as well as can be expected. Aged thirty-five, Lance-Corporal Riley, in peace times, is employed at Messrs. J. Cros- field and Sons' as a joiner. LANCE-CORPL. L 11. KNOWLES. Leg Badly Hurt By Fragment Of A Shell. One of the best-known of the Warrington Territorials, Lance-Corporal J. H. Knowles, has been wounded, but, happily, though his hurt is a severe one, it is not in a vital place. Lance- Corporal Knowles belongs to a patriotic family, for two of his firothers are also serving King and country, whilst three of his brothers-in-law are with the colours. An Old Volunteer. At the outbreak of war Lance-Corporal Knowles was acting as one of the school attend- anee officers under the Warrington Education Committee. He had served in the old Volun- teers, and, when the call for "men and still more 'nen " was so urgently put before the country, he re-joined his old battalion (the 4th South Lancashires), now become a Territorial unit. Lance-Corporal Knowles's home is at 49, Samuel-street, Warrington, and the news of his hurt first reached his wife at that address on Sunday morning, through a letter written by Lieutenant-Surgeon Chas. D. Law, who was for- merly resident-surgeon at the Warrington In- firmary, and who is now devoting his skill to the care of such of the " Terriers " as have the misfortune to be made billets for the enemy's bullets. Lieutenant-Surgeon Law's Tribute. Lieutenant-Surgeon Law's letter to Mrs., Knowles, was dated April 27th, and ran as follows: " I am sorry that I have to tell you that your husband was most unfortunately wounded this afternoon, whilst the village which we now are in was being shelled. A shell exploded close to

WOUNDED. PRIVATE JACK SMITH. Old Volunteer Who Re-joined At Out- break of War. News reached Warrington on Sunday morning that the names of several other Warringtonians had to be added to the Territorial casualty list, among them the name of Private Jack Smith. Private Smith has many friends in the town,

'and prior to volunteering for active service he made his home with his sister, Mrs. Jane Parr, at 10, Villars-street, Howley. The news that he had been wounded was conveyed on a field card j from him and receii,ed by his sister on Sunday j morning. It merely intimated that he had been hit, but gave no details as to where, how or when. Private Smith .is 35 years of age, and is a single man. He was keen on citizen-soldiering. and served for two years in the old Volunteers. When the Volunteers gave place to the Terri- torial Force exigencies of business for a time prevented him "carrying on" as he would have liked to do, but immediately war broke out he offered his services as a " Terrier " and, after he had passed the medical examination, they were accepted. One of Crosfield's Contingent. In pre-war days Private Smith was employed in the packing shed at Messrs. Crosfield's Soap Works, and he was much liked by fellow employes, many of whom have written him letters of encouragement since he "signed on." He was keenly interested in most manly sports, and also in Friendly Society work, being a mem- ber of the "Prince of Wales'" Lodge of Odd- fellows. Private Smith has two brothers serving in the Territorials. PRIVATE THOMAS PEACOCK. 1, oses A Leg In His Country's Service. News has been received by Mr. and Mrs. Peacock, of 6. Wilson-Patten-street, that their son, Private Thomas Peacock. of A Company, 4th (Territorial) Battalion, South Lancashire Regiment, was wounded on Monday, April 26th. "Took It In Very Good Part." The first intimation to hand took the form of a letter written by Lance-Corporal J. Williams, also of the Territorials. It ran as follows: " I am sorry to inform you that your son, Thomas, has been wounded by shrapnel in the ankle. He took it in very good part, and was in the best of spirits, and very cheerful. He will write and let you know his address and how he is going on at the first opportunity. Enclosed you will find his wallet, which he asked me to send to you. At the time of get- ting hit he was running for a stretcher for
PRIVATE JOSEPH HOWARD. Wounded.

Crosfield. At the time of his enlistment he was engaged in the tablet room of the works, where he was a favourite amongst his mates. He is an enthusiast—and a capable enthusiast—in the game of bowls, and has won honours, including the " Crosfield " Cup and Medal, and the "Peter Peacock" Gold Watch. PRIVATE A. HERSCHELL. Shot In The Arm Whilst Trench- Digging. While engaged in trench-digging behind the firing line, Private Alexander Herschel!, of A, Company of the Warrington Territorials was, a few days ago, wounded. Intimation of the fact was conveyed to his parents, Mr.. and Mrs. A. Herschel!, of 20, Kean-street, Warrington, in a letter written by a comrade, Private Henry Rowley. " Very Cheerful, and Asked to be Allowed to Walk." The letter ran as follows : I am sorry to inform you that my pal, your son, Alex, was wounded last night (Wednesday). We were ordered to go trench-digging behind the firing line, and had been digging for about 20 minutes when Alex was shot through the arm at the top. I am pleased to say it is not very serious, and he was very cfieerful. I helped to carry him to the dressing station, and he was talk- ing to-ine all the ,way: He even asked me to let him walk. We got him to the dressing station and got his wound dressed. Then he was taken to hospital in a motor conveyance. The Bullet as a Souvenir. - Private Herschel! now lies in the Vicarage' Hospital, Runcorn, where he has . been visited by his mother. She found him progressing favourably, and also saw the bullet, which had been taken from her son's arm. Private Herschel!, who has been VI the Terri- torials about two years, is 19 years of age, and was a Heathside School boy. He was at one time in the employment of Messrs. H. D.

Pochin and Co., Ltd., but latterly he *worked for Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd. Just previous to the outbreak of war, he was en4age,l on the extension of Messrs. Crosfield's works on the Cheshire side of the Mersey Needed at Raddop Court.
